Why the same printing. Zeno is written in Rust, so the Rust runtime shows floats with {:?}, fixed decimals with {:.2}, and text with the same quoting, exactly as zeno run does. It is the one target that cannot differ in the last digit.

24.19 WebAssembly: through Rust, with WASI

--target wasm writes the program in Rust, has rustc build it for wasm32-wasip1, and keeps the .wasm file. WASI is the system interface that WebAssembly hosts outside a browser give a program: the keyboard, the screen, the command line and files. The file runs in wasmtime, wasmer, or Node (tools/run-wasi.js). WebAssembly has no threads, so there the program runs on its one thread, built with a 32 MB stack, which holds 1000 nested calls.

Why through Rust. Rust builds WebAssembly well and has done so for years, and the Rust target already prints what zeno run prints; a WebAssembly printer of its own would be a second compiler to keep in step. This is also the one target where zeno build runs a compiler itself, because a .wasm file is not text a person would keep: what they want is the file that runs.

Why WASI and not the browser. The page target (24.10) is already the browser's. zeno build --web puts Zeno itself in a page as WebAssembly. What was missing was a program that runs anywhere a WebAssembly host does, the same file on every computer, and that is WASI.

24.20 Text in quotes: Zeno's own rule

A text shown inside a list, a dict or an object, or named in the message of an error, is in quotes. Inside them ", \, the new line, the carriage return and the tab are written as a program writes them (\", \\, \n, \r, \t). Any other control character (below a space, and U+007F to U+009F) is written as its code, \u{1b}, because it would not show on a screen. Every other character is written as it is.

Until now zeno run used Rust's {:?} for this, which escapes whatever Rust's tables of Unicode call "not printable" or "extending". That made ["தமிழ்"] print as ["தமிழ\u{bcd}"]: the last sign of the word is a combining one. The C that zeno build writes escaped five characters and nothing else, and the runtimes of the targets already followed the rule above. Three ways of running one program gave three answers. Now zeno run, the C runtime and every target quote a text the same way.

Why not Rust's rule everywhere. It needs Unicode's tables, which change with each version of Unicode, so the answer would depend on the version of Rust that built Zeno, and each runtime would need a copy of the tables. It also breaks words in Tamil, Hindi, Thai and every script that uses combining signs. strip and upper already keep to ASCII so that no table is needed (3.14); this is the same choice.

Why escape control characters at all. A list is shown to be read. An escape character or a zero-width control inside a text would change what the terminal does, or show nothing, and the reader could not tell "a" from "a\u{1b}".

Rejected. Escaping everything that is not ASCII: exact, but a program that prints a list of names in Tamil would print codes.

24.21 A float between two shortest texts takes the even one

A float is printed with the fewest digits that name it and no other float. Now and then two texts of that length are equally near: the float 1e15 + 0.25 lies exactly between 1000000000000000.2 and 1000000000000000.3. Zeno prints the one whose last digit is even.

Why. C, JavaScript, Python, Java and C# do, and so did the C that zeno build writes. zeno run printed the upper one, because Rust does, so zeno run and zeno build disagreed, and so did five of the targets. The even digit is also what the rest of Zeno does with a half: {x:.1f} rounds the exact value to even. It can only happen to a float that needs 16 or 17 digits. value::float_text puts Rust's answer right in that one case; the Rust target carries the same function.

Rejected. Teaching five runtimes to round up as Rust does: more code in more places, for the rarer habit.

24.22 A variable is read when its turn comes

Zeno works a line out from left to right, and reads a variable at the moment its turn comes. The lowering (24.3, 24.14) now keeps to that in four places where it did not:

  • f(b=two(), a=one()) runs two() first, as written. On JavaScript, Python, Java, C# and Rust it ran one() first, because the arguments had already been put in the order of the parameters.
  • x += f() reads x before f() runs, so a change f makes to x is lost, as in zeno run. Go and C++ read x after.
  • [x, bump()], x < bump() < y, f"{x} {bump()}", [x: bump()]: wherever a later part needs statements of its own (24.14), an earlier plain variable is copied first. Before, only earlier calls were copied, and a variable was read after the later part had changed it, on every target.
  • list[i] = value and object.field = value work out the list, the index and the value in that order.

Why. It is the rule of zeno run, and "it prints what zeno run prints" has no exceptions. None of the 319 programs changed a variable in the middle of a line that also read it, so none showed it.

Rejected. Copying every variable always: right, but each line of the written program would grow, and most lines change nothing midway. A variable is copied only when something after it on the line can run code.

24.23 Nesting is counted in JavaScript and Python too

24.15 had JavaScript and Python stop "where their own limit is". That is not the same program: zeno run stops at the 1000th nested call, with the name of the function and the line, and JavaScript ran more than 10,000 deep before it stopped with another message. Now both count as the other targets do: a call of a function of the program is Z.direct(f, line, ...), which counts it in, calls it, and counts it out again whether it returned or raised.

Why. A program that prints how deep it got, or that recurses 5000 deep on purpose, did something else in two of nine targets.

Cost. A call in Python is slower by about a third (fib: 2.3 s to 3.5 s), in JavaScript a little (0.12 s to 0.16 s). Correct first (24.2).

24.24 Corners of the library, pinned down

The review of the targets found places where zeno run did whatever the Rust it is built with does, and a target did what its own language does. Each now has a rule, which zeno run and all targets follow:

  • lines(). A line ends at \n. A \r just before that \n goes with it. A \r anywhere else, and one at the very end with no \n after it, stays in its line. It is written out in builtins.rs, not left to Rust's str::lines.
  • input(). The same for the line end. Bytes that are not UTF-8 become U+FFFD the way Rust, Python and browsers do it: one for each run of bytes that began a character and did not finish it, one for each byte that could not begin one.
  • range. A step past the last int ends the range. zeno run added the step without looking, which is a stop in a debug build and a wrong, endless list in a release build.
  • math.floor, math.ceil. Always an int: too big a float gives the biggest int, not-a-number gives 0, as math.round and zeno run do. Five targets gave the float back.
  • // and % of floats. -0.0 is kept where the arithmetic gives it (Python lost it).
  • JSON. The four hex digits of \u are digits (zeno run took \u+041); the second half of a pair is DC00 to DFFF; the blanks before a text that is not JSON, which the message leaves out, are JSON's four.
  • files. A path with nothing in it is "no file". A path through a file (notes.txt/x) "cannot be read".

Why list them. Each was found by a program written to look for it (tools/targets/edge-*.zeno), not by a user. They are small, but a rule that is whatever one compiler happens to do is not a rule (principle: unambiguous).

24.25 File names, and names in capitals

  • A program may have any file name. The Rust file names its own crate (#![crate_name]), so my prog.rs and 2048.rs build; the command that zeno build prints has -o, and quotes a name a shell would split.
  • go run refuses a file that ends in _test.go and does not see one that begins with _ or .. For those, the Go file gets program in its name: speed_test.zeno is written as speed_test_program.go.
  • Python looks for a module in the program's folder before its own library. A program called struct.py or re.py was taken for Python's module of that name. The runtime takes the folder off the list before it imports anything.
  • A name in capitals may be a macro of a C header (ERANGE, SIGINT, OVERFLOW). The C++ file says #undef for each such name of the program, after the runtime and before the program.
  • The words the list of 24.4 had missed (args, delegate, the sized ints of C++ and others) are in it.

Why #undef and not a longer list. The macros differ from system to system and there are hundreds; no list is complete. After the runtime nothing needs them.

24.26 The check holds the error to zeno run too

tools/targets.py (24.9) compared what was printed and whether the program stopped with an error. Now, when it stops, the message, the file and the line must be the same too. It also takes a corner program in several files (a folder with main.zeno), the words a program is started with (.args), and typed input that is not text (.stdin is bytes).

Why. "The same error" was promised (24.2) and not checked. The nesting difference of 24.23 would have been caught the first day.

24.27 TypeScript: the JavaScript, with the type any

zeno build --target ts writes the program as TypeScript. It is the program --target js writes, with a type on every variable, parameter and caught error, after src/runtime.ts, which is src/runtime.js with types. The type is any. The file passes tsc --strict, and Node (22.18 or newer) runs it as it is; tools/targets.py does both for every program.

Why any. What a Zeno value is, is found out while the program runs, by the runtime, in every target (24.2): that is how an int that overflows, a wrong unit or a missing field gives Zeno's message at Zeno's line. Go has any for this, Java Object, Rust an enum. TypeScript's types say what JavaScript would do with a value, and Zeno does not do what JavaScript does (1 + "a" is an error, an int is 64 bits). A type like number on a Zeno int would be a promise the program does not keep.

Why a typed copy of the runtime, and not // @ts-nocheck. A TypeScript project that takes the file should not have to switch its checker off for it. The copy costs little: a test (the_typed_runtime_is_the_runtime_with_types) takes the types out of runtime.ts and holds what is left to runtime.js, line by line, so the two cannot drift and what is tried for JavaScript holds for TypeScript.

Why the file is a module (it ends in export {};). In a TypeScript project every file that is not a module shares one set of names, so two built programs would both declare Z and neither would pass. A module's names are its own.

What changed in the JavaScript for it. The runtime took Node's file module with require("fs"), which a module does not have. It now asks Node for it by name (process.getBuiltinModule("fs")), which works in a script and in a module, so the .js file also runs where "type": "module" is set. It needs Node 22.3 or newer (20.16 in the 20 line); the oldest Node still kept up is 22.

Alternatives rejected. Real types worked out from the Zeno types (a second printer and a second runtime, and still wrong at the edges: a Zeno int is not a number). Running tsc in zeno build and keeping only the .js (then it is the js target).

24.28 PHP: its own ints and floats, lists in objects, use (&$x)

zeno build --target php writes a .php file that php runs (8.0 or newer), with src/runtime.php at its top. It is a port of the JavaScript runtime, and holds all 337 programs to zeno run.

  • An int is a PHP int, a float a PHP float. PHP keeps the two apart (3 and 3.0 are different values), and its int is 64 bits, so neither needs a box. PHP turns +, - and * that do not fit into a float instead of wrapping; the runtime sees that the answer is no longer an int and raises OverflowError.
  • A list and a dict are objects (ZList, ZDict) around a PHP array. A PHP array is copied when it is handed on; a Zeno list is shared, and xs.append(1) inside a function must be seen outside. PHP makes the key "1" the int 1; Zeno keeps them apart, so a str key is stored with an s before it.
  • An inner function names what it uses: function ($x) use (&$total). The & shares the variable. A PHP variable lasts for its whole function, so a shared variable declared in the body of a loop is unset where its block begins: the next round's is then a new variable, and the functions made in the round before keep theirs, as in Zeno.
  • No extension is needed. mbstring, ctype, bcmath and gmp are not in every PHP. Characters are counted and split with preg (always there) and by hand, and {x:.2f} works out the exact decimal text of the float with plain ints, a half going to the even digit as in zeno run.
  • A long chain is let go in a loop. PHP frees an object's fields from inside freeing the object, so a chain of 200,000 objects crashed it. ZInstance and ZCase hand their fields to a list that one loop empties, as the Rust runtime does.
  • PHP's settings are fixed at the start: no memory limit, floats written with all their digits, and a PHP warning stops the program as a fault of the runtime instead of being printed among the program's lines.

Alternatives rejected. Cells for shared variables, as the Python target has ($total->v everywhere, where PHP has a word for exactly this). mb_strlen and number_format (the first is not always installed, the second rounds a half up after rounding the float first, which is not what zeno run prints).

24.29 Zeno is built as one piece, so its speed does not move when code is added

Cargo.toml has codegen-units = 1 for a release build: the Rust compiler works on all of Zeno at once.

What happened. 0.5.0 added the targets, about 20,000 lines that nothing runs unless --target is given. No line of the VM changed, and bench/run.py --count showed it: within two in a hundred of 0.4.0's instructions, fewer on some programs and more on others. But timed, in four rounds on a quiet machine, zeno run --vm in the 0.5.0 build was slower than in 0.4.0's on every benchmark: fib 7 %, loop 5 %, sort 9 %, strings 1 %, trees 4 %, nbody 4 %. The built programs were not touched by it (their C is the same), nor was plain zeno run.

Why. By default the compiler cuts a program into sixteen pieces and works on each alone. Which functions land in one piece, and so which can be folded into which and what ends up beside what in the file, depends on everything else in the program. Adding code that never runs moved the VM's loop and its helpers about, and the processor's guesses and its cache did a little worse on the same instructions.

With one piece there is no cutting, so nothing unrelated decides it. The same source then runs fewer instructions than 0.4.0 (fib 2 % fewer, sort 1 %, strings 1 %) and, timed the same way, is within two in a hundred of 0.4.0 on five benchmarks (loop −2 %, sort −1 %, strings −2 %, trees −1 %, nbody −1 %) and 3 % above on fib, which is two hundredths of a second. Building Zeno takes 47 seconds where it took 36. The program is half a megabyte smaller.

The rule this is for. Partha, 2026-11-17: writing a program in other languages is a flag, and Zeno itself must stay as fast as it was. A count of instructions is not enough to show that; the check before a release that adds code is now both, the count and timed rounds against the release before.

Alternatives rejected. Moving the targets into a crate of their own (the VM's crate still changes with every other feature, so the same thing would come back). Whole-program lto on top of it (Zeno has no crates beside itself, so there is little for it to join; it took a minute to build and was not timed). Leaving it, as within the noise of this machine: it was the same direction on all six programs, four rounds running.

24.30 Lua: its own ints, a none of its own, try as a coroutine

zeno build --target lua writes a .lua file that lua runs (5.4), with src/runtime.lua at its top. The target's name is the language's, in full, as rust is: lua, ruby, dart and kotlin are short already, and rb or kt would have to be learnt.

  • An int is a Lua integer, a float a Lua float. Lua 5.4 keeps the two apart and its integer has 64 bits. Its +, - and * wrap around when the answer does not fit; the runtime looks for that (the signs of the two sides and of the answer) and raises OverflowError. That is why it is 5.4 and not LuaJIT or 5.1, where every number is a float.
  • none is Z.none, not nil. A Lua table cannot hold nil: {1, nil, 3} has a hole and no certain length. A Zeno list can hold none, and a dict can have it as a value. So none is one value the runtime makes, and nil never reaches the program.
  • A list is a table from 1, a dict a table of keys in order and a table of values. Lua's own table forgets the order keys were added in, and Zeno's dict keeps it.
  • try is a function handed to Z.try. Lua has no try; it has pcall, which calls a function and says whether it failed. A return, break or continue inside that function cannot leave what is around it, so the function gives back how it ended (1, 2, or 3 and a value) and the lines after the call do it, as in Go (24.13).
  • The body runs as a coroutine. pcall may be inside itself about 190 times and then Lua stops with "C stack overflow". A Zeno program may be 999 calls deep with a try in each (24.15). So Z.try does not call the body: it hands it to the loop in Z.start, which runs it as a coroutine of its own while the one that asked waits. However many trys are inside one another, Lua sees one pcall.
  • continue is goto. Lua has goto and no continue; the label is at the end of the loop's body.
  • Past 100 variables, a block keeps its own in a table. A Lua function may have 200 locals, and what an expression is worked out in counts toward a limit of 255. A program is one function, and a generated one can pass that.
  • Time. Lua has os.time, in whole seconds, and no sleep. If LuaSocket is there the runtime uses it. If not, time.now() is os.clock, the time the processor worked, and sleep counts it. A wait that keeps the processor busy is a poor wait; the other choices were to stop the program with a message (then a program that sleeps cannot be written in Lua at all) or to start sleep, the program of the system, for each wait (not there on Windows, and slow).

Alternatives rejected. nil for none, with a list that keeps its own length (every step that reads a list would have to know). pcall as it is, with the limit of 190 written down (a limit zeno run does not have). A repeat ... until true around a loop's body for continue (a break inside it then means continue, and the real break needs a flag).

24.31 Ruby: lambdas, loops that are blocks, and room for calls

zeno build --target ruby writes a .rb file that ruby runs (3.0 or newer, no gem), with src/runtime.rb at its top.

  • A Zeno function is a lambda, ->(r) { ... }. Ruby has three things like a function. A def does not see the variables around it, and a Zeno function does. A proc takes any number of arguments and its return leaves the method around it. A lambda takes the arguments it names and its return leaves the lambda.
  • An int is a Ruby Integer. It grows without end, so each step looks whether the answer still fits in 64 bits, as the Python runtime does.
  • for is a block: Z.each(xs, line) do |x| ... end. A block's parameter is a new variable each round, so the functions made in three rounds see three values. Ruby's own for x in xs has one x for all rounds.
  • while is Ruby's while, unless its body declares a variable an inner function uses. A variable first set inside a Ruby while belongs to what is around the loop: one for all rounds. So such a loop is written Z.loop do ... break unless cond ... end, a block, whose variables are new each round. Only such a loop, because a block costs a call each round and most loops make no function.
  • A name that begins with a capital gets z_ before it. In Ruby that is a constant: it cannot be set inside a function, and setting it twice is a warning. Total becomes z_Total. This is done in the Ruby printer and not in the shared list of names, since no other target minds.
  • # in a text is written \#. "#{x}" in Ruby fills in x.
  • The program starts itself once more. Ruby gives a program one megabyte for calls inside one another, and 999 Zeno calls, each some Ruby calls, can pass it. How much there is, is decided before Ruby starts (RUBY_THREAD_VM_STACK_SIZE), so the runtime starts the same file again asking for 64 megabytes. If that cannot be done, the program runs with what it has.

Alternatives rejected. Cells, as in Python (Ruby's blocks already do it). Every while as a block (slower for nothing). Running the program in a Thread with a bigger stack (a thread's stack size cannot be set in Ruby). Telling the reader to set the variable (the file must run by ruby hello.rb and nothing more).

24.32 Dart: Object?, one list of arguments, and the VM only

zeno build --target dart writes a .dart file that dart run runs (Dart 3 or newer), with src/runtime.dart at its top.

  • Every value is an Object?. Dart checks types before the program runs, and what a Zeno value is, is found out while it runs (24.2). Object? is Dart's any: dynamic would let a wrong call through to fail with Dart's message, and with Object? every use goes through the runtime, which gives Zeno's.
  • A function takes one list. (List<Object?> z_a) { Object? r = z_a[0]; ... }. All functions then have one type, and a call with names, defaults or a wrong count is lined up by the runtime, as in Go, Java and C#.
  • For the Dart VM only. There an int has 64 bits and wraps, and the runtime sees the overflow. Compiled to JavaScript for a page, a Dart int is a JavaScript number, and the checks would be wrong. --target html is the target for a page.
  • $ in a text is written \$. "$x" in Dart fills in x.
  • log10 is worked out as the C library does it. Dart has log and no log10, and log(x) / ln10 is one digit off for some inputs (log10(1000) gives 2.9999999999999996). The runtime does the steps of the C library's log10, so it prints what zeno run prints.
  • Printing waits. Dart's stdout.write hands the text to be written later, and a program that stops with an error could lose its last lines. The runtime writes the bytes itself and waits for them.

Alternatives rejected. dynamic (above). Real Dart types from the Zeno types (a Zeno int that overflows is still not a Dart int, and a second printer for every target is not worth what it gives).

24.33 Kotlin: the Java runtime in Kotlin, and fun, not a lambda

zeno build --target kotlin writes a .kt file. kotlinc compiles it to a .jar and java runs that. src/runtime.kt is src/runtime.java in Kotlin, for the same machine: an int is a Long, a list an ArrayList, a dict a LinkedHashMap, and sin and exp are Java's Math (24.16).

  • No cells. A Java lambda may only read the variables around it, so the Java target keeps a shared variable in a Z.Cell (24.13). A Kotlin function may change them, and a variable declared in a loop's body is new each round. The program is plain variables.
  • A Zeno function is fun(z_a: Array<Any?>): Any? { ... }. Kotlin has a shorter way, a lambda { a -> ... }. But a plain return is not allowed in a lambda, and its value is its last line. A fun with no name has return as Zeno has it.
  • A block of its own is if (true) { ... }. { ... } alone is a lambda in Kotlin, made and never called.
  • The file turns Kotlin's warnings off (@file:Suppress). A Zeno function that ends without a return gives none, so there is a return null after its last line, which Kotlin calls unreachable when that line was a return too; and a var that is set once "could be val". Both are what the rules write, as in C# (24.13).
  • The program runs in a thread with room for calls, as in Java (24.15): 999 Zeno calls, each some calls of the runtime, do not always fit in what a JVM gives its first thread.
  • The program comes first in the file, the runtime after, as in Java and C#, so the reader finds main at the top.
  • $ in a text is written \$, as in Dart.

The cost. kotlinc takes about ten seconds for any program, because the runtime, some 2,200 lines, is compiled with it each time. A jar of the runtime made once would be faster, and then the .kt file would not run by itself, which every target's file does (24.2).

Alternatives rejected. Calling the Java runtime from Kotlin (two files and a build). Kotlin for JavaScript or native (other machines, with other ints and other limits; one Kotlin is enough to say the program in Kotlin).

24.34 The words of the four languages, and a program that tries them

The list of words that get a _ (24.4, 24.25) took those of Lua (end, local, then, until, repeat, elseif), Ruby (begin, rescue, ensure, unless, redo, retry, alias, undef, defined, elsif, and _1 to _9, which in a Ruby block mean its arguments), Dart (late, required, factory, mixin, on, show, hide, part, library, external, covariant, deferred, extension, rethrow, sync, and List and identical, which the printed program itself uses) and Kotlin (fun, val, it, typealias, arrayOf, booleanArrayOf).

It is still one list for every target, so a variable end is end_ in JavaScript too, where it need not be. That keeps a program's names the same in every language it is written in (24.4), and it means the old targets are checked again with the new words: all of them still print what zeno run prints.

tools/targets/edge-names-2.zeno is the twenty-third corner program. It has a variable for each of about a hundred such words and for names that look like the runtimes' own (Z, ZRaise, z_ok, z_a, _G, self, it); variables, a class, its fields and a function with capitals; texts that say $5, ${x}, #{y}, #$z, #@w and [[x]]; functions made in the rounds of a while and of a for; break, continue and return from inside a try inside a loop; an error raised again through the trys of calls inside one another; and a function with 230 variables. The Lua coroutines, Ruby's Z.loop and the table of variables each came from a program like these failing first.

24.35 Multiply, then add, is two steps in C++ and Go too; and the check fails when a program differs

The first run of the weekly check with the four new languages (2026-11-17) showed a line that was not theirs: with the newest g++ (15.2), tools/targets/edge-ints.zeno printed in C++

1e308 % 3.0    4.9896007738368e291     where `zeno run` prints 0.0
7.0 % 0.1      -3.885780586188048e-16  where `zeno run` prints 0.0
1 % 0.1        -5.551115123125783e-17  where `zeno run` prints 0.0

Why. a % b on floats is a - b * floor(a / b). Zeno multiplies and rounds, then takes away and rounds. A processor with a fused multiply-add does both in one instruction and rounds once, and what is left is the tiny error of the product, where two steps leave 0. A C++ compiler may pick that instruction without being asked, and that g++ did. The C of zeno build has said "two steps" to its compiler since the first release (decision 12.5); runtime.cpp did not. With g++ 13 on the same kind of machine nothing showed, because that compiler was not using the instruction.

The rule. src/runtime.cpp now says it to each family of compiler (#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF for clang, #pragma GCC optimize("fp-contract=off") for g++, #pragma fp_contract(off) for Microsoft's), for the whole file, the program included. In src/runtime.go the product in % is written float64(y * q): Go may fuse too, on ARM64, and its rule is that a conversion written out rounds first. edge-ints.zeno has a line of a * b + c in a function, for every target. The other languages take two steps by their own rules (Java, Kotlin, C#, Rust, JavaScript, Dart) or run each step as an instruction of their own (Python, PHP, Lua, Ruby).

Not done. The Go runtime's own sin, cos and tan (24.16) are sums of products, and on ARM64 Go may fuse those: a last digit could differ there. It has not been seen and cannot be tried here; it is with the known limits.

The check did not fail. The step was python3 tools/targets.py | tee targets-report.txt, and without pipefail a step has the status of its last command, tee. So the run was green with a failed program in its report. The step now runs under bash with pipefail, and is red when any program differs.

Alternatives rejected. -ffp-contract=off in the command the user is told to run (the file must be right by itself, however it is compiled). A volatile in % only (a compiler that fuses there may fuse elsewhere in the file).

25. Starting another program

Partha asked (2026-11-17) for a program in Zeno that downloads a video from YouTube. examples/download.zeno is that program, and program.run is what Zeno needed for it. running-programs.md is the walkthrough.

25.1 The example starts yt-dlp, and does not fetch the video itself

download.zeno checks the address, starts yt-dlp with the right words, and says how it went.

Why. How YouTube hands out a video is not written down anywhere, and it changes every few weeks. yt-dlp is kept working by many people who follow each change; the same thing written in Zeno would work for a month. It would also need an encrypted connection, which Zeno has no library for. What the example shows instead is something nearly every real program does sooner or later: it uses a tool that is already there.

What its first lines say. That it is for videos the user has the right to keep: their own, one whose licence allows it, or one whose owner agreed. YouTube's terms of service allow no other download, and a reader of the example should not have to find that out afterwards.

Alternatives rejected. Fetching the video in Zeno (above). An http module first: the larger part of it is the encryption, and the video would still be out of reach.

25.2 program.run(name, words) starts a program, waits for it, and gives the number it ended with

import program

let ended = program.run("yt-dlp", ["--paths", folder, address])
if ended != 0 {
    print("that did not work")
}

Why a number. Every program on Linux, macOS and Windows ends with a whole number, and 0 means that all went well. A bool would throw away what the other numbers say: grep ends with 1 for "nothing found" and 2 for "could not look".

Why it waits. A line of a Zeno program is done when the next line begins. A program that went on while another ran would need a value for the one still running, and ways to ask it, wait for it and stop it. That is left for later (25.7).

Why in program. program.arguments() is the words this program was started with. program.run gives another program the words it is started with, and if that program is written in Zeno, its program.arguments() is exactly the list that was passed. The two are one idea seen from its two ends, so they are in one module, and import program is still the one line for "the programs on this computer".

Alternatives rejected. A module of its own (process, system): a module for one function, and a second name to learn beside program. run as a plain word like print: it would take a common name away from every program for something few of them do.

25.3 The words are a list, and no shell reads them

Each item of the list is one word for the other program, whatever is in it.

Why. The other way is one line of text that a shell takes apart: system("yt-dlp " + address) in C. Then a blank in a folder's name makes two words of it, and an address with & or ; in it is the end of one command and the start of another, which may be rm. That is one of the oldest ways a program is broken into, and it is there whenever the text comes from outside, as an address does. With a list there is nothing to quote and nothing to get wrong: "my videos" is one word because it is one item.

A program that wants what a shell does asks for a shell, and it shows on the line: program.run("sh", ["-c", "ls | wc -l"]).

Alternatives rejected. One str, split at blanks (then a blank inside a word needs quoting rules, which differ between Windows and the rest). Both a str and a list (two ways to write one thing, and the shorter one is the one with the hole).

25.4 The other program uses this program's keyboard and screen

What it prints appears where this program's lines appear, and what is typed while it runs goes to it. What this program printed before is on the screen first.

Why. yt-dlp redraws a line of progress as it goes, and a tool that asks a question can be answered. Nothing has to be kept in memory, however much the other program prints. It is also what happens when one program is started from another at a command line, so it is what a user expects to see.

25.5 A program that cannot be started is a FileError, and one that ends badly is not

FileError: there is no program `yt-dlp` to run
FileError: cannot run `notes.txt`

Why an error that is raised as a value. Whether the program is installed is known only when it is started, as whether a file is there is known only when it is opened (6.14). So a function that calls program.run says raises FileError or catches it, in a --strict check too.

Why FileError. A program is a file that is looked for in the folders the system keeps for programs, and what goes wrong is what goes wrong with a file: it is not there, or it may not be used. A kind of its own would be an eighth name for one function, and a program that handles both would write two except blocks that say the same.

Why a number other than 0 is not an error. The program was started and ran, which is all run promised. What its number means is the other program's business: for grep, 1 is an answer.

Stopped from outside. A program that was stopped by Ctrl-C or kill has no number of its own. run gives 128 plus the number of the signal, which is what a shell reports, so 137 for kill -9.

25.6 Only zeno run has it so far (provisional)

program.run works under zeno run, with and without --vm, and under zeno test. zeno build, in C and in LLVM, and zeno build --target refuse a program that uses it, with a message that names the line and says that zeno run can run it. That is how json is treated by zeno build (18.1). In a page it raises a FileError: a browser starts no programs.

Why provisional. In C, starting a program is fork and exec on Linux and macOS and CreateProcess on Windows, where the words have to be joined into one line by quoting rules of their own, and the list has to be read in each of the three ways memory is kept. For --target it is ten runtimes. None of it is hard, and all of it needs trying on three systems. The example that asked for run is a script, and zeno run is how a script is run.

Not provisional. A firmware build will never have it: a board has no other programs.

25.7 Left for later

  • program.run in a built program and in the targets (25.6).
  • Reading what the other program printed, and giving it text to read.
  • Going on while the other program runs; stopping it; giving up after a time.
  • The folder it starts in, and its environment variables.
  • program.exit(n): download.zeno can say in words that the download failed, and cannot yet end with a number that says so.

26. The libraries of other languages

Partha asked (2026-11-18): "Why should I leave Python?" A program in Zeno should be able to use what pip install put on the computer, and then the same for "every single language", done "without affecting the existing": whatever runs today runs the same, and the rest is there only "when we use some specific words, or import something". This chapter is the plan and its first part, Python. python.md is the walkthrough.

26.1 Three versions, in the order the languages allow

  1. Python, JavaScript (npm) and Java.
  2. The other languages with an interpreter of their own: Ruby, PHP, C#, Lua.
  3. C, Go and Rust.

Why this split. The first two groups have a runtime that can load a library by its name while it runs, so one way of working serves them all: start that runtime beside the program and talk to it (26.2). C, Go and Rust have none. A Rust crate is compiled into the program that uses it, and its generic functions do not exist until then. For those the way in is the C interface: Zeno declares the types of a function and calls a compiled library. That is a different piece of work, and it belongs to zeno build, which already writes C.

Why Python first. It is what was asked for, and its helper is the shortest. The other two of the first version use the same lines.

26.2 Python runs beside the program, as a program of its own

import python does not put Python inside Zeno and does not turn Python into Zeno. The first python.module starts the Python that is installed, and the two programs talk.

Why. Zeno is one file with nothing to install beside it. Python inside it would mean finding the Python library of each machine and loading it, which differs between Linux, macOS and Windows and between one version of Python and the next; a fault inside a library written in C would then end Zeno too. Started as a program, any Python 3 that is on the machine works, with every package it has, and a crash there is an error here.

The cost. Every field read and every call goes to another program and back, some tens of microseconds each. A loop of a million small calls is slow; a call that does real work, which is what a library is for, does not notice.

Alternatives rejected. Python inside Zeno (above). Rewriting libraries in Zeno, by hand or by a translator: most of what makes them worth having is written in C underneath. Only in --target py builds, where the program is Python anyway: zeno run could then not run the program, and running is how a program is written.

26.3 They talk over a socket of this machine, so Python keeps the screen

Zeno listens on a port that only this computer can reach, and hands Python the port and a word made up for the run. Python connects, says the word, and is listened to. Anything else that connects is hung up on.

Why not the two pipes every program has. They are Python's keyboard and screen. If the conversation used them, a print inside a library would be a line of the conversation, a progress bar would have no screen to redraw, and input() would read Zeno's questions. Each of those can be patched around, and each patch is something a library can see through. With a line of their own to talk on, Python's screen and keyboard are the user's, as they are when Python is started by hand, and as they are for a program that program.run starts (25.4).

Why JSON, one line each way. Every language of 26.1 can read and write it with what it comes with, and a line can be read by a person when something goes wrong.

26.4 python.module(name), and from there what is written is what Python does

let yt = python.module("yt_dlp")
let downloader = yt.YoutubeDL(options)
downloader.download([address])

Why a function, and not import python.yt_dlp. import a.b is a file of the program, a/b.zeno, found and checked before the program runs (7.1). A module of Python is found when Python is asked, and may not be there. A call that can raise says that; an import that can fail at run time would be a second meaning for one word.

Why nothing more than a dot and brackets. thing.name, thing(...) and thing[...] already mean a field, a call and an item. On a value of Python they mean Python's. There is no second way to write them and nothing to learn but the library.

A named argument is a keyword argument, dict(quiet=true), because that is what it is in both languages.

26.5 Numbers and text cross as themselves; everything else stays where it is

none, a bool, an int, a float and a str are the same thing in both languages and cannot be changed in place, so a copy is the value. Anything else that Python returns stays in Python, and Zeno holds the number it is kept under.

Why a list stays too. A list can be changed. If sys.path.append(folder) ran on a copy of sys.path, Python's list would not change, and nothing would say so. Bridges between languages that copied lists across have that trap, and the later ones do not copy. So append on a list of Python is Python's append, on the one list.

python.copy(value) when a list of Zeno is wanted. It says in the program that a copy is made, at the line where it is made.

What is exact. Only Python's own int, float, str, bool and None cross by value, not kinds built on them. A number of a library that is not one of these stays in Python, and builtins.float(x) makes a float of it. An int too big for Zeno's 64 bits stays as well.

26.6 What Zeno gives Python is a copy

A list or dict of Zeno that is passed arrives as a new list or dict of Python, with what is in it.

Why not the same list. For Python to hold a list of Zeno, Python would have to call into Zeno each time it reads an item, and Zeno is waiting for Python's answer at that moment. That is the same piece of work as a function of Zeno called from Python (26.11).

26.7 A Python value is not a condition, and not a number

if thing { } is refused as it is for any value that is not a bool (2.4), and so is thing + 1.

Why. Python decides for itself what counts as true: an empty list is false, a number is false when it is zero, and a class can say what it likes. Zeno has one rule, and a second rule for values that came from elsewhere would be the thing the language was made to leave out. len(thing) > 0 and thing is not none say which test is meant.

26.8 An error of Python is an error of Zeno

Python's ValueError, IndexError, KeyError, ZeroDivisionError and OverflowError, and the kinds built on them, are Zeno's kinds of the same names. OSError and its kinds are FileError. Every other is an Error. The message begins with Python's name for the error when that is not the kind's own name.

Why. A program should not have to know which language raised ValueError to catch it. And except Error catches everything already, with the name in the message for whoever reads it.

No Python, or no such module, is a FileError, like a program that is not installed (25.5): it is the same fact, something that was looked for on this computer and is not there.

26.9 The types are known when the program runs (provisional where marked)

A value from Python has the type json.parse gives (18.1). The checker lets it through, and --strict refuses it.

zeno run and zeno test have python, in both engines. zeno build in C and LLVM, --firmware and every --target refuse it. In a page it is a FileError.

Provisional: --target py. A program written out as Python could import the module directly, with no helper. It would have to behave as zeno run does at every line, which needs the same care as the rest of that target.

26.10 Which Python

python3, then python; on Windows python, python3, then py. ZENO_PYTHON names one outright. A name that may be something else (python can be Python 2, and on Windows a stand-in that only says where to get Python) is asked quietly for its version first.

Why the first on the PATH. It is the one the user's pip install installed into, and the one an active virtual environment puts first.

26.11 Nothing changes for a program that does not ask

import python itself starts nothing. Python is started by the first python.module, once. A program without the import runs the code it ran before: the new kind of value is one more case in places that already ask what kind of value they have.

The one thing that does change. python is now the name of a module that comes with Zeno, so a file of the program called python.zeno can no longer be imported under that name, and a package cannot have it. It is what happened to json and web when they were added, and it is the price of any new module. The message that lists the modules has one more name in it.

How that is held to. Every test from before passes, with that message as the only line changed in them, and before a release the speed is compared with the release before, by count and by timed rounds (24.29).

26.12 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to Python: progress callbacks, sort keys.
  • A name that is a word of Zeno (re.match). For now Python's own getattr reaches it. Whether a word may follow a dot is a question for the whole language, and it was decided once (5.19c).
  • A loop that takes items one at a time, for what never ends.
  • python in a built program, and in --target py (26.9).
  • The rest of 26.1. JavaScript is chapter 28 and Java chapter 29.

27. The registry: a package by its name

Partha asked (2026-11-18) for a central place to find packages, as crates.io is for Rust and npm for JavaScript. Until now a needs line said where a package is: a folder, or a git repository (8.3). 8.3 turned a registry down for 0.1, and said one could come later as a third kind of line with the two others left as they are. This is that. registry.md is the walkthrough.

Checked against "unambiguous and intuitive". The new line is an old line with the address left out (27.1). A version is still one exact thing, and now it cannot even move (27.2, 27.4). A name is looked up in one registry, which the program's own file names (27.13). A command that uses the network is one that was typed to do that (27.7). And publishing has one step that changes something, and it is the registry's, not the one on your machine (27.10).

27.1 needs units at "v1.2.0": a name, and a version

needs filters in "../filters"
needs units from "https://github.com/someone/zeno-units" at "v1.2.0"
needs units at "v1.2.0"

The third line names no place. The registry says which repository units is, and which commit of it is v1.2.0.

Why this spelling. It is the second line without from and its address. at means what it meant, and nothing new has to be learned: somebody who moves a package into the registry deletes an address from the lines that need it. A line with a name and nothing else is refused, with both ways to finish it.

Alternatives rejected. needs units "1.2" (the first idea, in 8.3): two texts side by side in the git line would then mean an address and a version by their order alone. needs units from registry at "v1.2.0": a word that says what the missing address already says. A separate file for registry needs: 8.2 again.

27.2 A version in the registry is the letter v and three numbers

v1.2.0. It is a tag of the package's repository, exactly as written. No number has a zero in front, so a version has one spelling.

Why the v. What stands after at is then the same text in the git line and in the registry line, and the same text as the tag that git tag made. With 1.2.0 in one line and v1.2.0 in the other, one version would have two spellings, and somebody would have to remember which line takes which.

Why three numbers and nothing else. A registry has to say which version is the newest, so versions need an order, and three numbers have one that everybody knows. main or a commit after at is still possible, in the line that names the repository: those are things a repository has, not things a registry lists.

Alternatives rejected. 1.2 standing for the newest 1.2.x: a range under another name, and 8.4 has no ranges. Any tag at all: then "the newest version" has no meaning. -rc1 and the like: left out until somebody needs one.

27.3 The registry is a git repository with one small file for each package

The packages stay in their authors' repositories. The registry holds index/<name> for each: its name, what it is for, where it is, who published it, and a line for each version with its commit.

Why. 8.3 gave four reasons against a registry: a server, accounts, uploads, and people taking names. This shape answers the first three and leaves the fourth small.

  • No server. A git repository on GitHub is free to host and is kept running by somebody else. Zeno has no library for encrypted connections (8.3), and needs none: it reads the registry with the git it already uses for every package.
  • No accounts of its own. Whoever publishes is somebody with an account where the registry is hosted (27.11).
  • No uploads. A package is fetched from where it already is. The registry never holds anybody's code, so it stays a few hundred bytes a package, and there is nothing to store, scan or pay for.
  • Names. See 27.11.

It is also something a reader can understand whole: open the repository and read a file.

Why one file for each package. Two people who publish at the same time change two files, and git joins that by itself. A version is one line added to one file, which is what a history of the registry should look like.

Why in Zeno's plain words. The file is read by the lexer that reads zeno.package and zeno.lock, so there is no second reader (8.2).

Alternatives rejected. A server that packages are uploaded to (crates.io, npm, PyPI): the usual shape, and all four of the reasons above. An index in git plus archives on a server (crates.io's own split): still the server. One big file: every change touches it.

27.4 The registry names the commit, and a published version never changes

The line for a version holds the commit the tag named on the day it was published. zeno fetch checks out that commit. It does not ask the repository what the tag names today.

Why. A tag can be moved, by mistake or on purpose. With the commit written down, moving it changes nothing for anybody: the version everybody has is the version everybody keeps getting. This is what an upload gives a registry with a server, and here it costs forty letters. Taking the same version in a second time is refused, and the message says so if the tag has moved.

If the repository no longer has the commit, the fetch stops and says that, and uses nothing.

27.5 The lock line begins as its needs line does, and with a lock nobody is asked

units at "v1.2.0" from "https://github.com/someone/zeno-units" commit "9f8e7d6..."

Why this order. A line of zeno.lock is the needs line it is for, without the needs, and then what zeno fetch found. For a line with an address that was the commit. For a line with a name it is the address and the commit, both from the registry.

Why the address is in the lock. So that a fetch with a lock does not need the registry. The lock already answers "what exactly is built?" (8.10), and where it comes from is part of the answer. A program with its lock builds next year, whatever has become of the registry.

27.6 This machine keeps one copy of the registry, where things are kept that can be fetched again

~/.cache/zeno on Linux, ~/Library/Caches/zeno on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\zeno on Windows, or the folder ZENO_CACHE names. Only the newest state is kept. It is brought up to date when a name has to be looked up, once in a run.

Why not in the program's folder, where packages/ is. zeno search is run where there is no program yet. And each program would fetch its own copy of the same list.

Why this is not 8.6 again. 8.6 turned down a file "in a folder you may not know is there" that changes what a program means. This copy changes nothing: it is a copy of what the registry says, the first line zeno fetch prints says the registry was asked, and deleting the folder only makes the next fetch get it again.

27.7 Three commands use the network, and each is typed to do that (widens 8.9)

zeno fetch, zeno search and zeno publish. run, check, build and test still read files and nothing else.

zeno search with no network shows the copy from last time, and begins by saying that this is what it shows.

27.8 about "...": one line that says what a package is for

A new line of zeno.package, at most 120 characters. A package needs it to be published, and not before.

Why. A list of names tells a searcher nothing. The line is in the package's own file, so it travels with the version: the registry shows the one of the newest version.

Alternatives rejected. Asking for it in the form: then it is in the registry and not in the package. The first line of a README: a second file with a rule about its first line.

27.9 A name in the registry is small letters, digits and _

2 to 40 of them, starting with a letter. Not a word of the language, and not a module that comes with Zeno.

Why small letters. The registry is a folder of files named after packages, and Windows and macOS take Units and units for one file. And nobody can publish a Units to be mistaken for somebody else's units. A package that is never published may still be called what any name of the language may be.

27.10 zeno publish checks, and changes nothing

It checks the package (the table in registry.md), and ends with how to ask the registry: the address of a form, for a registry on GitHub, or the line for whoever keeps one that is elsewhere.

Why it does not do the publishing itself. To add to a registry, zeno would have to hold something that proves who you are: a token in a file on your machine, a zeno login, and an encrypted connection to send it over. That is a secret to leak and Zeno's first dependency. As it is, the only thing that proves who you are is that you are signed in to GitHub in your own browser.

It also keeps the command honest. zeno publish can be run as often as you like, at any stage, to see what is still missing.

Alternatives rejected. Pushing a branch to a fork of the registry and opening a pull request: needs the fork, and GitHub's API to open the request. zeno login: above.

27.11 Zeno's own registry is asked by a form on GitHub, and the first to publish a name owns it

The form is an issue with two answers: the repository and the version. A workflow reads it and runs zeno registry accept (27.12).

  • Who is asking is the account that sent the form. GitHub says so, and it cannot be typed in.
  • They must publish their own repository: one that belongs to that account, or to an organization that shows them as a member.
  • The first to publish a name owns it. Later versions come from the same repository and the same account.

Why. This is the answer to "accounts" and to most of "people taking names" (8.3). Nobody can publish another person's repository under a name they would then own, and nobody can add a version to a package that is not theirs. What is left is somebody taking a good name for an empty package of their own. No rule stops that at the door without a person reading every request, so that is for a keeper of the registry to undo when it is reported.

Why a form and not a pull request (as Homebrew and winget do). A pull request has the asker write the registry's file, which then has to be checked line by line, by a program or a person. A form has two answers, and the registry writes its own file.

Provisional. The form takes repositories on GitHub. A package that lives elsewhere is added by a keeper by hand. And an owner is one account: handing a package on is a keeper's edit.

27.12 zeno registry accept is part of zeno

zeno registry accept <folder> <address> <version> --owner <who>

It fetches the repository at the tag, checks the package, and writes index/<name> and index.json in a clone of a registry. It commits nothing.

Why in zeno. What a package must be to be published is asked twice: by zeno publish, of a folder, and by the registry, of what the repository really holds. Both ask the same function (fits), and both read zeno.package with the one reader there is. A script in the registry's repository would be a second reader of that file, to keep in step by hand.

Why it commits nothing. Who commits, and how, belongs to whoever keeps the registry: a workflow for Zeno's own, a person with a terminal for a small one.

Why --owner is a word and not an account. What an owner is depends on where the registry is. The workflow passes the GitHub account; a company's registry can pass whatever it calls its people.

27.13 A program can name another registry, and there is one for each program

registry "https://git.example.com/zeno-packages"

Every name in the program is looked up there, in place of Zeno's own. It is the line in the program's own zeno.package that counts, as with memory.

Why. A company's packages are often not for the world. Since a registry is any git repository, one of your own costs nothing.

Why in the file, and not a setting of the machine. What needs units at "v1.2.0" means would then depend on a variable somebody set last year. In the file, whoever reads the program can see where its names come from.

Why one, and not a list to look through in order. With two registries, a name that is in both has two meanings, and which one a program gets depends on the order. That is how a package published in public under the name of a private one ends up in a company's build. One registry for a program, and a name has one meaning.

Alternatives rejected. A registry on each needs line. A list of registries. An environment variable (ZENO_CACHE is one, but it says where a copy is kept, and changes what no program means).

27.14 index.json is the same list for a browser, and the page reads it there

zeno registry accept writes index.json beside index: every package on a line of its own. zeno-lang.org/packages reads it from the registry when the page is opened.

Why. A page in a browser cannot run git. And a page that read the list when the site was built would be out of date until the site was built again, which is a step somebody has to take. This way a package is on the page a few minutes after it is published.

zeno itself does not read index.json.

27.15 Left for later

  • Taking a version out, or marking one as not to be used.
  • Handing a package to another owner, and more than one owner.
  • The form for packages that are not on GitHub.
  • A licence line, and running a package's tests before it is taken.
  • Versions before a release (v1.2.0-rc1).
  • Saying in the lock which registry a line came from.

28. The libraries of JavaScript

The second language of the first version (26.1): import node, for the library that comes with Node and for the packages of npm. node.md is the walkthrough. Everything in chapter 26 holds here unless this chapter says otherwise: Node runs beside the program (26.2), they talk over a socket (26.3), numbers and text cross and everything else stays (26.5), what Zeno gives is a copy (26.6), a value from there is not a condition (26.7), the types are known when the program runs (26.9), and nothing changes for a program that does not ask (26.11). What follows is what JavaScript made different.

28.1 The module is called node, and the values "JavaScript"

import node, node.module("fs"). A message says "a JavaScript value".

Why node. It is the program that is started, and the one whose rules decide where a package is looked for. JavaScript in a browser has no fs and no npm. import javascript would promise more than is there, and import npm would name the place the packages come from and leave out the library Node has without it.

Why the values are "JavaScript". A message about a value speaks of the language the value is written in. ZENO_NODE names the Node to use, as ZENO_PYTHON does (26.10). Only node is looked for: it has no second name.

28.2 node.global and node.new, because JavaScript has both

Python has everything in a module, builtins included, and makes an object by calling its class. JavaScript has neither: JSON, Math, Date and process are in no module, and a class has to be given to new.

node.global(name) gives what JavaScript has under that name everywhere. node.new(Class, a, b) is new Class(a, b).

Why not make Class(a, b) do new. Calling and new are two things in JavaScript, and one value can take both with different answers: Date() gives a str and new Date() a date. Guessing which was meant would be right most of the time, and wrong with nothing to say so.

Alternatives rejected. A module of pretend, node.module("global"): it reads like a package that might not be installed. A new word in the language: one module's need is not the language's.

28.3 A number that is whole is an int

JavaScript has one kind of number. One that is whole arrives as an int, and any other as a float.

Why. Nearly every whole number a library returns is a count, a size, an index or a year, and in Zeno those are ints: items[n] needs one. Had every number arrived as a float, each of them would need int(...) around it. The other way round costs less: an int goes where a float is wanted.

The cost. Math.sqrt(16.0) is 4 and prints so, where Zeno's own would print 4.0. JavaScript does not keep which was written, so there is nothing to go by.

Past what is exact. A whole number above 9007199254740991 arrives as a float: by then JavaScript's number is not exact, and an int would say that it is. An int of Zeno above that goes as a BigInt, since a number would silently round it, and a BigInt that fits 64 bits comes back as an int.

null and undefined are both none. Zeno has one nothing. A field that an object does not have is therefore none, with no error. That is JavaScript's rule and it is kept, because a library's own documentation is written to it.

28.4 Named arguments are the object of options

thing(1, key=3) is thing(1, {key: 3}).

Why. JavaScript has no named arguments, and its libraries agree on what stands in for them: one object, last. So the Zeno call reads as the same call does with Python (26.4), and a program does not have to build an object first for the common case.

Why refuse nothing. Whether a function takes options is not known before it is called. Giving named arguments to one that does not is one argument more than it reads, which JavaScript ignores.

node.global("Object")(a=1, b="x") makes such an object by itself, which is python.module("builtins").dict(a=1, b="x") for JavaScript. node.new takes no named arguments: no function that comes with Zeno takes any, and one exception would be a second rule.

28.5 A promise is waited for

A call or a field that gives a promise gives what the promise resolves to. One that is rejected is an error at that line.

Why. A Zeno program is one line after another. There is nothing it could do with a promise but wait for it, and writing that wait on every call would be a word that never changes. Because of it the whole promise side of Node works today: fs/promises, timers/promises, fetch.

The cost. A program cannot start two things and wait for both. That waits for the day a function of Zeno can be given to JavaScript (28.10).

28.6 What a method is called on

thing.name in JavaScript gives a function that no longer knows thing. The helper keeps, with each value, the object it was read from, and calls it on that. So start.getFullYear() works, and so does keeping start.getFullYear in a name and calling it later, which in JavaScript itself fails.

Why go further than JavaScript does. In Zeno a method taken from an object stays that object's: let get = box.get and then get() is box.get(). A Zeno program that reads a method and calls it later is written to that rule.

28.7 == is the same object; print is what the console shows

a == b on two values of JavaScript is a === b.

Why not compare what is in them. JavaScript has no such comparison, and each library that needs one writes its own. Inventing one here would give answers no JavaScript program gets. node.copy(a) == node.copy(b) compares what is in them, by Zeno's rule, and says so.

print(thing) shows what console.log(thing) shows, because that is what a person who uses the library has seen. A value that writes itself, a date or an error or a URL, is shown as it writes itself: str(thing) should be the text the value means.

28.8 An error of JavaScript is Error, or FileError

What JavaScript throws is an Error of Zeno, and its message begins with JavaScript's name for it (TypeError: ...). An error that the system gave, which is one with an errno and a syscall, is a FileError. No Node, and no such module, are a FileError too (26.8).

Why no ValueError or IndexError. JavaScript's RangeError and TypeError do not mean what Zeno's kinds mean: RangeError is thrown for a bad length and for a stack that is too deep. Matching names that only look alike would make except ValueError catch things it was not written for. Reading past the end of an array is not an error in JavaScript at all.

28.9 A module is looked for from the folder of the program

node.module("dayjs") looks in node_modules beside the .zeno file, then in each folder above. node.module("./helper.js") is a file beside the program. For Python the folder of the program is the first place looked in, before the installed packages, so a helper.py beside the program is python.module("helper").

Why. It is where each language looks for a program of its own, and it is where Zeno's own import looks (7.1). A program then finds its modules wherever it is run from. Looking from the folder Zeno was started in, which is what a helper started with -e or -c does by itself, would make zeno run project/main.zeno fail for a program that runs when started inside project.

This changed Python as chapter 26 first had it. It was in no release.

28.10 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to JavaScript. More of JavaScript needs it than of Python: map, on("data", f), a server.
  • Node ends when the program does. A server or a timer started there does not keep the program alive.
  • Starting two things and waiting for both (28.5).
  • node in a built program, and in --target js, as 26.9 has it for Python.

29. The libraries of Java

The third language of the first version (26.1): import java, for the classes that come with Java and for libraries that are jars. java.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for JavaScript (28): Java runs beside the program, they talk over a socket, numbers and text cross and everything else stays, what Zeno gives is a copy, a value from there is not a condition, the types are known when the program runs, and nothing changes for a program that does not ask. What follows is what Java made different.

29.1 java.type(name) gives a class, by its whole name

let ArrayList = java.type("java.util.ArrayList")

Why type and not class. class is a word of Zeno and cannot follow a dot (5.19c). type is also what the bridges from JavaScript to Java call it (Java.type in Nashorn and GraalVM), so it is the word a person who has done this before looks for.

Why the whole name. Java's own short names come from an import at the top of each file, which this program does not have. One rule, the name the documentation gives, is less to know than a list of packages that are looked in without being asked.

29.2 Calling a class is new

ArrayList() is new ArrayList().

Why here and not for JavaScript (28.2). In JavaScript a class can also be called without new, with another answer, so the two had to be told apart. A class of Java cannot be called at all, so the call has one meaning. It is also how an object is made in Zeno itself, and in Python.

29.3 A dot after a class is what is static; a method is kept until it is called

Math.PI, Math.max(3, 9), Thread.State.NEW. On an object, thing.name is its public field, or its method.

What java.type gives is not Java's Class object. That object has methods of its own (getName, getMethods), and Math.max would have to be looked for among them. So the helper has a value of its own for "the class as its name is written" (Type), and gives Java the Class object when a method asks for one. thing.getClass() still gives Java's.

A method not yet called is a value too (Bound), because Zeno reads names.add before it calls it, and because a method can be kept in a name and called later, as in Zeno.

Only what is public. A program of Java outside the class could use nothing else, and a library's private parts are not its promise.

29.4 Of several methods with one name, the arguments choose

Java can have valueOf(int), valueOf(double) and valueOf(Object) side by side. Each is given a number for how well the arguments of this call fit what it takes, and the lowest is called.

The order is Java's own as far as it has one: an int of Zeno is an int before a long, a long before a double, and a plain type before its boxed one; a method that takes its arguments one by one comes before one that gathers them (Object...).

Two that fit equally are an error, which lists what there is, and so is none that fits. A guess would call something, and the program would go on with the wrong answer.

Alternatives rejected. Saying the types in the call, as thing.method["int", "Object"](1, x): it is exact, and it is a second language to learn for the few calls that need it. It can be added for those if they turn up. Taking the first method that fits: which is first is not something Java promises.

29.5 An int that goes as an Object is an Integer if it fits

A collection of Java takes anything (Object), so the method does not say which whole number it wants. An int of Zeno goes as an Integer when it fits 32 bits and as a Long when it does not.

Why. It is what the number is when written in a Java program: 5 is an int there and 5000000000L a long. A library compares what it is given with numbers of its own, and Integer 5 does not equal Long 5 in Java. Always Long would be simpler to say and would fail quietly inside contains and get.

Every whole number that comes back is an int, whatever its size in Java, and float and double are a float. A float is written the short way it prints, 0.1, and not with the digits it gains as a double.

29.6 == is equals

Why not the same object, as for JavaScript (28.7). Java has both, and its own == on objects is the one programs are told not to use for values: two Strings or two Integers with one value can be two objects. equals is what a class of Java says its equality is.

print shows toString(). An array has none worth reading ([I@1b6d3586), so its items are shown.

29.7 An exception of Java is an error of Zeno

IndexOutOfBoundsException is IndexError, IllegalArgumentException is ValueError, IOException is FileError, each with the kinds built on it, and every other is Error. The message begins with Java's name for it.

Why these and no more. Each of the three means in Java what the kind means in Zeno, by Java's own description of it. That is not so for ArithmeticException, which is both a division by zero and an overflow, two kinds in Zeno; it stays an Error (28.8 has the same reasoning for JavaScript).

29.8 A library is a jar, and the program says where it is

java.jar("lib/gson.jar"), or a folder: every jar in it.

Why the program says it. Python and Node each have one place where install puts packages, and each finds them there by itself. Java has none: a jar is found only if the class path names it. So the program names it, at a line that can be read, with a path from its own folder (28.9).

CLASSPATH is read as Java reads it, and with none the folder of the program is looked in for classes, which is what java Main does in that folder.

Alternatives rejected. Every jar beside the program, without being asked: which jars are used would depend on what happens to lie in the folder. A name as Maven writes it (com.google.code.gson:gson:2.11.0), found in Maven's own folder: a library there usually needs others, and which ones is worked out by Maven from files Zeno would have to read as Maven does. A folder filled by Maven or by hand, and named, is whole.

29.9 The helper is compiled once, and kept

Java runs classes and not source. The helper's source is in the zeno file; the first run makes classes of it with javac, in the folder this machine has for what can be made again (the registry's, 27), and later runs start those.

Why. Compiling takes about a second and starting takes a fifth of one. Paying the second on every run would make a short program slow for good.

How it stays right. The folder is named by a number worked out from the source, so another version of Zeno makes its own. The classes are made in a folder of the run's own and given their name when whole, so two runs at once never share half of them. They are compiled for Java 11, so a later Java runs them as they are.

With no javac, Java is given the source, which Java 11 and later compile as they start. With no folder to keep them in, they are made in a folder of this run's own and taken away after.

Alternative rejected. The classes inside the zeno file, ready made: building Zeno would then need Java, and Zeno is built with Rust and nothing else.

29.10 A name in brackets, where a word of Zeno is in the way

System.in does not parse (5.19c). On a class, and on an object that has no items of its own, thing["name"] is thing.name: System["in"].

Why this is safe to mean two things. It is taken so only where [ ] has no other meaning: a class has no items, and neither has an object that is not an array, a list, a map or text. For JavaScript the same writing is the language's own rule (node.md).

29.11 The bridge is kept out of the functions every program runs

Every function of bridge.rs that the rest of Zeno calls is marked #[cold] and #[inline(never)], and so is what letting go of a value from another language calls.

What happened. With Java added, a sort on zeno run --vm took a tenth longer than in 0.5.1 (3.63 s to 4.02 s for a million numbers, best of 8 rounds each), while the count of instructions was 1 % lower. No line of the VM had changed. The places that hand a value to the bridge are ops::item, ops::set_item, ops::field and value::equal, which every program runs through, and the compiler had folded the bridge into them. So their code changed, and moved, each time the bridge did: ops::item was 2170 bytes with JavaScript added and 2129 with Java. It is 1800 with the bridge kept out, and does not change when the bridge does.

Why this is the fix and not a patch. 26.11 promises that a program which asks for no other language runs the code it ran before. The source said so already; the compiled program did not. #[cold] tells the compiler that these calls are rare, which they are in every program without the import and cheap beside the trip to another program in one with it.

After it. The same sort is within 2 % of 0.5.1. All six benchmarks, both engines, timed in alternating rounds against 0.5.1, are between 6 % faster and 4 % slower. The 4 % is nbody on the VM (16.51 s to 17.08 s); about half of it was there before the bridge was begun, and the rest is no more than this machine gives for one build timed twice (24.29).

What it does not fix. Where the compiler puts the VM's own loop still moves by a few bytes when code is added anywhere, and that alone is worth a few percent on one benchmark or another. Stable Rust has no way to pin it.

29.12 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to Java: lambdas, Comparator, Runnable.
  • A class of Zeno that extends a class of Java.
  • Saying the types of a call where two methods fit equally (29.4).
  • Zeno's checker reading Java's types, which Java has.
  • java in a built program, and in --target java, as 26.9 has it for Python.

30. The least C: zeno build --minimal

Partha asked (2026-11-18) for one more way to build: one that goes past the checks and writes only the C the program itself needs, so that the file is small and easy to read, with everything that is there now kept as it is. zeno build writes about 3,000 lines of C for a program of one line, because the whole runtime is pasted in front of it and every operation goes through a function that checks it.

30.1 A new option, and the builds that were there do not change

zeno build --minimal writes the least C that runs the program. Six things are done, each with its own section below: no check of any kind (30.2), no place in the source carried along (30.4), only the parts of the runtime the program uses (30.5), print as C's printf (30.6), each statement written the short way (30.7), and the C compiler asked for a small program (30.8). docs/minimal.md is the walkthrough.

Why a new option. He asked for what is there to stay. The C that every other build writes is, byte for byte, what it was before this chapter: 2,028 C files were compared, the 363 programs of the check (30.10) built nine ways, with the compiler before and after.

Why the word minimal. It is his word for it ("the minimum code"), and it says what the option is for, which is how --fast was named (23.1). --small promises a small program, and it is the C that gets small (30.11). --unchecked names one of the six things. --bare and --direct say less than minimal does to someone who has not read this.

Why not --target c. --target writes the program in another language with the rules of Zeno carried along in a runtime (24.2), checks and all. This is the opposite promise, and it is the same C backend as zeno build, so it is an option of that.

30.2 No check of any kind: a mistake does what the C does

other builds --minimal
xs[i] with i out of range IndexError reads or writes whatever memory is there
ages["Eve"] with no such key KeyError reads an item that is not there
overflow of + - *, of -n, abs(n), **, sum OverflowError no defined result
n // 0, n % 0 ZeroDivisionError what the processor does: on a computer the system stops the program
x / 0.0 ZeroDivisionError infinity, or NaN
math.sqrt(-1.0), math.log(0.0), math.asin(2.0) ValueError NaN or infinity
u8(300) ValueError 300 goes on as it is
n << 70, n << -1 ValueError no defined result
xs.pop(), min(xs) of an empty list, a slice from past the end an error no defined result
int(x) of infinity or NaN ValueError the biggest int, the smallest, or 0
a variable that became none again after it was checked an error used as if it held a value
free(p) twice stops, and says so no defined result

Why further than --fast. --fast is about time. It leaves out the checks that cost something in a tight loop and keeps the rest: a key that is not there, a whole number divided by zero. --minimal is about what is in the file. A check brings its message, the message is put together from pieces of text, and text needs memory: one check left in keeps zeno_fail, the error value, zeno_join, zeno_str_int and an allocator in a program that adds two numbers. It is all of them or the file is not small.

Why a whole number divided by zero is not caught here, when --fast catches it (23.1). There the reason was that the check is nearly free beside a division. Here the cost is not time. The table says plainly what happens, and it is what a C programmer expects of /.

What is not a check, and stays. -7 % 3 is 2 in Zeno and -1 in C, and -7 // 2 is -4 and not -3. A correct program relies on that, so % and // are still the runtime's zeno_mod and zeno_floordiv, each a few lines with the check taken out. x // 8 and x % 8 are still a shift and a mask (23.5).

30.3 The errors a correct program can meet stay

int("ten") raises ValueError, a file that is not there raises FileError, raise raises, try and except catch, and an error that nothing catches stops the program and says what it was. Running out of memory still stops the program and says so.

Why. These are not mistakes in the program. What a person types and whether a file is there are known only when the program runs, and the program was written to deal with them. A minimal build of a correct program must do what the checked build does (30.10), and it could not if these went.

30.4 No place in the source

A runtime function that can stop the program takes the line and the column it was called from as its last two arguments, for the message. In a minimal build no function has those two parameters and no call passes them, and the table of file names is gone. An error nothing caught prints its kind and its message:

error: uncaught ValueError: cannot turn "ten" into an int
