Why. Two numbers at every call are code at every call, and they are the first thing that makes the C look unlike C a person writes. With the checks gone, the only reader left for them was an error the program raised itself.

What it costs. That message does not say where. The checked build does: build that way to find it.

How it is done. The emitter writes a mark in place of line, col (a byte no C has in it), and the mark goes with the comma before it when the file is put together. In the runtime the parameters and arguments are taken out by name, token by token (without_positions in src/minimal.rs); the test that compiles the whole runtime for each kind of build holds that to being C.

30.5 Only what the program uses

The runtime and the program are cut into items (a function, a type, a variable, a #define, an #include), each asked for by its name. Starting from the statements at the top of the program, every item that is named is kept, and every item those name, until nothing new is named. The rest is not written. A header is kept when one of the names it brings is used. Comments between items are dropped, since they explain the runtime across all its builds; comments inside a function stay with it. A function is declared ahead only if something written before it names it.

Why not leave it to the C compiler. It already does this for the machine code: an unused static function is not in the program of any build, which is why the program shrinks much less than the C (30.11). What was asked for is the file: C that can be read, reviewed, and carried to another project.

Why the program's own unused functions go too. One rule, "what the program uses". Every function Zeno writes is static, so nothing outside the file could have called it.

Why by name, and not with a C parser. The runtime is ours and is written one way. Three things hold the cutting to its word: a unit test gives the whole minimal runtime of each kind of build to the C compiler; tools/minimal.py reads the C of every build it makes with the compiler's warnings on, and a function or variable left in unused, or used and not declared, is a failure; and the programs then have to run right.

The marks. What a minimal build leaves out of the runtime is between #ifndef ZENO_MINIMAL and #endif /* ZENO_MINIMAL */, with what stands in its place after #else /* ZENO_MINIMAL */. They are decided when the C is written, as the marks of ZENO_FIRMWARE are, so no built program has them in it, and every other build gets the text between them unchanged.

30.6 print is printf

print(f"{n} is prime")
print("total", total, "of", len(xs))
printf("%lld is prime\n", (long long)z_n);
printf("total %lld of %lld\n", (long long)z_total, (long long)z_xs->len);

Words written in the program go into the format. A whole number is %lld, text and a bool are %s, and print of words alone is puts. {n:5}, {n:<5}, {n:05} and {x:8.2f} are printf's own. A float is %s of zeno_float_text(x, (char[64]){0}), which writes it into bytes of the statement's own, because printf has no format for "the fewest digits that read back as the same float". {n:x} and {reg:08b} are written the same way by zeno_radix_text, and a quantity is %s ms. What printf would print differently is left to the runtime, and shown with %s: text lined up to a width (Zeno counts characters, printf bytes), ^, a float filled with zeros (printf does not fill inf), and a list, a dict or an object.

Why. print in every other build turns each value into text first, and text takes memory, so print(n) brought an allocator into a program that otherwise has none. With printf, a program of numbers has no runtime in it: examples/primes.zeno is 100 lines of C, and hello is one puts.

What it costs, measured. printf is a large function. On Linux a program whose print never ran it before has about 250 KB more of the C library in memory while it runs (ring: 1,564 KB to 1,812 KB): pages of the library that nothing had touched. What the program itself asks for goes down (30.11). On a board nothing is paged, and the function is in the image of the checked build as well, which writes its error messages with fprintf; there the cost is the stack printf uses while it runs. A program that prints words alone gets puts, and has no printf in it at all.

30.7 Statements the short way, and what stays as it was

x = (x + 1); is written x += 1;, and return (a * b); is return a * b;. The emitter puts every operation in brackets so that what is around it cannot change its meaning; around a whole statement nothing is left that could (tidy in src/emit_c.rs). The statements at the top of the program are the body of main, unless the program has a collector in it, which has to find the program's variables on the stack below main (docs/memory.md).

What stays. Names keep their z_: a Zeno program may call a variable printf, main or int. A whole number is still int64_t, because that is what an int is in Zeno. A temporary is still written where two values have to be worked out in the order Zeno gives them. A list still holds zeno_slots and not an array of int64_t (30.12).

30.8 The C compiler is asked for a small program

-Os in place of -O2. With --fast as well it is -O3 -fno-math-errno, since that was asked for by name.

30.9 What it goes with

Every kind of build that writes C: the collector, --owned, --no-collector, --firmware, and --memory and --fast beside them. --release adds nothing to it. --llvm, --web and --target refuse it with a sentence that says why.

Why not LLVM. Nobody reads the IR, so the half of this that is for a reader has no reader there, and the half that is for the machine --fast --llvm already does.

The smallest. --minimal --no-collector or --minimal --owned. A program that makes a list has to free it somehow, and with the collector that is about 500 lines of C that no option can make small.

30.10 How it is held to its word

tools/minimal.py builds every program of the check of the targets (24.9: the examples, the corner programs, every sample of the book) both ways for each of the four kinds of build, and the two must print the same, end the same way, and stop with the same message. A program that a check stops has no defined result in a minimal build, so it is found and left out: the C of the checked build is given a line that writes a mark in zeno_fail and zeno_bug, where every check ends. On 2026-11-18: 213, 193, 193 and 210 programs for the four kinds, all the same, and 17 to 20 left out for each. It runs on GitHub on a push that changes the C backend (.github/workflows/minimal.yml), on Linux with gcc and on macOS with clang.

30.11 What it buys, measured

python3 tools/minimal.py --sizes makes the table in docs/minimal.md. In short, for the examples:

  • The C is 23 lines for hello, about 100 for a program of numbers, and 300 to 1,000 for a program with lists, objects and text, from about 3,000 every time. Over all the programs of the check it is 7% of the bytes with no collector and 14% with one.
  • The program shrinks less, because the C compiler never put an unused function in it. Its code and constants (text, as size counts it) are a quarter to a third smaller for most of the examples: ring 8.1 KB to 4.5 KB with no collector, words 16.5 KB to 12.8 KB. At the ends, blink loses 6% (it had almost nothing to lose) and primes 82%, 11.4 KB to 2.1 KB. The file on disk moves in steps of 4 KB and often does not move at all.
  • Memory. What the program holds from start to end changes little, unless the program stops needing the pool (primes: 34.8 KB to 0.6 KB). What it asks for while it runs goes down wherever print made text: thermostat 1,360 bytes to 240.

30.12 Left for later

  • A list of whole numbers as an array of int64_t, and an object's fields read without a slot, which is what a person would write.
  • A top-level let of a number as static const, with its value.
  • % as C's own where both sides are known not to be below zero.
  • A print for a board with no printf.
  • The uncaught error's place, for a build that wants only that back.

31. A field with the name of a type, in C

Found while zeno build --minimal was checked (2026-11-18): tools/targets/edge-names.zeno ran with zeno run and every --target, and zeno build wrote C for it that the C compiler refused.

31.1 The parameter steps aside, and the field keeps its name

A class may have a field with the name of a class or an enum:

class point {
    point: int
}

Zeno has no rule against it, and zeno run runs it. In C a class is a type z_point, and the function that makes an object had one parameter for each field, called as the field is in the struct: z_point. Inside that function the parameter hid the type, so z_point *self was read as a multiplication. A field named as another class broke the list of parameters itself, and a case of an enum that carries such a value broke the same way. edge-names.zeno has it by another road: its class new_ is z_new in C, which is what its field new is.

Decision. Such a parameter is z2_point. The field stays z_point in the struct, where C keeps the names of fields apart from the names of types, so self->z_point = z2_point; is right.

Why z2_. It is how a second variable of one name is already written (z2_x), so nothing new is to be learned when reading the C. And no type can have that name: every type begins with z_.

Why only where the names meet. For every program without such a field the C is what it was, byte for byte: 2,028 C files compared, the 363 programs of the corpus built nine ways, and only the nine of edge-names.zeno differ. The names of all classes and enums are gathered before the first class is written, because the type may be written below the class that has the field.

Why not an error. "The entire language must be unambiguous and intuitive": a name that is right for zeno run and wrong for zeno build would be a rule of C showing through. Two classes that C would know by one name are still refused (same_in_c), since there a name would have to be made up for a type the program prints and compares.

32. A try on Windows, in C

Found while 0.5.2 was got ready (2026-11-18): the test a_minimal_build_prints_what_zeno_run_prints_for_a_correct_program passed on Linux and macOS and failed on Windows. The program it builds stopped at its first caught error and said nothing.

32.1 Under MinGW a try is a plain jump

A try in C is setjmp, and an error is longjmp back to it (5.5i). On Windows setjmp is a macro, and MinGW writes it as _setjmp(place, the frame of this function). longjmp then does not only jump. It walks the stack back to that frame with the machinery Windows has for the exceptions of C++ (RtlUnwindEx), so that the functions it passes can clean up.

On GitHub's Windows machine, with gcc 15.2 and -Os, that walk failed. The program of the test, built with --minimal and the collector, ended with the number 0xC0000028 (Windows' "bad stack") where int("4x2") is caught. A debugger showed the place: longjmp, then RtlUnwindEx, then the stop. The same C built with -O0, -O1 and -O2 ran to its end, and so did five examples with -Os. The same C built by gcc 13 ran under Wine at every level.

Decision. Under MinGW for x86-64 the runtime says _setjmp(place, NULL). With no frame, longjmp puts the registers back and jumps, and walks nothing. Every C build has these lines, and they do something only there.

Why. A Zeno program has nothing for the walk to do: its C has no clean-up code between a raise and its try. The walk can only go wrong, and where it went wrong the program could not say so. A plain jump is what _setjmp and _longjmp are on Linux and macOS (22.14), and what the LLVM build has asked for on Windows since it first ran there (12.8). So this makes the C build the same as the other, and Windows the same as the other systems.

Why not find what gcc 15 did. It was looked for and not found from here: no machine at hand has that compiler, and a build on GitHub's takes ten minutes. The reason above does not depend on it. Whatever made the walk fail, a program that does not walk cannot meet it.

Why not only with --minimal. -Os is where it was seen, and only --minimal asks for -Os. But the checked build has the same setjmp in the same functions, and nothing says -O2 is safe by more than luck with where the compiler put things. One way to jump, in every build.

What is left as it was. 32-bit MinGW already asked for no walk (_setjmp3(place, NULL) is its macro). Windows on ARM64 has only the setjmp that walks, and other compilers on Windows say setjmp in their own way, so those keep the macro. The trial workflow now builds six programs with --minimal on the machine it tries, and says where one that fails stopped.

33. A library written in Zeno

6.10 said of the methods of text and lists: "Once modules exist, what can be written in Zeno will be." Modules have existed since chapter 7, and since then Zeno has gained a VM, a second compiler and fifteen other languages to write a program in. A function of the library was by now written once for each: math.log2 is in builtins.rs, in runtime.c, and in thirteen other runtimes. That is why missing.md puts this first: every small gap of the library costs that much, until the library can be written in Zeno.

This chapter is the way to do it, the first functions written that way (6.21 had left them out "until something needs it"), and two mistakes that it found. library-in-zeno.md walks through the code.

33.1 A module that comes with Zeno may have a part written in Zeno

The folder library/ holds one .zeno file for each such module: library/math.zeno, library/random.zeno. The files are kept inside the zeno program (src/library.rs), so there is nothing to install beside it and nothing to find when a program runs.

math has both kinds of part. math.sqrt is built in, as before, and math.hypot is written in Zeno. A program does not see the difference: import math, then math.sqrt(x) and math.hypot(x, y), or from math import sqrt, hypot.

Why inside zeno, and not a folder beside it. A folder that has to be found is a way for it not to be found: a zeno that was copied to another machine, a folder of an older version. Every installer would have had to carry it. The files are small text.

Why one module can have both kinds. hypot belongs with sqrt. A second module, math2 or mathx, would make the reader learn which function lives where, for a reason that is about how Zeno is built and not about mathematics.

Turned down: writing these in Rust and C like the rest. hypot is one line of C. It is also a line in each of fifteen other runtimes, each with its own test, and the answers would differ in the last digit, because each language has its own hypot. Written in Zeno it is the same arithmetic everywhere, so it prints the same everywhere, and that is checked by the tests there already are.

33.2 The part is joined like a file of the program

modules.rs reads the part when a file of the program imports its module, gives its names the module's name in front (math.hypot), and puts its statements ahead of the program's own. From there on it is a file like shapes.zeno: the checker checks it, the interpreter and the VM run it, both compilers and every target compile it, and none of them was changed for it.

The part begins with strict, so every type in it is written, as every kind of build asks. It may keep things to itself with private. It imports the built-in part of its own module (import math, for math.sqrt), and nothing else.

In a message it is named library/math.zeno, with its own line numbers, like any file. zeno join shows it, which is a way to read the library.

Why last among the files, and first among the statements. A place in a message is a file's number and a line. The parts are read after every file of the program, so the program's files keep the numbers they would have had. Their statements still go first: a part uses nothing of the program's, and the top of any file may use the part.

33.3 Only what the program reaches is joined

Of a part's functions, the program gets the ones its files name, the ones those name, and so on. A program that calls math.gcd has math.gcd in it, and not hypot, sinh or clamp.

What is not a function comes whole when anything of the part is reached: the four numbers of random.

Why. A program for a board pays for every function in it. A library that came whole would be a reason to avoid it there, and firmware is what Zeno is for. The C compiler would drop most unused functions if asked, but the fifteen targets would not, and zeno build shows its C to be read.

How. The stage that gives names their full names already visits every use of a name. It now also notes which full names each function of a part uses, and Loader::join follows those from what the program's own files name.

33.4 A program that names nothing of a part is the program it was

A file that spells none of the names a part offers cannot be using it, and the part is then not read at all. If a file does spell one (let clamp = 3) and turns out not to mean the part's, the part is taken off the end of the files again. Either way the joined program is, to the last statement, what it was before parts existed.

Why it matters. "Nothing existing may change" is how every feature since 0.1 has been added. Here it holds by construction for every program that was accepted before: math.hypot and import random were both refused. tools/minimal.py and the test a_program_that_names_nothing_of_a_part_is_the_program_it_was hold it there.

The one thing that does change, as for json, web and python before it (26.11): random is now the name of a module that comes with Zeno, so a file of a program called random.zeno can no longer be imported under that name.

33.5 A part means the names that come with Zeno

A program may give abs, len or max a meaning of its own: they are names, and not words of the language. Joined to such a program, a part that says abs(x) would call the program's abs. What math.hypot does would then depend on who calls it.

Two things keep that from happening.

  1. A part uses no such name where it can do without. The part of math has its own private size in place of abs. random keeps its four numbers as plain whole numbers and cuts them to 32 bits with & 4294967295, so it needs no u32.wrap.
  2. Where it cannot, the program is told. random.pick needs the length of a list, and len is the only way to ask. A program that has a len of its own and reaches pick is refused, at its len: "this program uses random.pick, which is written in Zeno and uses the len that comes with Zeno. So the program cannot give len a meaning of its own here. Give this one another name". A program that does not reach pick keeps its len.

Why a refusal, and not a fix. The fix is a way for a part to say "the len that comes with Zeno" that nothing can hide. That is a change to how every engine looks a name up, and it is worth making once, for the files of a program as well: an imported file has the same trouble today, and is refused the same way (7.7). Until then the refusal is honest, rare, and can be lifted without changing any program.

33.6 import random goes at the top of a file

A module that comes with Zeno can be imported inside a function, where the import of a file cannot (7.5). A part written in Zeno is joined to the file, as a file of the program is, so its import belongs where theirs do. import random inside a function is refused with a message that says so. import math inside a function still gives the built-in part, and math.hypot there says to move the import to the top.

33.7 What math gained

What it is
math.hypot(x, y) the distance of the point (x, y) from (0, 0)
math.sinh(x), math.cosh(x), math.tanh(x) the hyperbolic functions
math.gcd(a, b) the greatest whole number that divides both
math.clamp(value, low, high) the value, kept between the two

hypot takes floats. math.hypot(3, 4) is refused, with the message every function written in Zeno gives: write 3.0. math.sqrt takes a whole number because the checker has a rule for it by name. A function written in Zeno has the rules of the language and no others, and "an int does not become a float by itself" is one of them.

hypot is the root of the sum of the squares, and exact where that is. math.hypot(3.0, 4.0) is 5.0. Sides whose squares would not fit in a float are first multiplied by 2-600, and tiny ones by 2600, which changes no digit of a float. Turned down: dividing by the longer side, which is the usual way and gives 13.000000000000002 for (5.0, 12.0).

sinh near zero is a series. (e**x - e**-x) / 2 takes one number from another that is nearly equal, and loses most of its digits. Below 0.25 the first six terms of the series are used. The three functions are made from math.exp, so their last digit is the machine's exp's, as exp's own is.

gcd is never negative, and gcd(0, 0) is 0, as in Python, C++ and Go.

clamp is written once for every type that < compares: whole numbers, floats, quantities in one unit, text. The three are of one type. The value is held against low first, so with low above high, which is a mistake in the program, the answer is low for a value below it and high otherwise. Turned down: an error for that case, as Rust and Java give. A function written in Zeno that raises must say raises, and then every clamp in every program would need a try.

33.8 random

What it gives
random.between(low, high) a whole number from low to high, both included
random.number() a float from 0.0 up to 1.0, never 1.0
random.pick(items) one of the items of a list
random.seed(n) starts the numbers again from n

The same numbers on every run, until the program seeds. A program that never calls seed gets the numbers of random.seed(0).

Why. A test that fails must fail again when it is run again. A simulation is compared with yesterday's. A board has nothing to make a first number from. And it is one rule for zeno run, a compiled program and every target, where "different each time" would be fifteen ways of asking a machine for something unpredictable. C does the same. Python, JavaScript and Go do not, and a game written in Zeno has to seed itself. It has nothing to seed from yet: the time of day is in missing.md, and random.seed of it will be the line to write.

This cannot be changed later without changing what programs print, so it is decided now and not left open.

Why sfc32. It needs four whole numbers of 32 bits, additions, shifts and one ^: no multiplication and no division, so it is quick on a processor that has neither. It passes the usual tests of randomness, which the short generators that C libraries use do not. It is written with nothing but operators, so it is the same on every engine. It is not for keys or passwords, and the file says so.

between includes both ends, so a die is between(1, 6). The ends can be given in either order. Every number is as likely as any other: bits are drawn under a mask that just covers the span, and a draw above it is thrown away, where the short way (bits % span) makes the low numbers come up a little more often. high - low must fit in an int, or the subtraction is an OverflowError like any other.

number has 53 bits, made from two draws as Python makes it, so every float it can give is as likely as any other.

pick of an empty list is an IndexError: there is no item to give.

Left out for now. shuffle, which takes items out of a list it was only lent (5.15e). A seed from the machine. Numbers that follow a bell curve.

33.9 Two mistakes this found

Two files could not both import a module that comes with Zeno. main.zeno and shapes.zeno each say import math. Joined, the program said it twice, and the checker answered "math is already declared in this block". No example had two such files. Now, as the files are joined, an import that an earlier file already made is left out. Twice in one file is still refused. The part of math imports math itself, so every program that used it would have met this.

A function of an imported file, used as a value, did not build. let f = shapes.area ran under zeno run, and zeno build wrote zeno_wrap_shapes.area, which is not a name in C. The wrapper is now named from the function's name in C, zeno_wrap_z_shapes_area. A function of the first file keeps the name it had, so the C of every program that built before is unchanged. [1.0, 2.0].map(math.sinh) is how it was found.

One thing seen and left. A file can use math without importing it, when another file of the program does: the joined program has one set of names. It is the other side of the first mistake, and mending it means the checker knowing which file a line is in.

33.10 What can be written this way next

What is only arithmetic and control: factorial, a search in a sorted list, a queue. JSON in a compiled program (18.5) is text and lists, and can be.

What cannot: anything that asks the machine. program.exit, the environment and the time of day need each engine. And the methods of text and lists stay built in, for the reason of 6.10: they are called as xs.insert(...), and they take items out of a list they were lent.

34. Ending a program, its environment, and the error stream

Three functions of the module program, each of which asks the machine, so each was written once for every engine: zeno run, the VM, C, LLVM and the fifteen target languages. A program that does not use them is unchanged: they are three new names inside program, and nothing else moved. Walkthrough: ending-a-program.md.

34.1 program.exit(code) ends the program, and is not an error

import program

if len(program.arguments()) != 2 {
    program.warn("usage: copy <from> <to>")
    program.exit(2)
}

The program ends there, and whatever started it (the shell, a script, program.run) is given code. What was printed is sent first. Before this, a program could end in two ways only: at its last line, with 0, or with an error nobody caught, with 1 (6.19). A tool that a script calls has to be able to say "no such file" with one number and "wrong words" with another.

No try stops it, and no except sees it, not even one that names no kind. It is not an error: a program that asked to end has not gone wrong. Python's sys.exit is an exception, and a bare except: that was written to catch something else swallows it; that is the kind of surprise Zeno is meant not to have. Inside both engines it travels up as an error that no try catches does (a Control::Fatal that says where the program ended, with the number kept beside it, 34.5), so the language beside a program (import python) is still told that the program is over. In C and LLVM builds it is C's own exit, which also runs the memory report. Each target language uses its own way to end at once (os._exit after the output is sent in Python, exit! in Ruby, std::_Exit in C++), never one an except written in that language could stop.

code goes from 0 to 255. That is what every system hands on: on Linux and macOS, exit(256) arrives as 0, which would turn a failure into a success. A number outside is a ValueError, raised where the call is, as char(0) is; a number written down outside is found by the checker before the program runs. A --minimal build has no checks (30.2), and there the number is cut to its last eight bits, as in C.

It does not count as the end of a path. A function that promises an int still has to return one on every path, program.exit or not. Why. Java, Go and C do the same. The rule "every path returns" stays one a reader can check without knowing which calls end the program, and the cost is one line in a rare case.

In a test (zeno test), a program cannot end in the middle of the run: the test fails, with "the program ended here, with program.exit(2)", and the next test runs. In a page, the program cannot end either: the turn that is running stops, and the page stays, with its buttons. In a firmware build it is allowed: an uncaught error there already ends with exit(1), and what ending means on a real board is for the board's runtime to say (missing.md, item 8).

34.2 program.environment(name) gives str or none

let home = program.environment("HOME")
if home is none {
    print("HOME is not set")
}

none when the environment does not say, which a program must handle (str or none, as input() gives). A name that no environment can hold (empty, or with = or a zero byte in it) is none too, and the machine is not asked: some systems would refuse it with an error, and C would read only the part before the zero. A value that is not UTF-8 is read as the words on the command line are, with U+FFFD where a byte cannot be read.

A function, and not a dict of everything. A dict would be a copy taken when the program started, of names the program never looks at, and it would have to be made in every target. One question, one answer.

It only reads. Setting a variable changes nothing for the program itself, only for programs it starts, and C's setenv is not safe beside other threads. If program.run ever needs to give a program an environment, that will be a word of run's.

The word is environment, whole, as Zeno's names are (1.4), not env or getenv.

A firmware build refuses it: a board has no environment, and a value the build needs is a const. A page has none, and gets none. A program built for WebAssembly sees what its host gives it: tools/run-wasi.js gives it Node's environment, wasmtime gives nothing unless asked with --env.

34.3 program.warn(text) writes one line on the error stream

program.warn(f"cannot read {path}, going on without it")

One str, and a line end after it. print takes any values, and showing every kind of value is a long piece of each backend; an f-string already turns anything into text, so one str loses nothing and costs fifteen short functions instead of fifteen long ones.

What was printed before it is sent first, so that on a screen that shows both streams the lines keep the order the program wrote them in.

The word is warn. Ruby and Perl have a warn that does exactly this. program.error(text) reads as if it raised an error, which it does not. print(text, to: errors) would make print the one built-in that takes a named argument for where its output goes, and every backend's print more complicated, for a rare need.

In a page, where there is one place for text, the line is shown with the rest. In a firmware build it goes where an uncaught error's message goes.

34.4 How the three are held to each other

tools/targets.py now holds every target to zeno run on two more things: the number the program ended with (it compared only "0 or not" before), and the lines written on the error stream before any error. Every program is started with ZENO_TARGETS=yes, so that tools/targets/edge-ending.zeno can read a variable whose value is known. Two changes came with that. go run ends with 1 whatever the program ended with, so Go programs are built first and then run, as C++ and Rust ones were. And tools/run-wasi.js hands the program Node's environment instead of an empty one.

In cargo test, both engines give a Ran: what was printed, what was warned, the error if any, and the number at the end. A test sets the environment the way it sets what is typed (with_environment), and that environment goes to the built programs it runs as well.

34.5 The end travels as an error no try catches

Decision. Inside zeno run and the VM, program.exit(3) keeps 3 aside, for the thread the program runs on, and stops the program with Control::Fatal, the kind no try catches, with the message "the program ended here, with program.exit(3)". At the end of the run, Ran::ended finds the 3 and makes it a run that went well, ending with 3. A page's turn does the same, and the page stays. A test that calls a function that ends the program shows that message, as it did.

Why. It first had a kind of its own, Control::Exit, beside Control::Raise and Control::Fatal. Counted before 0.6.0, the VM ran 1 to 3 % more instructions than in 0.5.2 on every benchmark (fib +2.1 %, loop +3.1 %, sort +2.7 %), and the whole difference was inside its loop, at lines that had not changed (let base = frame.base alone ran 3.9 million more on fib 25). The loop is one large function, and a sixth kind of Control changed how the Rust compiler kept its values in registers. Without it the counts are those of 0.5.2 again. What a program does is the same either way: nothing catches the end, everything above it is told, and the number reaches the shell.

The other choice. Keeping Exit and finding another change that gave the loop back its registers would have been luck, and the next change anywhere could undo it. Carrying the end in a kind that already exists leaves the loop as it was in 0.5.2.

34.6 On Windows a built program asks for the environment in UTF-16

C's getenv answers on Windows in the machine's code page, so a value in Tamil on a machine set up for English came out of a built program as question marks, where zeno run printed it. Windows keeps the environment whole, in UTF-16, and program.environment now asks it (GetEnvironmentVariableW) and turns the answer into UTF-8, as program.arguments does for the command line. The three functions of Windows are declared inside the function that uses them, so that a --minimal build, which keeps only the functions a program uses, keeps them with it. Turned down: _wgetenv, which is Microsoft's C library's own and reads a copy made when the program started.

34.7 What the VM reaches outside itself sits in a box of its own

program.warn gave the VM one more field, the text it collects for the tests, and the board had grown with its inputs, ports and converter. Both sat in the VM before the stack and the frames, which every instruction reads, and pushed them 48 bytes further on. With that, bench/loop.zeno ran 6% slower by the clock than in 0.5.2 while running the same instructions to the last digit: callgrind showed the two builds' inner loop identical but for those two offsets. It was measured, not guessed: with the output, the warnings, the board, the page and the keyboard moved into one World behind a pointer, the same program is within 1.5% of 0.5.2 by the clock, and the others are level or faster (nbody 4% faster).

So the rule: what an instruction reads on every step (the stack, the frames, the handlers) stays together at the front of the VM, and what only a call of a built-in reaches goes in the box, where it can grow without moving anything.

35. A case of an enum can stand for a number

enum Reply {
    Ack = 6
    Nak = 21
}

let byte: u8 = u8(Ack)        # 6, to send
let reply = Reply(byte)       # Reply or none, from what came back

Every protocol, every register field and every error code is a number with a name. Before this, a program kept the numbers in consts and the meaning in an enum, and wrote the match between them by hand, once for each direction. Walkthrough: enum-numbers.md.

35.1 Ack = 6, for every case or for none

The number is written out, a whole number with or without a minus, in any base Zeno reads (0x15, 0b1010). A const or a sum is not taken: the list of numbers is meant to be read off the page, as the table in a datasheet is.

Every case has one, or none does. C numbers the cases it is not told about (one more than the case before), which makes the number of a case depend on where it is in the list: adding a case in the middle changes the numbers after it, and a message sent by the old program means something else to the new one. In Zeno nothing has a number that was not written. Why not a number for every enum, counted from 0? The same reason: a number that nobody wrote cannot be relied on, so it is better not to have one at all.

Only a case that carries nothing. A Fault(code: int) is not one number; giving it one would say that every fault is the same.

No two cases the same. Reply(6) has to give back one case. C allows two names for one number; Zeno has const for a second name.

The number is an int, the size Zeno counts in. A case that has to fit a u8 is turned into one with u8(Ack), which is checked like every conversion: a number too big for a u8 is an OverflowError there.

35.2 int(Ack) gives the number, Reply(6) gives the case or none

Both ways are conversions, written as conversions are. int(x) and u8(x) already turn a value into a number, and the name of a type called like a function already makes a value of that type (a class). So int(Ack) and Reply(6) need nothing new to be read. Turned down: a field, Ack.number. A case is not an object, and a field would read as if it could be changed. Turned down: Ack as int. Zeno has no as, and does not need a second way to convert.

Reply(6) gives Reply or none, because most numbers are no case at all, and a byte that came over a wire can be anything. The checker makes the program look at the none before it uses the case, as it does for input() and program.environment. Turned down: raising a ValueError for a number that is no case. Not knowing a code is the ordinary case for a program that reads from outside, not a mistake, and none makes the program say what it does then.

int(Ack) cannot fail, and u8(Ack) fails only as u8(n) does.

A plain enum without numbers is refused in both, and the message says how to give it numbers. A case is not secretly a number in Zeno, as it is in C.

Comparing a case with a number is still refused (Ack == 6): a Reply and an int are different things, and int(Ack) == 6 says which one is meant.

35.3 How it is built: two functions written beside the enum

The checker knows which calls these are, since it knows that Ack is a case of an enum with numbers and that Reply is one. It notes each, as it notes a count += 1 on a sized number (10.27), and checked rewrites the program. Beside the enum, in the same block, it writes

function Reply..number(value: Reply) -> int {
    match value {
        case Ack { return 6 }
        case Nak { return 21 }
    }
}
function Reply..case(number: int) -> Reply or none {
    if number == 6 { return Ack }
    if number == 21 { return Nak }
    return none
}

and int(Ack) becomes int(Reply..number(Ack)), Reply(6) becomes Reply..case(6). No program can write a name with two dots in a row, so the names are no one else's, and an enum declared inside a function gets its two functions inside that function.

Why not in each engine. Every engine, every build and all fifteen target languages can already run a function with a match and an if. Written this way, the feature is the same everywhere from the first day, with nothing to keep in step: tools/targets/edge-enum-numbers.zeno passes in all of them unchanged. An enum whose numbers no call uses gets no functions, so a program that only writes the numbers, as documentation, builds to the same code as before.

What it costs. Reply(n) tries the cases one after another, which for the dozen cases of a protocol is as fast as a table. An enum of hundreds of cases would want a table or a switch, which the C compiler may make of the ifs on its own.

35.4 Left for later

A loop over the cases (for reply in Reply.cases), which other languages have and which a menu or a test of every code wants. It needs a list of an enum's cases as a value; it is the next thing for this chapter. A case that is a set of bits (Read | Write), for a register of flags: that is a different thing from one number per case, and wants a type of its own.

36. Bytes

import files

let frame: list[u8] = [0x7E, 0x01, 0x00, 0xFF]
files.write_bytes("frame.bin", frame)
let back = files.read_bytes("frame.bin")     # list[u8]
print(back[0])                                # 126

A firmware image, a capture from a logic analyser, a record a board wrote to its flash: none of these is text, and until now Zeno could not open them (6.16). This chapter is the first of three about bytes. It gives a file as its bytes. The second stores a list[u8] one byte to an item in C and LLVM (5.13a), and the third gives a list a fixed length. Walkthrough: bytes.md.

36.1 files.read_bytes gives a list[u8], and files.write_bytes takes one

A byte is a u8, and a file of bytes is a list[u8]. Zeno has had both since 0.1, so nothing new has to be learned: an item is a number from 0 to 255, len is the size of the file, for b in bytes walks it, and every method of a list works. Turned down: a bytes type of its own, as Python and Go have. It would be a second kind of list, with its own methods to learn and its own rules for what goes in. What a bytes type buys is a compact list, and that is a question of how a list[u8] is stored, which the second part of this chapter answers for every list[u8], not only the ones that came from a file.

Two functions with names of their own, beside read and write. Turned down: files.read(path, binary: true). What a call gives back would then depend on the value of an argument, and the checker would have to know it; read_bytes says on the page what it gives.

Everything the file holds, as it holds it. No byte is changed, and none is refused: a zero, a byte that is no UTF-8, a "\r\n" all arrive as numbers. The errors are those of files.read: no file, or one that cannot be read (a folder, or a file this program may not open), as a FileError that every kind of build can catch. There is no third, because nothing is required of the content.

write_bytes makes the file, or replaces what was in it, as files.write does, with one byte for each item. The list is a list[u8], so its items fit in a byte, and a number written out that does not fit is refused before the program runs (256 does not fit in a u8 (0 to 255)). A list of ints is refused too: it may hold anything, and turning it into bytes would have to drop what does not fit. [u8(n) for n in numbers] says where the check is. The one list whose items are not known until the program runs, one that came from json.parse, is looked at item by item, and an item that is no byte is a ValueError that names it.

The list is new at each call, so it can be kept by an owner in a build with no collector: let frame: owned list[u8] = files.read_bytes(path).

How it is built. zeno run and the VM read the file with Rust's std::fs::read. C and LLVM call zeno_files_read_bytes in runtime.c, which reads in pieces of 512 bytes into a list with room for the whole file, and in a firmware build says whether it worked, as files.read does. Each target language uses its own way of reading a file as bytes (list(f.read()) in Python, File.binread(path).bytes in Ruby, os.ReadFile in Go).

36.2 A list[u8] is stored one byte to an item

In C and LLVM every list was an array of eight-byte slots, so a file of a megabyte, read with read_bytes, took eight megabytes. Now a list[u8] keeps one byte for each item. Nothing in the language changes: the same program prints the same thing, and only the memory it takes is different (an 8 MB file read and written back takes 13 MB in all, where it took 64 MB).

Every list[u8], not only the ones from a file. [1, 2, 3] where a list[u8] is wanted, [u8(n) for n in numbers], a field payload: list[u8], a map whose function gives a u8: each is stored packed. A program cannot tell the difference, so there is no choice to make and nothing to write. Turned down: a bytes type (36.1), and turned down: packed list[u8], a word that asks for it. Both would put a question of storage on the page that the compiler can answer alone, and the second would leave the slow way as the one a beginner meets first.

Only list[u8]. A byte is what files, protocols and buffers are made of; a list of u16 or i32 is rarer and takes eight bytes an item still. Packing them is the same work again for each width, and waits until a program asks for it.

How it is built. The runtime keeps one struct for a list, zeno_list, with a length, the room and the items. For a list[u8] the items are bytes, read through ZENO_BYTES(list), and a set of functions does for them what the list functions do for slots: zeno_bytes_of, zeno_bytes_append, zeno_bytes_at, _pop, _insert, _copy, _concat, _slice, _str, _eq, _find, _contains, _reverse, _clear, _sort, _sort_by, _sum and _best. A byte goes into and comes out of them as an int64_t, so the code around them does not change. sort is a counting sort, since there are only 256 values; find and contains are memchr; == is memcmp.

The checker marks each place a list is made whose type is list[u8] (a list written out, a comprehension, a call such as read_bytes), and the emitters make a packed list there. The kind the emitters share gains Kind::Byte, which appears only as the item of a list: an item read out of one is an int again, as a field of a small type is (5.13a). A packed list and a list of slots never meet: where one would be stored as the other the emitter stops with an error, so that a place the checker did not mark is found by the tests and not by a program that prints the wrong numbers. The one comparison between them that a program can write, bytes == [1, 2, 3] where the right side is a list[int], has its own function, zeno_bytes_eq_ints.

The interpreter, the VM and the fifteen target languages are as they were: there a list of numbers is already the language's own.

36.3 [0] * 64 repeats a list

A buffer starts as so many zeros, and writing sixty-four of them out is no way to say it. list * n makes a new list with the items of list, n times over, as in Python: [0] * 64, [0x7E, 0x00] * 3. Where a list[u8] is wanted the numbers written in it must fit in a byte, as in any list written out, and the new list is stored packed (36.2).

One way round. 3 * [0], which Python also takes, is refused with a message that shows [0] * 3. Two spellings of one thing is one too many (principle 1).

Not for lists of lists, dicts or objects. [[0] * 3] * 3 is the best-known trap in Python: the three rows are one row, and setting grid[0][0] sets all three. A list holds such values by sharing them, so * would always make that trap, and it is refused with a message that shows the comprehension, [[0] * 3 for i in range(3)], which makes each row. Numbers, text, bools, enum values and none are never changed in place, so repeating them is safe.

A count below zero is a ValueError, where Python quietly gives an empty list. A negative count is a mistake in the program, and an empty list would carry it further before anything showed it. A count of zero gives an empty list.

How it is built. The checker types list * int as the list, and refuses the cases above. zeno run and the VM build the list in ops.rs. C and LLVM call zeno_list_repeat, or zeno_bytes_repeat for a list of bytes, which is one memcpy for each repeat; with no collector a list of text takes its own copies, as + does. The target languages each have their own way in the mul of their runtime (Python's own *, Ruby's Array#*, a loop elsewhere).

36.4 list[u8, 64]: a list of a fixed length

var buffer: list[u8, 64] = [0] * 64
buffer[0] = 0x7E
buffer.append(1)      # error: `append` would change how many items this list has
print(buffer[64])     # error: 64 is outside a list of 64 items

A buffer in firmware nearly always has a size that is fixed when the program is written: a frame of 8 bytes, a block of 512, a ring of 64. C writes uint8_t buffer[64], Rust [u8; 64], Go [64]byte. In Zeno it is list[u8, 64]: a list that always has 64 items.

The length is part of the type, and is a number written in it. list[u8, 64] reads as "a list of u8, 64 of them", and a number in the [ ] can never be mistaken for a type. Turned down: a word of its own, such as array[u8, 64]. It would be a second kind of list, with its own name to learn, for what is a list that cannot grow. Everything a list does that leaves its length as it is works the same way. Turned down: [64]u8 or u8[64], the order of Go and C: Zeno writes a type's name first and what it holds after (list[u8], dict[str, int]), and a length is one more thing it holds.

What gives one a value. A list written out with exactly that many items ([0x7E, command, 0, 0x7F]), [0] * 64, or another list of the same type and length. The count is checked before the program runs: this list has 2 items, and a list[u8, 8] always has 8. A list whose length is only known when the program runs ([0] * n, a list[u8] from somewhere else) is refused, with a message that says so.

What it does. Everything a list does that leaves the length as it is: an index, xs[i] = v, len, for, in, ==, find, sort, reverse, slice, map, filter, sum, min, max, + (which makes a new, ordinary list), printing. append, pop, insert and clear are refused, with a message that says to give an item a new value instead. A position written as a number is checked before the program runs: buffer[64] on a list[u8, 64] is an error then, not an IndexError later.

Where it can go. A list of a fixed length goes where one of the same type and length is wanted: a variable, a parameter, a field, what a function gives back, an item of a list[list[u8, 4]]. It does not go where an ordinary list[u8] is kept, such as a let that says list[u8] or a field of that type: whatever held it there could append to it, and the first holder would find a list longer than its type says. The message says to write list[u8, 64] there, or copy the items with .slice(0).

A function that never changes the length can be given one. This is the case that matters most: checksum(data: list[u8]) should take a buffer as well as any other list. The checker reads the function: if it only reads its data, gives items new values, walks it, or passes it on to a function that does the same, a list of a fixed length goes there. If anything in it could change the length (data.append, or keeping data in a variable, a list or a field, or returning it, or handing it to a function the checker cannot read), the message names that line: this list always has 8 items, and `pad` may change how many its `data` has: it calls `data.append` (line 11). The same holds for a generic function such as first[T](xs: list[T]). Turned down: refusing every function that takes a list[u8], which would make each library function be written twice, and turned down: a check when the program runs, which would turn a mistake the checker can see into an error that waits for the program to reach it, and would need a mark on every list in all fifteen target languages.

How it is built. The checker has one more type, Ty::Fixed, the item and the length. Whatever only looks at a value (the arguments of print, len and the other built-ins, an index, a loop, the object of a method) sees it as the list it is, so none of that had to change. The places that keep a value see the length, and src/lengths.rs reads a function's body to answer whether it changes the length of a parameter. Every engine and every build stores a list of a fixed length as a list: the length was made sure of before the program ran, so nothing is left to check while it runs. A list[u8, 64] is packed one byte to an item, as any list[u8] is (36.2).

36.5 Left for later

A list of a fixed length that takes no block from the pool. Today list[u8, 64] in a build with no collector is a block from the pool, as any list is. Since its length is known, its items could sit inside the object that has it as a field, or on the stack of the function that makes it, with nothing to give back. That is the next step for this type.

Text from bytes, and bytes from text (the UTF-8 of a str, and a str from bytes that are UTF-8), which a protocol that carries a name wants. It is a pair of functions with an error for bytes that are not text, and waits until a program asks. files.append_bytes, for a log of records, the same. A file read in pieces, for a file too big to hold, waits for cleaning up at the end of a block, as it does for text.

37. The libraries of Ruby

The first language of the second version (26.1): import ruby, for the library that comes with Ruby and for gems. ruby.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for JavaScript (28) and Java (29): Ruby runs beside the program, they talk over a socket, numbers and text cross and everything else stays, what Zeno gives is a copy, a value from there is not a condition, the types are known when the program runs, and nothing changes for a program that does not ask. What follows is what Ruby made different.

37.1 ruby.require loads, and ruby.constant names

ruby.require("date")
let Date = ruby.constant("Date")

Why two functions, where Python has one. In Python import gives the module, and everything is reached from it. In Ruby require gives nothing: it loads a file, and what the file brings are constants that every program can then name. One library can bring several (net/http brings Net::HTTP and URI), and many constants need no library at all (Math, File, Kernel). A ruby.module that guessed the constant from the name of the library would be right for date and wrong for net/http, yaml (YAML) and active_support.

Why these names. require is the word Ruby has, so it is the one a person looks for. constant is what Ruby calls every name that begins with a capital letter, a class, a module and RUBY_VERSION alike, so one function covers them. It takes the name as Ruby writes it, "Net::HTTP".

require gives none. Ruby's gives true the first time and false after, which says nothing a program of Zeno needs.

37.2 A call has brackets

In Ruby day.year is a call. In Zeno thing.name with no brackets is the method itself, to be called later, as it is for a value of JavaScript (28.6) and Java (29.3), and that rule holds for a value of Ruby: day.year() calls, and day.year is the method.

Why not call it as Ruby does. A dot that sometimes calls is the ambiguity the language was written to be without: words.push would have to mean "call with nothing" or "the method" by a rule the reader cannot see. With brackets every call in a Zeno program looks like a call, whichever language answers it. Python, JavaScript and Java already agree with Zeno here, so Ruby is the one that bends.

The method not called yet prints as a sentence that says so, since the commonest mistake is to leave the brackets off as Ruby allows.

37.3 send for the names Zeno cannot write

empty?, sort!, +, class and raise cannot follow a dot in Zeno. They are reached through send, which is Ruby's own method for calling a method by its name: words.send("empty?").

Why not let ? and ! into a name after a dot. ? and ! are not part of any name in Zeno, and letting them in for one module would change what the lexer reads for every program, which 26.11 rules out. It would also not reach the operators or the words.

Why not the name in brackets, as for Java (29.10). In Java an object that has no items has no use for brackets. In Ruby almost everything has []: an Array, a Hash, a String, a Struct, a class (Hash["a", 1]). words["empty?"] already means something there. send means one thing, and is what a Ruby programmer would write.

Where a name has no method and the same name with ? or ! has, the error says how to write it.

37.4 A symbol stays in Ruby; ruby.symbol makes one

:up and "up" are different values in Ruby, and a Hash keeps them apart. If a symbol arrived as a str, the program could not give it back as what it was, and hash[key] with a key Ruby gave would look under the wrong key. So a symbol is one of the values that stay, and ruby.symbol("up") is how a program writes :up.

In a copy it is its name. ruby.copy makes plain data of Zeno (26.5), and a dict has keys that are str or int. A Hash with symbol keys is the commonest Hash in Ruby, so the copy would be refused for most of them if a symbol could not be a key. As a value it is copied the same way, so that one rule covers both.

No looking under both. ages["bob"] does not also try :bob. A Hash can hold both keys, and then which one was meant would be a guess.

37.5 Text and bytes are one String

Ruby has one class for both. A String comes across as a str when it is text: as it is when Ruby has it in UTF-8, turned into UTF-8 when it is in another encoding, and read as UTF-8 when Ruby has no encoding for it (ASCII-8BIT), which is what a socket, Net::HTTP and File.binread give. Bytes that do not read as UTF-8 stay in Ruby.

Why read the unlabelled bytes as text. Most of what Ruby hands out without an encoding is text: the body of a web page, the output of a program. If those stayed in Ruby, the first thing most programs do, fetch something and look at it, would give a value that len and + refuse.

What it costs. Whether such a String arrives as a str depends on what is in it, where everywhere else it depends on the kind of value: the bytes of a file that happens to hold only text arrive as a str. Python has bytes and JavaScript has Buffer, so they have no such case. Nothing is lost by it, because a str given back to Ruby is the same bytes. A program that must have bytes whatever they are reads them through something that stays in Ruby: File.open(name, "rb"), and its each_byte().

37.6 An exception of Ruby is an error of Zeno

ZeroDivisionError and KeyError have Zeno's kinds of the same name. IndexError and StopIteration are IndexError, ArgumentError is ValueError (it is what Ruby raises for a value a method cannot use, Integer("x")), Errno::... and IOError are FileError, and the rest are Error with the name Ruby gave in front. RuntimeError is the exception raise "text" makes, and its name says nothing, so the message is the text alone, as for a plain Error of JavaScript (28.8).

ArgumentError is also what Ruby raises for the wrong number of arguments. That is a mistake in the program and not a value, but Ruby does not tell the two apart, so neither can Zeno.

37.7 A loop goes through what each gives

for item in thing takes everything thing.each gives, as Ruby's own for does, and of a Hash its keys, as for a dict.

Why each and not to_a. They are the same for most things and differ for some: a table of csv gives its rows to each and its header as well to to_a. A loop is each.

Something with no end is refused. 1.. and loop would be gone through forever before the loop began (26.12). A Range with no end and anything whose size is infinite raise ValueError and say what to write (first(n)).

37.8 A library is looked for from the folder of the program

As for Python and JavaScript (28.9): the folder of the .zeno file is the first place require looks, so a helper.rb beside the program is ruby.require("helper"). A Gemfile there is the one Bundler uses, when the program requires bundler/setup and BUNDLE_GEMFILE does not already name another.

Why Bundler is not required for the program. A Gemfile beside a program does not say that the program must run under it, and under Bundler every gem that the Gemfile does not name is hidden. A program of Ruby says require "bundler/setup" when it wants that, and so does a program of Zeno.

37.9 Left for later

  • A block: a function of Zeno given to map, each, File.open. It is the callback that 26.12 leaves, and Ruby needs it more than the others.
  • A loop with two names over a Hash, giving the key and the value. It gives a count and the key, as over the list of keys that the loop takes. The same holds for a dict of Python and a Map of Java.
  • A class of Zeno that inherits from a class of Ruby.
  • ruby in a built program, and in --target ruby, as 26.9 has it for Python.
  • Rubies before 3.1 and other Rubies (JRuby, TruffleRuby) are not tested. The helper uses nothing newer than Ruby 2.6.

37.10 On Windows the helper is a file

Everywhere else Ruby is started with -e and the helper as one word. On Windows a program is handed its command line as one text and cuts it into words itself, and Ruby cuts it by rules of its own: a \ followed by spaces and then a " takes the " out of the count, and a word with * or { in it is looked up as the name of a file. The helper arrived cut short at a line that ended in \, Ruby stopped on a syntax error, and Zeno said there was no Ruby. So on Windows the helper is written once into the folder for what can be made again (registry::cache), under a number worked out from it, and Ruby is given the file. Turned down: only mending that line, which was done too: the next line of the helper to trip a rule nobody knows by heart would bring the fault back, and only on a machine no test here runs on. Why not a file everywhere: -e needs no folder to write in, and works.

38. The libraries of PHP

The second language of the second version (26.1): import php, for what comes with PHP and for Composer packages. php.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for the others (28, 29, 37): PHP runs beside the program, they talk over a socket, numbers and text cross and objects stay, what Zeno gives is a copy, a value from there is not a condition, the types are known when the program runs, and nothing changes for a program that does not ask. What follows is what PHP made different.

38.1 php.type, php.callable and php.constant, because PHP keeps the three apart

In Python everything a module has is reached with a dot from the module. PHP has no value for a module, a class or a function: a class is named by new and ::, a function by being called, a constant by being written. Each lives in its own table, and one name can be in all three (count is a function, and many classes have a method and a constant called that). So there is one way in for each.

Why these names. type is the word Java's module uses for a class (29.1), and class cannot follow a dot. callable is what PHP itself calls a value that can be called (is_callable, Closure::fromCallable), and function is a word of Zeno. constant is PHP's own constant(). Each takes the name as PHP writes it, with its namespace: "Carbon\\Carbon", "Shop\\total", "DateTime::ATOM".

php.require(path) reads a file of PHP that is not in a package, from the folder of the program, as require_once does. It gives none, as Ruby's (37.1).

38.2 An array of PHP crosses whole

An array of PHP is a value and not an object: given to a function it is copied, as a list of Zeno is not. It is what a list and a dict are in PHP, both at once. So it comes across as one of them, whole: a list where its keys are 0, 1, 2 and so on in order, a dict for any other. explode(",", "a,b") gives a list of Zeno, which append and len and everything else of Zeno work on.

Why not leave it in PHP, as a list of Python stays (26.5). A list of Python is an object: two holders see one list, and changing it is seen by both, so a copy would not be the same thing. An array of PHP is never shared, so a copy is exactly what PHP would hand to another function. Leaving it would only make every result of PHP's functions, nearly all of which are arrays, go back to PHP for each item.

An empty array is a list. PHP cannot tell [] from an empty map. A list is the commoner, and an empty list and an empty dict print differently but are both empty.

38.3 A function that changes its argument is given a variable

sort(&$array) and preg_match($p, $text, &$matches) change what they are given and give back something else. Given a list of Zeno, they would change the copy PHP made of it, and nobody would see it. php.variable(value) is a variable that lives in PHP. Given to such a parameter, PHP changes it, and .value reads it after.

A list given where a variable is wanted is an error, before the function is called. PHP knows which parameters are written &$, so the helper asks it. A program that gave a list and saw nothing happen would have no way to find out why.

Why not change the list of Zeno after the call. Zeno would have to say which argument came back changed, for every call to every function, and write it into a list the program may not expect to change. php.variable says it at the line.

38.4 Classes, functions and methods are values the helper makes up

php.type("DateTime") gives a value that the helper made for the class, since PHP has none. Calling it is new. A dot after it is the constant of that name, or the static property, or the static method. A dot after an object is the method of that name, or the property.

The method before the property. PHP lets a class have both with one name, and a dot in Zeno is one thing. A method is what a program of PHP more often reaches by a name, and the property is still reached with the name in brackets, thing["name"], which on an object that has no items of its own is the property first.

A name in brackets for the words of Zeno. Size::from and a property for cannot follow a dot. As for Java (29.10) the name in brackets reaches them: Size["from"]("l"). An object of a class that has items of its own (ArrayAccess) keeps its brackets for them.

38.5 Named arguments are PHP's

name=value is PHP 8's name: value, by the name of the parameter. This is why PHP 8 is the oldest PHP the module says it works with: the rest of the helper would run on 7.4.

38.6 A warning of PHP is an error of Zeno

PHP reports most of what goes wrong in its functions by a warning on the screen and a value of false: file_get_contents of a file that is not there. A program of Zeno would go on with the false, and fail somewhere else. So the helper turns a warning into an error, and the error has the kind of what the warning says: FileError for a file, Error for the rest. A notice and a deprecation only advise, and PHP prints them as it always does. @ before a call in PHP, which hides its warning, has no form in Zeno, so a warning is not hidden.

DivisionByZeroError is ZeroDivisionError. ValueError, InvalidArgumentException, DomainException and JsonException are ValueError. OutOfBoundsException and OutOfRangeException are IndexError. Everything else is Error, with PHP's name for it in front, but for the plain Exception and Error, whose name says nothing.

What it costs. PHP has no exception of its own for a file, so whether a warning or a RuntimeException is a FileError is read from its text: "Failed to open stream", "No such file or directory", "Permission denied" and a few others. These are the system's words, which PHP passes on, and are the same in every PHP 8.

38.7 Bytes that are not text stay in PHP

A string of PHP is bytes. Where they read as UTF-8 they are a str, as for Ruby (37.5), and bytes that do not stay in PHP. There an item is a byte as an int, len is how many, and for goes through them, since a program that kept bytes wants them as numbers.

38.8 The helper's names begin with zeno_ and Zeno

A Composer package puts its functions and classes into the one program PHP runs, beside the helper's. PHP refuses a second function of one name, so a package with a keep or a back would stop the helper from starting. Every function of the helper begins with zeno_, and every class with Zeno.

38.9 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to PHP: array_map, usort, preg_replace_callback. It is the callback that 26.12 leaves.
  • A class of Zeno that extends a class of PHP.
  • php in a built program, and in --target php, as 26.9 has it for Python.
  • Only PHP 8.3 is tested. PHP 7.4 would run all but named arguments, and is not tried.

39. The libraries of Lua

The third language of the second version (26.1): import lua, for Lua's own library and for modules from LuaRocks. lua.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for the others (28, 29, 37, 38). What follows is what Lua made different.

39.1 lua.require and lua.global

lua.require(name) is Lua's require, which gives the module, as Python's import does. So unlike Ruby's (37.1) it gives what was loaded. lua.global(name) is what every program of Lua has without a require, string, table, os, and is named as Node's (28.2), which is the same thing.

39.2 Lua is talked to over named pipes

Every other helper connects back over a socket of this machine. Lua comes with no sockets, and the one library that gives them, LuaSocket, is written in C and has to be built for each Lua. What Lua does have is io.open, and on Linux and macOS a named pipe is a file it can open. So Zeno makes two pipes with mkfifo, in a folder only this user can open, and Lua opens them as files: one Lua writes and Zeno reads, one the other way. The names are removed as soon as both ends are open, so once Lua has started there is nothing to clean up.

Why not stdin and stdout, which every Lua has. The helper leaves the screen and the keyboard to Lua (26.3): a library that prints, or asks, works as it would in a program of Lua. On stdout the lines would be mixed with what Lua prints, and a module written in C prints around anything the helper could put in the way.

Windows has no such pipe. Its named pipes are not files that io.open can make, so there the helper uses LuaSocket if it is installed, and says so if it is not. The same is done where mkfifo is not there. The rest of the bridge does not know which it is: a link is something to read lines from and something to write them to.

39.3 A function gets self when it is a method

Lua writes object:name(x) and module.name(x), and only the colon gives the function its object. Zeno has one dot, and the call cannot say which is meant. The function can: one written function Class:name() has a first parameter called self, and Lua 5.2 and later say what a function's parameters are called. A function read from a table is given the table when its first parameter is self.

Lua 5.1 cannot say, and neither can a function written in C. For those, a function that the table has from its metatable is a method, and one the table holds itself is not. This is how Lua makes an object: its methods are in the class, which is the metatable's __index, while a module is a plain table that holds its functions. A function read from a userdata, a file or a socket, is always given it, as their methods are all called with a colon.

When the rule is wrong, the name in brackets is Lua's own t["name"], which gives the function as it is, and the program passes the object itself: p["length"](p).

Why not a second way to write a call, such as p.call("length"). Zeno's dot already means the method of an object for every other language, and almost every call of a library is told apart by the rule. A second form would have to be written at each of those calls, for the few the rule gets wrong.

39.4 Several values are a list

A function of Lua gives any number of values. None is none, one is that value, and several are a list of Zeno with all of them: string.find("hello", "l") is [3, 3].

Why not the first only, as Lua does in an expression. What comes second is often what the call was for: the count of gsub, the captures of find, the next position of string.unpack. Lua's own local a, b = f() takes them all, and Zeno has no such assignment.

nil and a message is an error. This is how most functions of Lua say they failed (io.open, os.rename, load), and what a program of Lua passes to assert. Given back as [none, "message"], it would be a list, which is not none, and a program that tested the result would go on. When the first of two or more values is nil and the second a string, the call raises Error with that message, and FileError when a number comes third, which is the number of the system that Lua's file functions give. A single nil is still none: string.find with no match.

39.5 A table stays in Lua, and counts from 1

A table is shared in Lua, as a list of Python is, so it stays (26.5). Its items are where Lua has them, and t[1] is the first. lua.copy makes a list of a table whose keys are 1 to its length, and a dict of any other.

Why not shift the index by one. t[1] in Zeno would then be t[2] in Lua, and a key that is a number would mean one thing in a table that is a list and another in one that is not. Everything a program reads about Lua says t[1]. The list that lua.copy makes is Zeno's, and counts from 0 as every list does.

for over a table gives the items of a list and the keys of any other, as Zeno's own for does for a list and a dict. Over a function it is Lua's generic for: the function is called until it gives nil, which is what string.gmatch and io.lines give.

39.6 Numbers

Lua 5.3 and later know whether a number is an integer, and it arrives as what it is. Before 5.3, and in LuaJIT, every number is a float, and a whole one within 2^53 arrives as an int, as in JavaScript (28.3).

39.7 Named arguments are a table of options

As for JavaScript (28.4): Lua has no named arguments, and a library takes a table of options last instead. f(1, loud=true) is f(1, {loud = true}).

39.8 An error of Lua is an Error

Lua's errors are values with no kind, usually a string, so every error of Lua is an Error with the value as its message. The position that Lua puts in front of a message names the helper when an error is raised from a function of Lua's library, so that position is taken off. The one other kind is the FileError of 39.4.

39.9 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to Lua: table.sort(t, f), callbacks.
  • Windows, which needs LuaSocket and was not tried.
  • lua in a built program, and in --target lua, as 26.9 has it for Python.

40. The libraries of C# and .NET

The fourth language of the second version (26.1): import csharp, for the types that come with .NET and for packages of NuGet. csharp.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here as it does for the others, and .NET is close to Java (29): classes, methods of one name that take different things, a helper that has to be compiled. Where Java decided a question the same way, 29 has the reason, and what follows is what .NET made different.

40.1 The module is csharp

Why not dotnet, which is the runtime and the command. Every other module is named for the language its libraries are written in, and the name is what a person reads in the documentation of a library: "a library for C#". F# and Visual Basic run on .NET too, and what they make is used the same way, but nearly every package of NuGet is written in C# and documented with it. cs is the target of zeno build --target cs (24), which writes a program, and is the wrong word for using a library.

csharp.type(name) is named as Java's (29.1), and calling it is new (29.2). csharp.assembly(path) is Java's java.jar: an assembly is what .NET calls a .dll.

40.2 A type is named as C# writes it

"List<int>", "Dictionary<string, List<int>>", "int[]", "int?", and "string" for System.String. .NET's own way to write a generic type, "System.Collections.Generic.List1[System.Int32]", is whatType.GetType` takes, and nobody writes it in a program.

A name with no namespace is looked for in the namespaces a new project of C# has without a using: System, System.Collections.Generic, System.IO, System.Linq, System.Net.Http, System.Threading, System.Threading.Tasks.

Why, when Java's types need the whole name (29.1). For Java the packages looked in would have been a list Zeno chose. This list is C#'s own: every project made by dotnet new since .NET 6 has these namespaces without asking (its "implicit usings"), so a person who writes C# already writes File, Math and List<int> with no namespace. A name that is not found with its namespace is tried there only after, so a whole name always means what it says.

40.3 Of several methods, the arguments choose, and a named argument is a parameter

The choice is Java's (29.4), with C#'s order: an int of Zeno fits an int before a long and both before a double; a list fits an array or a List<T> as well as its items fit theirs, a class before an interface; int? takes what int takes, one step later. Two that fit as well are an error that lists both.

A named argument is given to the parameter of that name, Math.Round(2.567, digits=1). C# has named arguments of its own, unlike Java (29) and Lua (39.7), so name=value means in Zeno what name: value means in C#. The message that says no method fits lists each with the names of its parameters, so the names can be found.

A method that hides one of its base class's (new in C#) is the one there is: JObject.Parse and JToken.Parse take the same arguments, and C# calls the first on a JObject.

A generic method is given its types from the arguments: Task.FromResult(7) is Task.FromResult<long>(7). A type that no argument says is object. Writing the types in the call, as C# can, is the rejected alternative of 29.4.

40.4 A Task is waited for

A method that takes time, such as one that reads the network, gives a Task, and C# writes await before the call. Zeno waits for it, and the call gives what the task gave: none for a plain Task.

Why not give the Task. Zeno has no await for a value of another language, and a Task that is not waited for does its work while the program goes on, or not at all if the program ends first. Every library of .NET that reads a file or the network has methods that end in Async, and each would need a second call to be of use.

40.5 Numbers go as long, and are made what the parameter is

Every whole number of Zeno arrives as a long, and becomes int, short, byte or an enum when the method takes one and it fits, as C# turns 5 into what it is given to. A float becomes a float or a decimal the same way. Every whole number that comes back and fits 64 bits is an int, and a decimal stays in .NET, since a float of Zeno would change it.

Why not Java's rule (29.5), Integer when it fits: that was for a collection that takes Object. A collection of .NET says its type (List<int>), and the number is made that type when it is given.

40.6 A package is found from the project beside the program

.NET has no folder that every package goes to, as pip and npm have, and NuGet installs a package only into a project. So the program uses the project beside it: dotnet new classlib and dotnet add package in its folder (or one above), and Zeno reads obj/project.assets.json, which dotnet writes and which names each .dll of each package, and of every package it needs, and where NuGet keeps it. A type is then found in them by its name, as in .NET's own.

Why not a name and a version in the program, as csharp.package("Humanizer.Core", "3.0.10"). The packages a package needs, and which of their versions, are worked out by NuGet, and the file that NuGet writes is the answer. Zeno would otherwise have to work them out as NuGet does. It also leaves the project as .NET has it: dotnet builds it, updates it and lists what it has, and the code of C# beside the program is built into it (csharp.assembly of its bin folder).

Why not install what is missing. No other module installs anything (26), and a program that fetches from the network when it is run is a program that does something it does not say.

40.7 The helper is built once with dotnet build, and kept

As Java's (29.9): the source is in the zeno file, the first run builds it in the folder for what can be made again, under a number worked out from the source, and later runs start what was built. .NET takes some seconds where javac takes one, so this matters more.

It is built for the .NET that builds it, read from dotnet --version, and it may run on a later one (RollForward). .NET cannot compile a single file as it starts, as Java 11 can, so where it cannot be built dotnet run is started instead, which says why: there is no SDK, only the runtime.

40.8 An exception of .NET is an error of Zeno

IOException and those under it, and UnauthorizedAccessException, are FileError; KeyNotFoundException is KeyError; IndexOutOfRangeException and ArgumentOutOfRangeException are IndexError; ArgumentException and FormatException are ValueError; DivideByZeroException is ZeroDivisionError; OverflowException is OverflowError. Every other is Error. The message begins with .NET's name for it, as Java's does (29.7).

Why more than Java's three. .NET has an exception of its own for each of these, where Java's ArithmeticException was two kinds. Each means in .NET what the kind means in Zeno, by .NET's own description.

40.9 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to .NET: an event, a Func<T>, the lambdas of LINQ.
