  • An extension method called with a dot on its object.
  • What a method puts back in an out or ref parameter.
  • csharp in a built program, and in --target cs, as 26.9 has it for Python.

41. f32: a float of 32 bits

let gain: f32 = 0.1
var total: f32 = 0.0
for i in range(10) {
    total += gain
}
print(gain, total)          # 0.1 1.0000001
let wide: float = total     # an f32 goes where a float is wanted

Most boards with a float unit (a Cortex-M4F, an M33, an ESP32) have one of 32 bits. A float of 64 bits is done there in software, many times slower, and a sensor's reading, a filter's coefficient or a PID gain never needed 16 digits. f32 is a float of 32 bits, as C's float, Rust's f32 and Java's float. It is the fifth item of missing.md. Walkthrough: f32.md.

41.1 The name is f32

f32, beside u8 and i32. A sized type in Zeno is named by what it holds and how many bits: u for a whole number without a sign, i with one, and now f for a float. Rust and Zig spell it the same. Turned down: float32, Go's, which is longer and breaks the pattern; single, C#'s and Pascal's, which says nothing to anyone who has not met it; and C's own float, which Zeno already uses for the 64-bit one.

41.2 A sum of f32s is an f32, and a sum with a float is refused

An f32 with an f32, or with an int, gives an f32. + - * / are done in 32 bits, and // % ** in 64 and rounded once to 32, which is the same answer to within the last bit and the same in every engine. An int beside an f32 is turned into a float and then into the nearest f32, so gain * 3 is an f32. A comparison compares the two f32s.

Why not "arithmetic gives an int" (2.8a)? A sized whole number is a way to store a number, and the danger is a sum that wraps; doing the sum in an int takes that danger away. An f32 is a way to compute: the point is that the board's float unit does the sum. Making every sum a float would put the sums back in software, which is the thing f32 is for avoiding.

An f32 with a float is refused before the program runs, with a message that says what to write:

error: `+` between f32 and float would have to choose between 32 bits and 64. Write `f32( )` around the float to work in 32, or `float( )` around the f32 to work in 64

Either answer is a guess. C picks 64 bits silently, so a single 1.5 in a filter written in floats turns the whole sum into software doubles, which is a classic slow bug on a microcontroller. Picking 32 bits silently would throw away digits the float had. The principle is "one meaning" (4), and here the program has to say which one.

A written float is not a float value, and adapts (41.4): gain + 1.5 is an f32 sum.

41.3 An f32 goes where a float is wanted

Every f32 is exactly a float, so nothing is lost, and asking for float( ) each time would be noise: an f32 is given to a function that takes a float, put in a float variable, or returned as one, and is widened on the way. This is the rule of sized whole numbers (2.8c), which go where an int is wanted.

A list[f32] is not a list[float], for the reason a list[u8] is not a list[int]: lists are shared, and whoever held it as a list[float] could put a float in it that is not an f32. The message says to copy it, [float(x) for x in readings].

41.4 A written float is rounded to the nearest f32

let gain: f32 = 0.1 needs nothing more. A number written in the program where an f32 is wanted, or beside an f32 in a sum or a comparison, is made the nearest f32 before the program runs. 0.1 has no exact f32, as it has no exact float, and the nearest one is what anyone writing 0.1 there means. Turned down: C's 0.1f, a mark on every number in a filter, which says nothing the type does not.

A written number too big for an f32 is an error before the program runs: let a: f32 = 1e39 says 1e39 does not fit in an f32, whose largest is about 3.4e38. A written number too small becomes the nearest f32, which may be a subnormal or 0, as in every language.

A float value is not rounded by itself. let a: f32 = x, with x a float, is refused, and the message says to write f32(x). Most floats are not f32s, so the rounding is a step the program should show.

41.5 f32(x) makes one

f32(x) takes an int, a float or an f32 and gives the nearest f32. A float too big for an f32 is an OverflowError, a try can catch, as a whole number too big for a u8 is a ValueError for u8(n); f32(inf) is inf and f32(nan) is NaN, which are f32s. An int is first made a float, as everywhere: f32(16777217) is 16777216.0. float(x) and int(x) take an f32.

41.6 math works in 64 bits

math.sqrt(gain) gives a float. The functions of math take a float, and an f32 goes in by 41.3. Each gives the same answer in every engine and target, because each language's 64-bit sqrt, sin and the rest agree, and not all of them have 32-bit ones. abs, min, max and sum keep an f32 an f32: they choose or add, and sum adds in 32 bits, one item at a time.

41.7 What a build writes

C writes float. A sum of two f32s is C's float sum, a field is four bytes, and -O2 uses the float unit's own instructions. Division by zero is a ZeroDivisionError, as for a float, except in a minimal build, which has no checks.

LLVM keeps an f32 in a double and rounds after each step. For + - * / this is the same answer bit for bit: a double has more than twice the bits of an f32 and two more, so rounding the exact double answer to 32 bits gives the answer a 32-bit unit gives. It kept the backend's slots and calls unchanged.

Every target language has a type for an f32 in its runtime and does the same rounding: Go's float32, Java's and Kotlin's Float, C#'s float, C++'s own tag, Rust's f32, and a small class with the value in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Ruby, PHP, Lua and Dart, which round with their own 32-bit tools (struct, Math.fround, pack, string.pack, Float32List). tools/targets/edge-f32.zeno holds them all to zeno run.

41.8 An f32 is printed with the fewest digits that read back as it

print(gain) shows 0.1, not 0.10000000149011612: the shortest number that, made an f32 again, is the same f32, then written as a float is. That is what Rust, Java and C# print for one. print(float(gain)) shows every digit of the float it is, for when that matters.

41.9 Left for later

  • json.write of an f32, and f32("0.5") from text.
  • A format such as {x:.2} with no f after it, for an f32.
  • math in 32 bits (sqrtf), when a program shows it is too slow.
  • pointer[f32] and a register that holds an f32.
  • An f32 field in LLVM takes eight bytes, where C takes four.
  • A generic function copied for T = f32 that changes a number written once in it rounds it for every copy.

42. u64: a whole number of 64 bits with no sign

function fnv(text: str) -> u64 raises OverflowError {
    var h: u64 = 0xcbf29ce484222325
    for c in text {
        h = h ^ u64(c.code())
        h = u64.wrap(h * 0x100000001b3)
    }
    return h
}
let hash = fnv("hello")
print(f"{hash:016x}")             # a430d84680aabd0b
print(u8.max, i16.min, u64.max)   # 255 -32768 18446744073709551615

A hash (FNV, CRC-64, xxHash), a random generator (xorshift, PCG), a counter of microseconds since boot, a 64-bit register, a file offset past 8 exabytes: each is a whole number of 64 bits with no sign, and Zeno's int has a sign. u64 is that number, as C's uint64_t, Rust's u64 and Go's uint64. With it come the limits of every whole type, u8.max to u64.max, which Rust spells u8::MAX. It is the sixth item of missing.md. Walkthrough: u64.md.

42.1 The name is u64, and there is no i64

u64, beside u8, u16 and u32. The pattern of 2.8 names a whole type by its sign and its bits. Rust and Zig spell it the same. Turned down: uint64 (Go), longer and outside the pattern, and ulong (C#), which says nothing of the size.

There is no i64. It would be a second name for int, which is already a signed number of 64 bits, and two names for one type is two meanings (4): a reader would ask how they differ. int.max and int.min are its limits.

42.2 A sum of u64s is a u64, checked

+ - * // % ** between two u64s give a u64, and a result past 18446744073709551615 or below 0 is an OverflowError, as an int sum past its end is (2.4):

the result is too big for a u64
the result is below 0, and a u64 never is

/ gives a float, as it does for ints. & | ^ ~ << >> work on the bits; a shift is 0 to 63, and << that pushes a 1 off the top is an OverflowError, as for an int.

Why not "arithmetic gives an int" (2.8a)? That rule makes u8 + u8 an int so that the sum cannot wrap. An int cannot hold half the numbers a u64 holds, so the sum would fail where the u64 did not. The answer stays a u64 and is checked instead.

Why checked, when C and Go wrap? For the reason ints are (2.4): a silent wrap is a wrong number that looks right. A program that wants the wrap says so with u64.wrap (42.6), and a reader sees it.

42.3 A u64 meets only a u64 or a written number

A u64 with an int value, a float, or any other type is refused before the program runs, with a message that says what to write:

error: `+` between u64 and int would have to choose between a u64 and an int. Write `u64( )` around the int to work in u64s, or `int( )` around the u64

Either guess can be wrong. Making it a u64 fails when the int is below 0; making it an int fails when the u64 is past int.max. C picks unsigned silently, so -1 < x is false for every unsigned x, one of its best known traps. The principle is "one meaning" (4), and here the program says which.

A written number adapts, as it does for f32 (41.4): h * 3, h == 0, h > 1000 and [h, 7, 8] need nothing more, and the list is a list[u64]. A written number below 0 beside a u64 is an error before the program runs (-1 does not fit in a u64).

A u8, u16 or u32 does not mix with a u64 by itself either, because their sums are ints (2.8a). u64(x) never fails for one, and the message says so.

42.4 Conversions say what they check

Write Gives Fails when
u64(n) a u64 n is below 0: OverflowError
int(x) an int x is past int.max: OverflowError
u8(int(x)) and the like that type it does not fit
float(x) the nearest float never
str(x) its digits never

A u64 does not go where an int is wanted by itself, though a u8 does (2.8c): every u8 is an int, and half of the u64s are not. The message names the conversion. A u64 does not go where a float is wanted either: a float holds 53 bits exactly, so most u64s past 2**53 would change, and the program should show the step.

42.5 A written number past int.max is a u64

let x: u64 = 18446744073709551615 is written as it reads. The lexer reads a whole number up to the largest u64, and the checker accepts one past int.max only where a u64 is wanted:

error: 18446744073709551615 is too big for an int (-9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807). Only a u64 holds it: write it where a u64 is wanted, as in `let x: u64 = 18446744073709551615`

A number past the largest u64 says so, in decimal or hex: this number is too big. The largest whole number Zeno holds is 18446744073709551615, the largest u64. This replaces the lexer's old "number is too large", which said nothing of where the end is. Turned down: a mark such as Rust's 5u64 or C's 5ULL, a mark on each number that says nothing the type does not.

42.6 u64.wrap keeps the low 64 bits

u64.wrap(h * 0x100000001b3) is the multiplication cut to 64 bits, which is what a hash or a random generator means; u64.wrap(a + b), u64.wrap(a - b) and u64.wrap(a << n) are the same for those operators. u64.wrap(n) of an int keeps its 64 bits read with no sign: u64.wrap(-1) is u64.max. This is the rule of u8.wrap (2.8b), the same word for the same idea, and Rust's wrapping_mul.

Why a wrapper around the sum, and not a function wrapping_mul(a, b)? The sum reads as a sum, and the one word at the front says everything inside wraps. Turned down: Go's and C's silent wrap (42.2), and a separate type that always wraps (Rust's Wrapping<u64>), which hides the wrap at each use.

42.7 Every whole type has .max and .min

u8.max, u8.min, i8.max ... u32.max, int.max, int.min, u64.max and u64.min. Each is the number of its type: u8.max is a u8 of 255, and u8.max + 1 is the int 256 by 2.8a. Before this, a program wrote 255 or 2147483647 by hand, and a digit wrong in one is hard to see. Rust spells it u8::MAX; Zeno already reads . as "of", and max and min are the words Zeno uses for the larger and smaller (max(a, b)). Turned down: C's UINT8_MAX, a name in capitals for each type, and Java's Integer.MAX_VALUE.

The floats have no .max yet (42.10).

42.8 What a build writes

C writes uint64_t. + - * are checked with the compiler's __builtin_add_overflow and its two friends, which are one instruction and a branch. --release, --fast and --minimal drop the checks and wrap, as they do for ints, so the C there is C's own +. --firmware carries the OverflowError as a value, as for every error.

LLVM keeps a u64 in an i64, which has no sign of its own, and uses the unsigned instructions: udiv, urem, icmp ult, lshr, uitofp. The checks call the same runtime functions as C.

Every target language has a u64 in its runtime: Go's uint64, Rust's u64, C#'s ulong, Kotlin's ULong, C++'s own tag over uint64_t; Java's long with its unsigned methods (Long.compareUnsigned, Math.unsignedMultiplyHigh); a small class over a big whole number in Python, Ruby, JavaScript, TypeScript (a BigInt) and Dart (a BigInt); and a class over the 64 bits in PHP and Lua, which have only signed ints and do the unsigned steps by hand (Lua's math.ult, PHP's sums in pieces of 32 and 16 bits). tools/targets/ edge-u64.zeno holds them all to zeno run.

42.9 A u64 prints its digits, and x its bits

print(h) shows the decimal digits, all twenty of 18446744073709551615 when it is the largest. {h:x}, {h:X} and {h:b} show the bits with no sign, so {u64.wrap(-1):x} is ffffffffffffffff; {h:016x} pads with zeros, as a hash is shown. {h:d}, a width, < > ^ and {h:.2f} work as for an int.

42.10 Left for later

  • A u64 as a key of a dict, in range( ), or as an index. Each is refused before the program runs today; int( ) makes one an int.
  • pointer[u64] and a register of 64 bits.
  • json.write of a u64 (a ValueError today), and u64("123").
  • A u8, u16 or u32 going where a u64 is wanted by itself. Each fits, so this is safe; it needs the sized types' sums to have a type first.
  • float.max, float.min and f32.max.
  • u8(x) and u8.wrap(x) straight from a u64, without int( ) between.
  • A u64 field in a firmware struct is 8 bytes in C; packed layouts of registers are item 9 of missing.md.

42.11 The new numbers cost the old ones nothing

f32 and u64 each brought a test to the top of every a + b, and arms for none, u64 and the pins to the test of a == b. Counted by bench/run.py --count, a program of strings ran 0.85% more instructions in the VM than in 0.5.2 and one of trees 0.54% more, though neither has an f32 or a u64 in it. Two causes, both found with callgrind and not guessed from timings:

  • value::equal grew too big for the compiler to copy into each operator, so every == became a call. It is now two parts: the common pairs (int, string, bool, none) in a small part that is copied in, and every other pair in a second part that is called. The answers are the same for every pair.
  • The two tests for f32 and u64 asked four questions of every operator. They are now one question per side (f32 and u64 sit next to each other in Value, so "is it either" is one comparison), and the work for them lives in its own function, narrow_binary.

After both, against 0.5.2, the VM ran fib, loop and sort to the same count within 0.03%, strings 0.07% fewer, trees 0.08% more and nbody 0.13% more.

The interpreter (zeno run with no --vm) showed the same thing a third time: fib ran 0.8% more instructions, every one of them in ops::binary, which had grown. The VM had long answered two ints and two floats itself before calling it. That short part is now ops::fast_binary, ops::binary tries it first for whoever calls, and the long part is binary_rest. The interpreter's fib went from 12,888 million instructions to 12,499 million, 2.2% fewer than in 0.5.2, and the VM's counts did not move. The rule stays that a feature a program does not use costs that program nothing (decision 34.5 is the same lesson for program.exit).

43. Units made of units: V * A is W

let supply = 3.3 V
let draw = 20 mA
let power = supply * draw
print(power, power.mW)          # 0.066 W 66 mW
print(supply / draw)            # 165 ohm
print(1 / 2 ms)                 # 500 Hz
print((5 W * 2 h).Wh)           # 10 Wh

Units are what Zeno has that C does not (1.15), and until now they stopped at the sums a firmware program does every day: the power a board draws, the resistor for a current, the energy a battery gives, the frequency of a period. A program took the numbers out, multiplied, and put a unit back by hand, which is the very slip units exist to catch. It is the seventh item of missing.md. Walkthrough: units-made.md.

43.1 A closed list of what units make

Zeno makes a unit from two others only when the pair is on a list:

Write Gives
voltage * current, either way round power
current * resistance, either way round voltage
power * time, either way round energy
power / voltage, power / current current, voltage
voltage / current, voltage / resistance resistance, current
energy / time, energy / power power, time
a number / time, a number / frequency frequency, time
time * frequency, either way round a plain number

These are Ohm's law, power and energy, and periods, which are nearly all the sums with units in a firmware program. Any other pair is refused before the program runs, and the message lists these.

Why a list, and not an algebra of dimensions? An algebra (F#, the uom crate of Rust, Boost.Units) makes m * m a unit of its own, and V * s / m too, and then needs a name for each answer or shows it as kg*m^2*s^-3. That is a feature the size of the rest of the units, and most of what it makes has no name a firmware engineer would use. A list keeps 1.15's rule that every unit has a name on the list, so a typing slip is still an error, and it says in one table what works. A pair can be added to the list later without changing any program that works now. Turned down: making a unit for a pair that is not on the list, because a V * V in a program is far more often a slip than a sum.

43.2 The answer is in the unit with no prefix

3.3 V * 20 mA is 0.066 W, and .mW makes it 66 mW. Each side is first put in the unit of its kind with no prefix (V, A, ohm, W, J, s, Hz), the numbers are multiplied or divided, and the answer is in that unit of its own kind.

Why not the "finer unit" of 1.15? "Finer" compares two units of one kind, and here the answer is a third kind. A rule from the prefixes (mV * mA is uW) would need units that are not on the list, and two programs that work out the same power would print it in two units. One rule, the same every time, is "no prefix"; .mW says the rest, as .ms does for time.

J is the energy with no prefix. A program that wants watt-hours writes .Wh, as it writes .ms.

43.3 Time times frequency is a plain number

10 ms * 1 kHz is 10.0, the number of cycles, as 1 s / 1 ms is 1000.0 by 1.15. A count of cycles has no unit on the list, and a float is what it is.

43.4 A number over a time is a frequency

1 / 2 ms is 500 Hz, and 1 / 1 kHz is 0.001 s. Only time and frequency turn over: 1 / 2 V has no unit on the list and is refused. A unit binds to its number, so 1 / 2 ms needs no brackets.

43.5 Every engine and build, the same digits

The interpreter, the VM, C, LLVM and all fifteen target languages scale each side the same way, x * times / over with the same numbers, and then multiply or divide once, so they print the same digits. In C and LLVM the scales are known when the program is built, and a sum is one or two instructions; a quantity is still a double with its unit known only to the compiler. Division by zero is a ZeroDivisionError, except where a build has no checks.

43.6 Left for later

  • More pairs: charge (mAh, for battery life), speed (m / s), rpm and Hz.
  • A unit a program names itself.
  • sum of quantities, which still wants + in a loop (1.15).

44. The libraries of C, Go and Rust

The third version of using other languages' libraries (26.1): import c, for a library of C, and for a library of Go or Rust built with the C interface each of them has. c.md is the walkthrough. Chapter 26 holds here too: nothing changes for a program that does not ask, the helper runs beside Zeno and not inside it, and what can be refused is refused with a message that says what to do. What follows is what C made different.

44.1 The module is c, and it has one function

c.library(library, declarations). Every other language could be asked what a thing is: Python has dir, Java has reflection. C cannot. A library of C knows the names of its functions and nothing of what they take or give, and that is only in the header. So the program says it, and the words it says it in are the ones it would copy from the header: "double cbrt(double x);". That is one thing to learn for a person who knows C, and nothing new to learn for the library.

Why not read the header itself. A header is written for the C preprocessor: macros, #ifdefs for each system, other headers it includes. Reading it right is the work of a C compiler, and the whole of <stdio.h> is hundreds of declarations a program does not use. The program declares the few it calls, and may still #include the header, so that the compiler checks that the two agree (44.3).

Why c and not native or ffi. The module is named for the language its libraries are written in, as python and csharp are (40.1). Go and Rust come through it because what they give C is a library of C (44.6).

44.2 The library is named as the compiler would be told it

One text or a list: a bare name is -l ("z" is -lz), a name with / or the ending of a file (.c, .so, .a, .o, .dylib, .dll) is a file, found from the program's folder, and a word that starts with - goes to the compiler as it is. none is the C library every program has. A person who has built with the library in C already knows what to write.

Why a .c file may be given. A board's firmware has C already (a checksum, a protocol), and testing it from a Zeno program on the computer, with no board, is the first thing a firmware engineer will want. Building it with the rest costs nothing more.

44.3 The C compiler works out the types

Zeno writes a small file of C with a function for each declaration, which takes the arguments from a table and calls the real one, and builds it with the library. What a type is (a whole number with a sign or without, how many bytes, a float, a pointer) is worked out from that file by the compiler, with _Generic, so that uLong, size_t and time_t are known on this machine exactly as C knows them, and a declaration that disagrees with an included header is the compiler's error.

Why not libffi. It does the same at run time, but it is one more thing to have installed, and it believes the declaration without a header to check it against. A C compiler is there already wherever zeno build is used.

It is built once. The result is kept in Zeno's cache, under a number made from the declarations, the files given and when they last changed. The first run takes about half a second; the next is immediate.

44.4 The library is loaded by a helper in C

As for every other language, the library runs in a helper beside the program (bridge.c, built once and kept), spoken to over the same lines (26.3). A fault in C (a pointer that is wrong, memory that is not there) stops the helper, and Zeno stops the program with an error at the line that called it, instead of crashing with no word of where.

What it costs. A call goes to the helper and back: under a tenth of a millisecond, which is nothing for a checksum of a frame and too much for a call in a loop of a million. The calls with no cost are the ones zeno build makes (44.8).

44.5 Values go across as C would take them

  • A number is checked to fit the type the function takes, and is an OverflowError if it does not, as u8(300) is. A uint64_t above the top of int comes back as u64 (42).
  • A str given for a char * (or any pointer to bytes) is copied with the \0 C expects. A char * given back is copied into a str, or a list of bytes if it is not UTF-8.
  • A list given for a pointer is lent: copied into memory of the type it points to, and copied back into the list afterwards, unless the pointer is to const. That is how a buffer is filled.
  • Any other pointer given back is kept as it is: given back to C, compared with ==, printed. Zeno never looks inside it and never frees it: a library that hands out memory has a function to free it, which the program calls, as it would in C. NULL is none.

Why lend a copy, and not the list's own memory. A list of Zeno is not laid out as an array of C is (its items are values, which may be of any size), and a list may change length while C holds it. A copy for the length of a call is the one that cannot go wrong.

44.6 Go and Rust come in through C

A library of Go built with -buildmode=c-shared or c-archive, or of Rust built as a cdylib or staticlib with extern "C" functions, is a library of C, and c.library takes it. There is no import go or import rust: neither has a way to load a library and ask it for its functions at run time, as Python or Java do, and both of them build the C interface well. Building it is done by their own tools (go build, cargo), which a person who writes Go or Rust already uses.

44.7 What is refused, and why

  • A function that takes ..., such as printf: the types of what it takes are not in its declaration. The message says to declare it with the types the program gives, or to write a function of C that calls it.
  • A function given as an argument (a callback): a function of Zeno lives in Zeno, and C would call it from inside the helper. It can come later (44.9).
  • A struct given or given back whole, not through a pointer: its fields would need a type of Zeno for each struct. A pointer to one is fine, and is kept as any other pointer is.

44.8 Nothing changes for a program that does not ask

import c itself starts nothing; the first c.library builds and starts the helper. Every function that does it is out of the way of the rest of Zeno (#[cold], never inlined), so that the speed of a program without it does not move.

The one thing that does change, as in 26.11: c is now the name of a module that comes with Zeno. A file of the program called c.zeno can no longer be imported as import c, and a package cannot be called c. One test had three files called a, b and c importing each other; it now calls the third one d, and that, with the message that lists the modules, is the only line of the tests from before that changed.

--target refuses import c with a message, as it refuses import python. zeno build takes it (44.10).

44.9 Left for later

  • A function of Zeno given to C as a callback.
  • Structs by value, with a class of Zeno for each.
  • The address of a variable (&huart2), which for now a function of C gives.
  • Reading the declarations from a header, for a library with many functions.
  • zeno build --llvm, which writes LLVM and not C.

44.10 zeno build calls C as C does

Partha asked for it next, for a vendor's HAL on a board, and it is the place where import c costs nothing: the C that zeno build writes calls the declared function by its name, with no helper and nothing in between, and the C compiler links the library in. Every build does it: --firmware, --no-collector, --owned and --minimal.

What made it possible: the checker knows the declarations. When the library and the declarations are written out as texts in c.library(...) (nearly always), the checker reads them, as zeno run does, and gives each function a type: int for a whole number of C, u64 for uint64_t, float, bool, str or none for a char * given back, and a new type, a C pointer to thing, or none, for any other pointer given back. So a wrong argument is found before the program runs, in zeno run too, and the C build knows what to write. A declaration worked out while the program runs still works with zeno run, unchecked, and zeno build asks for it written out.

Why a name only a header gives is a whole number. Zeno does not read headers (44.1), so it cannot know what uLong or HAL_StatusTypeDef is. Nearly every such name passed by value is a whole number or an enum; a few are floats, and those few have names headers share (float32_t). The C compiler sees the real type and says so if the two disagree, and a pointer to such a name is kept as a pointer, whatever it points to. Turned down: asking the C compiler first, as zeno run's stubs do. The checker would then need a compiler, and for a board, the board's compiler and its headers, just to say whether a program is right.

The same answers as zeno run. A number is checked to fit the type the function takes, with the same message; a list is lent, copied in and back; text given back is copied. A test holds every build to what zeno run prints (emit_c::tests). Two differences, both of C: a list[u8] given for bytes is handed over where it is, with no copy, which a program cannot tell apart from the copy and back; and text that is not UTF-8 is printed as the bytes it is, where zeno run shows \u{fffd}. tools/minimal.py, which holds --minimal to what the checked build does, builds the libraries in as zeno build does.

A file of C may not be the build's own C. zeno build modbus.zeno writes modbus.c, and the example's checksum was in modbus.c too: the first build would have written over it. The build now refuses, and says which file, and the example's file is crc.c.

44.11 A declaration with no ( is a value

A HAL is used through its constants as much as its functions: GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_5, GPIO_PIN_SET, HAL_OK. They are macros or constants of an enum, which no library holds as a symbol, so they cannot be looked up as a function is. "uint16_t GPIO_PIN_5;" says there is a value of that name and type, and hal.GPIO_PIN_5 reads it by its name, as C would: in zeno run, in the stubs, which are compiled with the header; in zeno build, where it is written.

Not declared again. C cannot declare a macro (uint16_t GPIO_PIN_5; would become uint16_t ((uint16_t)0x0020);), so a value is only read, and the header declares it. A variable of the library's own file of C, with no header, is written extern, as C writes it, and is declared as it is written.

44.12 No import cpp

C++ was the one big language left. It is skipped, for now and on purpose:

  • Firmware libraries are C. The HAL of every chip vendor, CMSIS, FreeRTOS, lwIP, FatFs: all C. What firmware needs is in 44.10.
  • The C++ interface is not one thing. Names are mangled differently by each compiler, classes and templates have no form a program outside C++ can call, and a library built by one compiler cannot always be called by another. Every language that uses C++ libraries (Python, Rust, Go) mostly does it through a layer of C.
  • That layer already works here. A library of C++ with extern "C" functions is a library of C, and c.library takes it, as it takes Go and Rust (44.6).

44.13 A missing function is said the same way on every system

A declared function the library does not have is found on Linux when the stubs are loaded, and the helper says "the library m has no name, which was declared". The linkers of Windows and macOS find it earlier, when the stubs are built, and what they say names a temporary file that is different each time. Their lines ("undefined reference to", "undefined symbol:", "_name", referenced from:) are read, and when the name is one the program declared, the error is the one Linux gives. Any other complaint of a linker is still shown as it was said.

45. Inputs: a pin the program reads

from board import input_pin, pull_up, led

let button = input_pin(2, pull_up)    # pressed joins pin 2 to ground
if button.is_low() {
    led.on()
}
print(button, button.is_high())       # InputPin(2) true

Until now a pin could only be driven: is_on() read back what the program had written, and 3.15b kept inputs off the list for 0.1 because they want a real board. A board that cannot read a button is not much of a board, and it is the first half of item 7 of missing.md. Walkthrough: inputs.md.

45.1 An input is a type of its own

input_pin(2) gives an InputPin, and pin(2) still gives a Pin. An InputPin has is_high(), is_low() and number. It has no on, off or toggle, and a Pin has no is_high; each is an error before the program runs that names what to write instead. Underneath, an input pin is its number, as a pin is (3.15), and costs what an int costs.

Why two types? An output is driven and an input is read, and on the hardware a pin is one or the other at a time. Rust's embedded-hal splits them the same way, into OutputPin and InputPin. Driving a button's pin is a short circuit waiting to happen, and the checker can see it. Turned down: a mode set while the program runs, as Arduino's pinMode(2, INPUT). The mode then lives in the board and not in the program, and on() of an input is found on the bench.

45.2 It is read with is_high and is_low

An input says is_high() and is_low(), and not is_on(). A button usually joins its pin to ground, with a pull-up holding the pin high the rest of the time, so a pressed button reads low. "On" would then mean the opposite of "pressed", or of "high", depending on who reads it. High and low are what the data sheet and the scope say, and they mean one thing. Both are given so that a test reads as it is meant: if button.is_low(), and not if not button.is_high().

is_on() of a Pin stays as it is. For an output, "on" is what the program drove it to, and nothing that works today changes.

45.3 The pull is said where the pin is made

input_pin(2, pull_up), input_pin(2, pull_down), or input_pin(2) with nothing pulling it. pull_up and pull_down are values of the board module, of the type Pull, as led is a value of the type Pin. They are imported like anything else (from board import pull_up, or board.pull_up), a function can take a Pull and pass it on, and one prints as its name.

Why there? The pull is set in the same register write that makes the pin an input, and the schematic decides it once: a button with no resistor of its own needs the pull-up, for as long as the board is on. Turned down:

  • A word of the call that is not a value, as register(u8, ...) takes a type. A program's own variable called pull_up would then mean one thing in the call and another outside it.
  • A str, input_pin(2, "up"). A typing slip would be found when the program runs, if at all.
  • A bool, input_pin(2, pull_up=true). Two of them would let a program ask for both pulls at once.
  • An enum with the cases up and down. An enum's cases are names of their own in Zeno (Ack, not Reply.Ack), so it would take two common words from every program that imports it.

A Pull is the str of its name underneath, so printing one, comparing two and keeping them in a list work as they do for any str. The checker keeps a Pull and a str apart.

45.4 A fifth function in the board layer

A compiled program that makes an input pin calls zeno_board_input(pin, pull), with 0 for nothing, 1 for a pull-up and 2 for a pull-down, and reads the pin with zeno_board_read, as is_on already does. With ST's HAL it is one HAL_GPIO_Init.

Only such a program calls it. The part of the runtime that does is marked #ifdef ZENO_INPUT_PINS, and the build keeps it only when the program makes an input pin. So a board header written for the four functions (5.12) still builds every program that reads no pin, and the C of such a program is what it was before, line for line. A program that does read one, built over such a header, gets the C compiler's message naming zeno_board_input, which is the function to write. Turned down: asking every header for the fifth function, which would break every header there is for a feature most of their programs do not use.

45.5 On a computer nothing presses the button

On the simulated board a pull-up reads high, a pull-down low, and a pin nothing pulls keeps the level it had (they all start low, as before). That is what a pin with nothing wired to it does, near enough. Making an input prints nothing. The lines the simulated board prints are what the program drives, as a logic analyser on an output shows it; a pull is weak, and is not driven.

So under zeno run a button is never pressed. A board of one's own (5.12b) can press it: the test a_button_is_pressed_on_a_board_of_its_own builds examples/doorbell.zeno over a header whose button is down for three reads, and the bell rings once. That is how firmware is tested on a desk. Turned down for now: pressing a button under zeno run, from a file of times and levels. It is worth having, and wants its own design: what the file looks like, and whether the clock moves by itself while a program waits for a press.

45.6 Nothing changes for a program that reads no pin

led, pin, register, Pin and every line the simulated board prints are as they were, and so is the C of every program that makes no input pin. board gains input_pin, pull_up and pull_down, and Zeno gains the type names InputPin and Pull; a program's own class of either name comes first, as one called Pin does (3.15). --target builds still refuse the board module.

45.7 Left for later

  • Pressing a button under zeno run (45.5).
  • Waiting for an edge, and an interrupt when one comes: item 7 of missing.md, with the rule for a variable an interrupt shares.
  • Debouncing in the library: a press read twice, some milliseconds apart.
  • button as a value of the board, as led is, for boards that have one.
  • An InputPin as a key of a dict, which a Pin cannot be either.
  • Running it on a real board. The STM32 sketch in board.md gains its fifth function, and like the other four it has not been tried on hardware.

46. A serial port

from board import serial

let port = serial(1, 115200 baud)
port.write("ready\n")
let byte = port.read_byte()           # u8 or none
if port.has_byte() {
    port.write_bytes([0x06])
}

A serial port is how a board talks: to a terminal on a desk, to a GPS module, a modem, another board. It is the second part of item 7 of missing.md, after inputs (45), and the one that list put first among the rest. Walkthrough: serial.md.

46.1 A port is a type of its own, and a number underneath

serial(1, 115200 baud) gives a Serial, which has write, write_bytes, read_byte, has_byte and number, and prints as Serial(1). As a pin is (3.15), a port is a kind of its own to the checker and its number in the built program, so it costs what an int costs, and a list of ports, a port in a field and a function that takes one all work. A port the board does not have is a ValueError, as a pin is: the simulated board has ports 0 to 3.

46.2 The speed has a unit: baud

serial(1, 9600) is refused: the message says to write 9600 baud. Two bare numbers side by side do not say which is the port and which the speed, which is the reason sleep(500) is refused (3.15a). baud joins the list of units (1.15) as the one unit of a kind of its own, so a speed in Hz is refused too. A speed of 0 or below is a ValueError.

Why not Bd, or kBd? Data sheets write "115200 baud", and the speeds a port is set to are written out in full, so one unit with no prefixes is enough. Left for later: 1 / 9600 baud, the time of one bit, which would join the list of units made of units (43.1).

46.3 Text and bytes are sent by two methods

port.write(text) sends the bytes of the text's UTF-8, and nothing else: no line end is added. port.write_bytes(bytes) sends a list[u8] as it is. A port only looks at the list, so in a build where a list has one owner it is lent for the call.

Why two? It is how files.write and files.write_bytes already are (36.1), so neither is a guess, and the checker can say which one was meant. Turned down: one write that takes either, which would need a rule for a list written in place ([1, 2] is a list[int] until something says otherwise). Turned down: adding a line end, as print does. A protocol decides its own line ends (\r\n for a modem), and a port that added one would be wrong for half of them.

46.4 read_byte waits; has_byte does not

port.read_byte() gives the next byte, waiting for it, as a u8 or none. It is none only when no byte can come any more. port.has_byte() says whether a byte has come that has not been read, without waiting. A console, a modem or a protocol reads in order and can wait, and is shortest written with read_byte; a loop that also blinks a light asks has_byte first. These are Arduino's Serial.read() and Serial.available(), and MicroPython's uart.read(1) and uart.any().

Why none and not a byte that never comes? On a board no more bytes is never, so a firmware program can treat none as the end. On a computer it is the end of what was typed (Ctrl-D, or the end of a file piped in), and a program that reads lines stops there, as one that reads input() does (23). Turned down: read_byte giving none for "nothing yet", which would make every reader a loop with a wait in it, and a reader on a computer spin for ever once the input ended.

Left for later: read_line, a timeout, and reading many bytes at once. A line is a few lines of Zeno over read_byte (examples/console.zeno), and the library written in Zeno (33) is where it can go once a board has been tried.

46.5 Four more functions in the board layer, for a program with a port

#define ZENO_SERIALS 4                                       /* how many ports */
void zeno_board_serial_open(int port, double baud);          /* set its speed */
void zeno_board_serial_write(int port, const uint8_t *bytes, size_t count);
bool zeno_board_serial_ready(int port);                      /* no waiting */
int  zeno_board_serial_read(int port);                       /* waits; -1: no more */

Only a program that makes a port calls them, by the rule of 45.4: the part of the runtime that does is marked #ifdef ZENO_SERIAL_PORTS and kept only for such a program. A board header written with four functions, or five, still builds every program with no port, and the C of every such program is what it was. Writing takes a buffer and a count and not a byte at a time, because a board's driver (ST's HAL_UART_Transmit, a DMA) sends a buffer.

46.6 On a computer every port is the terminal

What a port sends is written out as it is, with no line of its own, and what it reads is what is typed, a byte at a time. That is a serial monitor: the window where a firmware engineer reads what a board says and types back. The end of what was typed is the end of the port: read_byte gives none and has_byte is false. A terminal hands over a line at a time, so on a computer has_byte waits for the next line, where on a board it never waits.

Turned down: a line for each write, as the pins have (pin 7 on). A pin's level is an event a logic analyser shows; the bytes of a port are text, and a line around every write("hel") would cut a sentence in pieces. Every port of the simulated board is the one terminal, so a program with two ports sees both there; a board of one's own (5.12b) keeps them apart, and is how the tests wire a port back to itself.

46.7 Left for later

  • read_line, a timeout, and reading many bytes at once (46.4).
  • 1 / 9600 baud as the time of one bit (46.2).
  • Parity, stop bits, flow control. The board header sets them; 8N1 is what nearly every port is.
  • A byte arriving by interrupt, with the rule of item 7 for what an interrupt may share.
  • Running it on a real board, with ST's HAL underneath, as in serial.md. Like the rest of the board layer it is a sketch until then.

47. Reading a voltage: an analog pin

from board import analog_pin

let sensor = analog_pin(0)
let level = sensor.voltage()          # 1.65 V
if level < 1200 mV {
    print("low")
}
print(sensor.count(), "of", sensor.max_count)    # 2048 of 4095

A thermistor, a potentiometer, a battery through a divider, a current through a shunt: most of what a board measures arrives as a voltage on a pin, read by its analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). It is the third part of item 7 of missing.md, after inputs (45) and the serial port (46). Walkthrough: analog.md.

47.1 An analog pin is a type of its own

analog_pin(0) gives an AnalogPin, which has voltage(), count(), max_count and number, and prints as AnalogPin(0). It is the pin's number underneath, as every pin is (3.15). It has no on and no is_high: those belong to a Pin and an InputPin, and the message says which to make. Three types for three things a pin can be is the rule of 45.1 carried on: the checker knows which a pin is.

47.2 voltage() is in volts, and count() is the converter's own number

sensor.voltage() gives a quantity in V. Units are what Zeno has that C does not (1.15), and this is where a firmware program meets its first real one. level < 1200 mV, level * 20 mA (a power, 43) and level.mV all work, and level < 1200 is refused.

sensor.count() gives the number the converter counted, an int, and sensor.max_count the count that stands for the whole reference (4095 for 12 bits). A program that wants a share, as for a potentiometer, writes sensor.count() / sensor.max_count, and one that does its own sums on counts, as C code does, can.

Why both? A voltage is what the reading means, and a count is what was measured; a lookup table for a thermistor is indexed by count, and a battery is compared in volts. Turned down:

  • A bare count only, as Arduino's analogRead. 512 means nothing until one knows the bits and the reference, and those are the board's, not the program's.
  • A float from 0 to 1 only, as Mbed's AnalogIn.read(). It has no unit to check, and the program multiplies by the reference by hand, which is the slip units are for.
  • read(), which does not say what comes back.

The voltage is the count's share of the largest count, times the reference, worked out in that order by every engine and build, so the whole scale is the reference exactly and they print the same digits.

47.3 The board says its bits and its reference, and has two functions

#define ZENO_ANALOG_BITS 12           /* the converter counts 0 to 4095 */
#define ZENO_ANALOG_REFERENCE 3.3     /* the volts its largest count stands for */
bool zeno_board_analog(int pin);      /* make the pin one the converter reads; false if it cannot be */
int  zeno_board_analog_read(int pin); /* what it counts on the pin now */

Only a program that makes an analog pin calls them, by the rule of 45.4 (#ifdef ZENO_ANALOG_PINS), so a header without them still builds every other program. A pin the converter cannot read is a ValueError ("pin 7 of this board cannot read a voltage"): on most chips only some pins reach the converter, and the board is what knows which.

47.4 On a computer nothing is wired

On the simulated board a pin that is high reads the whole reference (3.3 V, a count of 4095) and one that is low reads 0 V. Every pin can be read, the converter has 12 bits, and making an analog pin prints nothing, as making an input prints nothing (45.5). It is what a voltmeter on the pin would show: a pin the program drove high, or one a pull-up holds, is at the supply. A board of one's own (5.12b) feeds real readings: the test a_voltage_is_read_on_a_board_of_its_own has a 10-bit converter against 5 V that reads a ramp.

47.5 Left for later

  • Feeding a voltage to a pin under zeno run, with pressing a button (45.5): one design for both.
  • Averaging, a sample time, and choosing the reference. The board header sets them.
  • Reading several pins in one sweep, and a reading by interrupt.
  • A voltage written out: a DAC, and PWM, which is next.
  • A temperature from a thermistor, in the library written in Zeno.

48. A PWM signal: a pin switched on for a share of the time

from board import pwm_pin

let lamp = pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz)
lamp.duty(0.25)               # on for a quarter of each millisecond

let servo = pwm_pin(10, 50 Hz)
servo.pulse(1500 us)          # on for 1.5 ms of each 20 ms

A pin is only ever high or low. Switched fast by a timer of the chip, it dims a lamp, sets the speed of a motor and tells a servo its angle, with no work from the program between two changes. It is the fourth part of item 7 of missing.md, after inputs (45), the serial port (46) and reading a voltage (47). Walkthrough: pwm.md.

48.1 A PWM pin is a type of its own, made with its frequency

pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz) gives a PwmPin, which has duty(share), pulse(time) and number, and prints as PwmPin(9). It is the pin's number underneath (3.15). It has no on and no off: a Pin has those, and the message says that all the time on is duty(1.0). It is the fourth thing a pin can be, by the rule of 45.1.

The frequency is given when the pin is made, and it has a unit. pwm_pin(9, 1000) is refused: "the frequency of a PWM pin has a unit, as in pwm_pin(9, 1 kHz)". A frequency worked out from a period, 1 / 20 ms, is one too (43). Why when it is made? The frequency belongs to the wiring: a servo wants 50 Hz and a lamp wants more than the eye sees, and neither changes while the program runs. A timer is set up once with it. Turned down: a frequency with a default, as Arduino's analogWrite has (490 Hz on some pins and 980 Hz on others, which nobody remembers), and a frequency set by a method after the pin is made, which leaves a pin with no frequency in between.

A new pin is off all the time, as a new Pin is low. A frequency of 0 Hz or less is a ValueError.

One pin has one signal. Making a second PwmPin for a pin that has one starts the signal again, off, at the new frequency, and both values then drive it, as two pin(9) drive one pin.

48.2 duty takes the share of the time on, from 0.0 to 1.0

lamp.duty(0.25) is on for a quarter of the time. A float, since a share is a number with no unit, and 0.0 to 1.0 since that is what a share is. Outside that range is a ValueError that says the range and gives an example. Turned down:

  • A count from 0 to 255, as analogWrite(pin, 64). The 255 is one timer's width and means nothing on another, and 64 does not say "a quarter" to anyone reading.
  • A percentage, 0 to 100. Zeno has no % unit, and duty(25) beside duty(0.25) would be the ambiguity the language is built to keep out. A program that thinks in percent writes duty(25 / 100).
  • Clamping a share above 1.0 to 1.0. A wrong sum would then run a motor at full power in silence.

The name is the word on the data sheet: the duty cycle.

48.3 pulse takes the time on in each period

servo.pulse(1500 us) is on for that long in each period. A servo and an electronic speed controller are told a time, not a share: 1 ms to 2 ms, whatever the period. Without pulse the program would write duty(1500 us * 50 Hz), and must then know the frequency in two places. The time has a unit, and a bare number is refused. A time below zero or longer than one period is a ValueError that says how long the period is.

pulse(t) is duty(t * frequency) and nothing more. The two are two ways to say one thing, and each is the plain way for one kind of device.

48.4 One function in the board layer

bool zeno_board_pwm(int pin, double hertz, double duty);

It starts or changes the signal on a pin, and answers false if the pin cannot make one. On most chips only the pins a timer reaches can, and the board is what knows which, so making such a pin is a ValueError: "pin 7 of this board cannot make a PWM signal". Making a pin calls it with a duty of 0, and duty and pulse call it with the same frequency and the new share. The runtime keeps each pin's frequency and checks every range, so the board sees a pin it has, a frequency above 0 and a duty from 0 to 1.

One function, not three (open, set, close): every call carries the whole signal, so a board has nothing to remember, and one that must set up its timer can do it when the frequency changes. Only a program that makes a PWM pin calls it (#ifdef ZENO_PWM_PINS), by the rule of 45.4.

48.5 On a computer each change is printed

The simulated board prints a line when a signal changes: pin 9 pwm 0.25 at 1000 Hz, and led pwm 0.5 at 2500 Hz for the LED's pin. It is the line pin 9 on (5.12a) for a pin that is partly on. Setting the duty a pin already has prints nothing, as turning on a pin that is on prints nothing, and so making a pin that has no signal yet prints nothing. A pin that was on is turned off first, with its own line, since a timer takes the pin over. Every pin can make a signal there. Reading such a pin, with is_on(), says off: the simulated board has no time in which the pin would be high.

48.6 Left for later

  • Reading back the duty and the frequency of a pin.
  • Changing the frequency of a pin that is made (a buzzer playing a tune), which today is a second pwm_pin.
  • The timer's resolution: a board with an 8-bit timer rounds 0.001 to nothing, and the program is not told.
  • Two pins of one timer that must share a frequency, complementary outputs and dead time for a motor bridge.
  • A voltage from a real DAC, and a tone.
  • A trial on a real board. The board function is written for the simulated board and for test boards only.

49. A ticker: a steady beat the program keeps time by

from board import ticker

let beat = ticker(10 ms)
while true {
    let came = beat.wait()        # until the next tick: 1 when on time
    step()
}

A loop that ends with sleep(10 ms) takes 10 ms and the time its work took, so it runs slow, by a different amount each round. A control loop, a sampler and a clock need rounds that are the same length whatever the work takes, and need to know when a round ran over. It is the fifth part of item 7 of missing.md, the "timer" there. Walkthrough: ticker.md.

49.1 A ticker is made with its period, and is a type of its own

ticker(10 ms) gives a Ticker, which has wait(), ticks(), restart() and period, and prints as Ticker(10 ms). Its ticks are one period apart, counted from when it is made: the first is one period later. The period has a unit, and a bare number is refused: "the period of a ticker has a unit, as in ticker(10 ms)". A period of no time or less is a ValueError.

Why not timer? Timer is already what web.every gives, a call that waits and can be stopped (web.md). And on a microcontroller "a timer" is five things: it makes PWM (48), counts pulses, measures them, wakes the chip and keeps a beat. The name says which one this is. Go and Mbed call theirs a ticker too.

Why in board and not in time? time is in all fifteen target languages, and a ticker there would have to be written fifteen times before it was any use. It is built for the loop of a firmware program, where the other parts of board are, and a program on a computer imports it from there the same way.

49.2 wait() and ticks() both say how many ticks have come

beat.wait() waits for the next tick. beat.ticks() never waits. Each gives the number of ticks that have come since the program last took them, and takes them. wait() gives 1 when the loop kept up and more when it was late; ticks() gives 0 when no tick has come.

if blink.ticks() > 0 { led.toggle() }      # a loop with several beats
seconds += second.ticks()                  # a clock that loses nothing
if beat.wait() > 1 { late += 1 }           # a loop that knows it ran over

Why a count and not a bool? A count is the whole truth: a clock adds it and stays right, and a control loop multiplies it by the period and has the time that went by. A bool would lose the ticks that came while the program was busy. Turned down:

  • Running the late ticks one after another, as last += interval does on an Arduino. A program that fell behind would then run its loop in a burst, with no waiting, to catch up, which is the last thing a motor wants. The program is told how late it is and decides.
  • Dropping late ticks in silence, as Go's Ticker does. That a round ran over is what a firmware engineer most needs to know, and is what C code most often does not check.
  • ticks() that only looks, with a second call to take them. Two calls leave a moment between them in which a tick can come.

Zephyr's k_timer_status_get and k_timer_status_sync are the same pair. The ticks stay where they were due: taking them late does not move the next one, so a loop does not drift.

beat.period is the time from one tick to the next, in ms, the unit now() counts in, so came * beat.period is the time that went by.

49.3 restart() starts the period again

idle.restart() makes the next tick one period from now and forgets the ticks that had come. It is how a ticker measures quiet: a program restarts it at each byte or each press, and idle.ticks() > 0 then says that nothing came for a whole period. That is a timeout and a debounce, which 45.7 and 46.7 left open.

49.4 It asks the board for nothing new

A ticker is kept on the board's clock and its sleep (zeno_board_now and zeno_board_sleep, 5.12), so a board header with the first four functions runs it. Why not a hardware timer each? A chip has a handful, and PWM takes some. Comparing with one clock gives a program as many beats as it wants, at the clock's resolution. A sleep may end a little early, so wait() reads the clock again until the tick has come.

Only a program with a ticker keeps this part of the runtime (#ifdef ZENO_TICKING, by the rule of 45.4), so the C of every other program is what it was.

49.5 A board keeps a fixed number of tickers

Sixteen, unless the board header says another number with ZENO_TICKERS. Each is two doubles in a table. Making one more is a ValueError: "this board keeps 16 tickers, and this would be one more. Make each ticker once, outside any loop". Why a fixed table? A firmware build with no collector has no malloc (pool.md), and a number underneath is what every other value of the board is (3.15). A ticker is not given back, so one made in a loop uses the table up, and the message says so. zeno run keeps the same sixteen.

49.6 On a computer

The clock is the computer's, and a ticker prints nothing: there is no line to show, as there is none for sleep. A program in a page cannot wait, as it cannot sleep, and is told to ask with ticks().

49.7 Left for later

  • A function the board runs at each tick: an interrupt, which is next.
  • Giving a ticker back, and one tick only (after).
  • A ticker in the fifteen target languages.
  • A period finer than the board's clock and sleep can keep.
  • A trial on a real board.

50. Interrupts: the board counts, and the program asks

from board import falling, input_pin, pull_up

let button = input_pin(2, pull_up)
let press = button.interrupt(falling)

while true {
    press.wait()              # the chip sleeps until the button goes down
    ring()
}

A pulse from a wheel sensor lasts a millisecond, and a program that looks at the pin now and then misses most of them. A chip's answer is the interrupt: the hardware notices the edge itself, whatever the program is doing. It is the last part of item 7 of missing.md, which asked for "a safe way to share a variable" with an interrupt, "and the rule should be one sentence". Walkthrough: interrupts.md.

50.1 An interrupt is made from an input pin and an edge

button.interrupt(falling) gives an Interrupt, which has wait(), edges() and number, and prints as Interrupt(2). From then on the board counts those edges of the pin. rising, falling and either are values of the board module, of the type Edge, as pull_up is a Pull (45.3), so a function can take one and a str in their place is refused.

Why from an InputPin, and not interrupt_pin(2, falling)? The pin is still read: a program that counts presses also asks whether the button is down now. And what holds the pin is said once, where the input is made. An Interrupt is the pin's number underneath (3.15), and it is a type of its own so that wait() exists only on a pin whose edges are being counted, which the checker then knows (45.1).

One pin has one interrupt. A second interrupt( ) on a pin starts the count again with the new edge, as a second pwm_pin starts the signal again (48.1). A chip has one such setting a pin.

50.2 wait() and edges() both say how many edges have come

press.wait() waits for an edge. press.edges() never waits. Each gives the number of edges counted since the program last took them, and takes them, as wait() and ticks() do for a ticker (49.2), for the same reasons: a count loses nothing, and a bool would.

print(turns.edges(), "turns this second")     # a rate, with a ticker
if press.edges() > 0 { ring() }               # a loop that does other things
press.wait()                                  # nothing else to do: sleep

50.3 The program's own code never runs inside an interrupt

That is the rule, in one sentence. The board counts what happened, and the program asks for the count when it chooses to. There is no function of the program that the hardware starts by itself, so there is no variable shared with one, and nothing to get wrong.

Why not a function that runs when the edge comes, as C, Arduino and Rust have?

  • The shared variable. In C the handler and the loop both write count, the programmer marks it volatile, and count += 1 in the loop still loses an edge that lands between its read and its write. No compiler sees it, and it shows up once a week. Rust refuses it, with critical sections and its ownership rules through the whole language; in Zeno owning is one way to build a program, not the language.
  • The runtime. A handler that joins two strs, or appends to a list, while the program is half-way through doing the same, breaks the pool both draw from. Refusing that needs the checker to know of every function whether it could allocate or raise, which is the ground of item 9.
  • What a handler is for. Nearly every handler in firmware does one of two things: counts, or sets a flag for the loop to see. Counting is both. The board's own handler is two lines of C that cannot be wrong, and it is written once, in the board header.

What this gives up: an answer inside the interrupt itself, within microseconds of the edge: bit-banging a protocol, or reading the second line of an encoder at the edge of the first. Those stay in C, which a firmware build calls directly (44.10).

Also turned down: functions run between two statements of the program, an event loop, as a page has (web.every). It is safe, but the compiler must then place the points where they may run, in four engines, and it is one answer to item 14 (tasks), which should be designed whole. It can be layered on counting later without changing it.

50.4 Three functions in the board layer

bool zeno_board_interrupt(int pin, int edge);   /* count from now on: 1 rising, 2 falling, 3 either */
int  zeno_board_edges(int pin);                 /* how many since last asked; start again from none */
int  zeno_board_edges_wait(int pin);            /* the same, after waiting for at least one */

Why is the wait the board's, and not a loop over zeno_board_edges and a sleep? Looking at the count and going to sleep must be one step, or an edge that lands between the two is slept through. On a Cortex-M that is: interrupts off, look, WFI, interrupts on. The board knows how its chip does it. A pin with no interrupt is a ValueError ("pin 7 of this board cannot count its edges"), and only a program with an interrupt calls the three (#ifdef ZENO_INTERRUPTS, 45.4).

50.5 On a computer the program drives its own edges

Nothing is wired to the simulated board, so the edges counted are the ones the program drives on that pin itself, with pin(2).on(), as if a wire joined the two. It is the rule of 47.4, where a pin the program drove high reads as 3.3 V. Making an input with a pull is not an edge.

A wait() with no edge counted is a ValueError there: "the board says no edge can ever come on pin 2, so the program would wait for ever". Nothing can drive a pin while the program waits, and a message is kinder than a program that hangs. The board function says it by answering 0, which a real board never does.

50.6 Left for later

  • A function of the program run for each edge, with item 14.
  • Waiting for the first of several: an interrupt or a ticker. Today a loop asks each and sleeps a little in between.
  • When an edge came: the width of a pulse, which a chip's timer can capture.
  • Debouncing a button in the board. Today the program does it, with a ticker (49.3).
  • Interrupts of a serial port or a converter. A board header may use them inside its own functions already.
  • Pressing a button under zeno run (45.5).
  • A trial on a real board.

50.7 The interpreter keeps the board behind a pointer, and what the clock said about loop

Before 0.7.0 went out, zeno run was timed against 0.6.0, as every release is. bench/loop.zeno took 3 to 5% longer, and ran the same instructions to the seventh digit (84,061,204,209 where 0.6.0 ran 84,061,205,164). Building each commit since 0.6.0 put it at this chapter's: the commit before it is level.

What was changed. The interpreter held the board inside itself, between its other fields, and this chapter gave the board two more tables, 576 bytes. The VM had the same trouble in 0.6.0 and keeps what a program reaches outside itself in a box (34.7). The interpreter now keeps the board in one too. That gave back about one part in a hundred, and no more.

What was measured, and left. The rest is not in what the code does. Three things say so:

  • The same build, started under names of four lengths, takes 9.80 to 10.39 seconds: where things land in memory moves the time by 3% either way, for 0.6.0 as for this one.
  • A simulation of the cache (cachegrind) finds the same reads and the same writes in both, and next to no misses in either.
  • With both versions built another way, so that no branch crosses a 32-byte boundary (-C llvm-args=-x86-branches-within-32B-boundaries), every branch of the interpreter lies somewhere else, in both. The difference is then 1%: 10.13 and 10.25 seconds, each the mean of four names.

So the time is lost in where the code of the interpreter's loop happens to lie for this processor (an Intel Xeon of the Emerald Rapids kind), and which branch it is was not found. Another processor, or the next change anywhere in Zeno, puts things elsewhere. The builds that are released are made by another linker for another C library, and their code lies differently again.

That option is not turned on for the release. It was made for a fault of older Intel processors, which this one does not have, and here it only served to move the code. It was tried for ten minutes on one machine and one benchmark, it makes every build larger, and what it does to the other five benchmarks and to the VM was not measured. If zeno run is ever to be made steadier by the clock, how its code is laid out is the first thing to look at, and it is written down here for that.

zeno run, seconds 0.6.0 0.7.0
fib 3.10 3.07 −0.9 %
loop 33.39 34.51 +3.4 %
sort 14.86 14.41 −3.0 %
strings 3.22 3.24 +0.7 %
trees 24.45 24.35 −0.4 %
nbody 58.31 58.32 0.0 %

51. One step to a board: zeno build --board

zeno build --board boards/qemu-cortex-m3 examples/blink.zeno
Wrote blink.c
Built blink.elf for the board in `boards/qemu-cortex-m3`.
Run it with: qemu-system-arm -M lm3s6965evb -nographic -semihosting -kernel blink.elf

Item 8 of missing.md is "one step from a .zeno file to a board", and has three parts: the cross-compiler in the same command, a runtime with no printf and no exit, and checks without GCC's built-ins. This chapter is the first part. It was built first because it is what lets the other two be tried: before it, nothing Zeno wrote had ever run on a processor other than the computer's. Walkthrough: board-build.md.

51.1 --board names a folder, and the folder says how

A board is a folder with a file called zeno.board in it, and zeno build --board <folder> builds the program for it. The file names the board's C compiler, its flags, the files of C that are built with every program, the linker script, and the command that runs or loads the result:

compiler "arm-none-eabi-gcc"
flags "-mcpu=cortex-m3" "-mthumb"
header "board.h"
sources "startup.c" "system.c"
script "link.ld"
link "-nostartfiles" "-Wl,--gc-sections"
run "qemu-system-arm" "-M" "lm3s6965evb" "-nographic" "-kernel"

Why a folder. Decision 5.12c turned cross-compiling down, because "those tools exist, differ for every vendor, and are what a firmware engineer already has set up", and a --target thumbv7m would be "a second, worse copy of each of them". That reason still holds, and the folder respects it: Zeno knows no processor, no flag and no vendor. It reads the names of the tools the engineer already has, and types the command they would have typed. What 5.12c did not weigh is that the command is long, is the same for every program on a board, and was typed again for each one.

Why not on the line, as missing.md first had it (zeno build --cc arm-none-eabi-gcc, with the flags in zeno.package). A line with a compiler, six flags, two files and a linker script on it is the command 5.12c already had. And the flags are not the program's: the same program is built for two boards, and one board runs many programs. Written in zeno.package they would be copied into every program, and a program for two boards would need two packages. The header with the board's functions (5.12b) already lives apart from the program. The flags, the startup file and the linker script belong beside it.

Why the file is read as zeno.package is (8.1): one lexer, so a comment starts with # and text is written as in a program. Each word in quotes is one word of the command, and no shell reads the line, so a path with a space in it needs no second kind of quoting, and the same file works on Windows.

Why a path and not a name (--board nucleo). A name needs a place where names are looked up, and there is none yet (51.9). A path is what the engineer's own board will always be.

51.2 Eight lines, and one of them must be there

compiler is the only line a board must have. about, compiler, header, script and run are said once; flags, sources and link any number of times, and the words add up in the order written.

A file is named as it is in the board's folder (header, sources, script), wherever the command is typed, so a board can be moved and shared whole. A file that is named and not there is said before anything is built, by its name, and so is every other mistake in the file, with its line. A cross-compiler's own message for a missing linker script is three lines about ld.

Why flags and link are two lines. -mcpu must be said when compiling and when linking; -nostartfiles only means something when linking. One compiler command does both here, so one list would work today. Two lists say what each word is for, and stay right if the two steps are ever run apart.

Why header is a line of its own and not -DZENO_BOARD=... under flags. It is the one flag Zeno itself defines the meaning of (5.12b), a file that must exist, and the difference between a board with pins of its own and one with the simulated pins. A board with no header line gets the simulated board, which is what makes the emulated board of 51.6 so small.

51.3 A build for a board has no collector

--board builds the C that --no-collector builds: every list and object has one owner, and memory comes from a pool whose size is fixed when the program is built (5.9). --collector with --board is refused, with the reason.

Why. The collector takes its memory from the system 64 KB at a time, and first looks for garbage when 4 MB are in use (22.5). That is right for a computer and cannot fit a chip that has 64 KB in all. A collector made for a chip is a piece of work of its own (51.9). Until it exists, building one in would give a program that links and then stops at its first list.

Why not leave the choice to the line, so that --board alone gave an ordinary build and --board --no-collector this one. Because the shorter command would then be the one that does not work. The option that names a chip gives the build made for a chip.

--minimal, --release, --fast and --memory go with it and mean what they mean elsewhere. --llvm, --web and --target are refused: the board's compiler is handed C, and those write something else. (clang can make code for a chip from IR; nobody has asked.) --board belongs to build alone: zeno run and zeno check with it are refused, because a board changes nothing in what they do.

51.4 What the compiler is asked, and in what order

<compiler> -O2 <flags> -I<folder> [-DZENO_BOARD="<header>"]
    -o <name>.elf <name>.c <sources> [-T <script>] <link>
    <the libraries of C the program declares> -lm

One command compiles and links. Zeno's own flag comes first and the board's after it, so the board has the last word: with flags "-Os", GCC takes the later -Os over the earlier -O2. The board's folder is on the path of headers, so the header is found by its plain name, and it and the sources can include the vendor's headers beside them. The libraries of C a program declares with import c are built in as in every C build (44.10): a vendor's HAL is C, and this is where it meets the board. Only the hint to the loader about where a library lies (-Wl,-rpath) is left out, since a chip has no loader.

The compiler is the board's, and CC is not read. CC says which compiler builds for this computer, and many people have it set. A board build that obeyed it would hand ARM flags to the computer's compiler.

When the compiler is not installed, the C has been written, and the message gives the whole command, to run once it is.

51.5 The program is <name>.elf, and run is shown, not run

The file is <name>.elf, whatever the processor: it is what a cross-compiler writes, what QEMU, OpenOCD, pyOCD and gdb read, and a .bin or a .hex is one objcopy away from it. It also cannot be mistaken for the program zeno build makes for the computer, which has no ending.

zeno build prints the board's run command with the program in it, and does not run it. The program is the last word, or stands where a word says {program}, since some tools take a sentence ("program {program} verify reset exit").

Why not run it. For QEMU it would be harmless. For a real board run writes to the chip's flash, and build has never changed anything but files in the folder it is typed in. Doing it in the same command is an option for later, and one that should be asked for by name (51.9).

51.6 The board that comes with Zeno needs no hardware

boards/qemu-cortex-m3 is the board QEMU emulates as lm3s6965evb: an ARM Cortex-M3 with 256 KB of flash and 64 KB of RAM. The folder is four files: zeno.board, a linker script, startup.c (the table of vectors, the first values of the variables, a millisecond clock on the SysTick timer, then main) and system.c (the handful of functions newlib leaves to a system).

Why an emulated board first. Nothing in Zeno has run on hardware, and that needs a board on a desk (missing.md). An emulated chip needs nothing, runs in the tests of every change, and still differs from the computer in the ways that matter to the C: a processor of 32 bits under whole numbers of 64, no floating point in the processor, another C library, a start with no system before it, and 64 KB. Why this one: of the Cortex-M boards QEMU has, it is the one with the most emulated (pins, serial ports, timers, a converter), which the next steps will use.

It has no header: its pins are the simulated ones, a line of text for each change, as under zeno run. That is what lets every example be compared with the computer byte for byte. The simulated board sleeps and reads the clock with two POSIX functions (nanosleep, clock_gettime); the folder says the board has them (-D_POSIX_TIMERS=1) and system.c supplies them on the SysTick clock. So the runtime needed no third family beside "Windows" and "everything else" (5.12).

What a program prints goes out of the first serial port, which QEMU joins to the terminal, and what it reads comes in from it. The message of an error nothing caught goes to the debugger (ARM semihosting, which QEMU answers), and so does the end of the program, with its answer: QEMU ends with 0, or with 1 after an error. On a real board with a probe attached the same two calls reach the debugger on the desk. So a test can tell what was printed from what went wrong, and knows when the program is over, with nothing added to Zeno's C.

The clock is real. sleep(500 ms) takes half a second of QEMU's time. A clock that only moved when the program slept (as in the test of 5.12b) would be quicker and would hide the one thing a start-up file most often gets wrong, its interrupt.

51.7 Every program, on the board and on the computer

tools/board.py builds each example, each sample of the book and each corner program of tools/targets/ twice, with --no-collector for the computer and with --board for the Cortex-M3, and the two must do the same: print the same text, end the same way, and stop with the same message. Then again with --minimal, for the programs no check stops. On the day it was written: 228 of 228 in the build that checks, and 212 of 212 in the minimal one.

Left out, and counted: a program a build with no collector refuses; a program with words on its line or with files; and a program that reads what is typed to its end, which a serial port does not have. A number with a fraction may differ after its fifteenth digit. cosh(1.0) is 1.5430806348152437 from the computer's C library and 1.543080634815244 from newlib: the next number along. Both are within the last place, the function is the C library's and not Zeno's, and holding them to one answer would mean writing the mathematics again. Zeno's own printing of a float is the same on both: in the first run of the check, which made no such allowance, this was the only number in any program that differed.

The workflow board runs it on a push that changes the C backend, the runtime or a board. cargo test cortex_m3 is the short form, one program with every part of a board in it, and skips the run where the tools are not installed.

51.8 Found on the way

  • A list that is the default of a field was freed while the object still held it, in every build with no collector, since those builds exist. class Bag { items: list[str] = [] }, made as Bag(): the list was made beside the call and freed when the statement ended. Two samples of the book did this, and tools/minimal.py had counted them as passing, because the checked build and the minimal build both ended with the same signal and so "did the same". The board did not: its memory is laid out otherwise, and it printed something else. A place that keeps what it is given (a field, a take parameter) now owns the default made for it, as it owns a [] written in the call, and tools/minimal.py fails a program that the system stops, but for three that are meant to end that way.
  • PRIx64 is not there on every C library. The runtime printed a register's address with it, and the newlib that Ubuntu ships does not define it for this compiler. It is %llx with a cast now, which is C99 everywhere.
  • main is given its two arguments by the board's start-up, a name and no words, because the program's main takes them when the program asks for its arguments.

51.9 Left for later

  • The rest of item 8: print and the end of the program through functions of the board, so that no C library is needed, and the checks without GCC's built-ins.
  • A header for the emulated board that drives its real registers, as a second board: the pattern for a real one, tried as far as QEMU emulates it.
  • A collector made for a chip (51.3).
