  • --board by name, a board line in zeno.package, boards as packages in the registry, and the emulated board carried inside the zeno program, which today needs a copy of the repository.
  • Loading the program in the same command, asked for by name (51.5), and a .bin or .hex beside the .elf.
  • --llvm for a board.
  • An end to what is typed over a serial port, so that a program that reads to the end can be tried on a board.
  • A trial on a real board.

52. print, and the end of a program, through the board

A build for a board (chapter 51) still stood on a C library. print was fwrite to a stream, the message of an error was fprintf, input was fgetc, and a program that stopped called exit. On a computer those four are given. On a chip somebody has to bring them: boards/qemu-cortex-m3 does it with newlib and a file of the functions newlib leaves open, and hello took 9,772 bytes of flash there, most of it the C library's streams. A board with a vendor's library and no streams at all could not be built for.

This chapter is the second part of item 8 of missing.md. A board's header may now bring the four itself, and then nothing in the runtime writes, reads or stops through the C library. hello takes 936 bytes.

#define ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS

static void zeno_board_print(const char *bytes, size_t count) { ... }
static void zeno_board_warn(const char *bytes, size_t count)  { ... }
static int  zeno_board_typed(void)                             { ... }
static void zeno_board_stop(int status)                        { ... }

Nothing in the language changes, and nothing a program prints changes, on a computer or on a board.

52.1 Four functions, and one line that says the board has them

A program reaches outside itself in four ways, pins aside. It prints (print, the question of input). It says something beside what it prints: a warning (program.warn, 34.3), and the message of the error that stops it. It reads what is typed (input). And it ends before its last line: program.exit(code) (34.1), or an error.

the board writes for what it must do
zeno_board_print(bytes, count) print, input's question send these bytes where printed text goes
zeno_board_warn(bytes, count) program.warn, an error's message send them where a person looks for trouble
zeno_board_typed() input the next byte typed, after waiting for it, or -1 if none can ever come
zeno_board_stop(status) program.exit, an error the program is over; 0, the number it gave, or 1 after an error

Why bytes and a count, and not one character at a time. A serial port with a queue, a USB endpoint and a debugger's channel all take a run of bytes at once, and a call for each character is a cost a board cannot take back. A board that can only send one writes the loop itself, in three lines. Why a count and not text that ends in a zero: the runtime knows the length already, and the board would count it again.

Why warn is a function of its own. A computer has two streams so that what a program prints can go to a file while what goes wrong stays on the screen (34.3). A board has the same two readers: the thing the program talks to, and the engineer. A board with one wire writes zeno_board_warn as a call to zeno_board_print, and that is then a choice somebody made.

Why -1 from typed. input gives none when nothing more can be typed, and reading a file on a computer ends. A serial port never ends, so a board on one never answers -1 and input waits. A board with nothing to read from answers -1 at once.

Why one line says it, #define ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS, and the four are not simply looked for. C cannot ask whether a function exists. And the headers that were there before this chapter have pins and a clock and no printing: without the line they build as they did, on the C library (the rule of 45.4: what was written before a part existed still builds). Why all four together, and not each when the program uses it, as the parts of the board are (45.4). A program that never calls input still must not pull in fgetc, and a board that prints by itself and reports its errors through stderr is a board whose errors go nowhere. The four are one decision, "this board has no streams", and one line makes it.

52.2 The runtime has one way out

Every place in runtime.c that wrote to a stream, read from one or called exit now goes through five functions at the top of the file: zeno_out, zeno_out_now (what was printed is to be seen before a wait), zeno_say, zeno_typed and zeno_stop. They are written out once, below the board, in two halves: the board's four, or the C library's.

The messages no longer go through fprintf. There were under twenty of them (error: out of memory, the uncaught error with its file and line, the memory pool that is full, the report of --memory), and between them they used %s, %d and %zu. zeno_sayf does those three in under forty lines. fprintf does everything, and on newlib everything is 20 KB of flash, in every program that can fail, which is every checked one.

On a computer nothing changes. The same bytes go to the same stream in the same order: what was printed is still pushed out before anything is said on the error stream, so the two keep their order on a screen. All the tests that were there pass as they were.

One place stopped a program with abort: the memory lent to a function of C for a list (44.10), when there was none to lend. On newlib abort raises a signal, which asks for a system with processes, and examples/modbus.zeno did not link for the second board. It says error: out of memory and stops with 1 now, as every other place that runs out does, on a computer too.

What still asks the C library for something on such a board: copying and measuring memory (memcpy, memset, strlen, which every compiler for a chip brings), and a number with a fraction, which snprintf makes into text and strtod reads. A float in a program still costs 28 KB of newlib. That is the next part (52.9).

52.3 A program that reaches its last line returns from main

zeno_board_stop is called by program.exit and by an error. A program that simply ends is not stopped: main returns 0, as any C program does, to whatever called it, which on a board is the start-up file.

Why not call zeno_board_stop(0) there too. The start-up file calls main and has to say what comes after it in any case, for C that was not written by Zeno as well. A second way to the same place would be a second thing to get wrong. The header and the start-up file are one board, and on the board that comes with Zeno they share one function (board_stops).

52.4 --minimal for a board never writes printf

A minimal build writes print as printf (30.6), and only what the program uses. For a board that is changed in two ways.

In a build for a board, print goes through the runtime's zeno_print, and not to printf. On a computer printf is free: it is in a library every program shares. On a chip it is copied into the program, and newlib's is 20 KB. The first run of the size table after 52.2 showed it: with fprintf gone from the runtime, the build that checks had become smaller than the minimal one on the board with a C library (examples/buffer.zeno: 15,888 bytes checked, 33,584 minimal), and the whole difference was printf. And a board that prints by itself has no printf to call at all.

Why for every board, and not only for one whose header says ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS. One rule, "a build for a board", needs no reading of the header's C, and is the smaller program on both kinds of board.

For a board with a header line, both halves of 52.2 are written and the header chooses, as in a checked build. Zeno would have to read the C of the header to know which half is wanted, and the line may stand in a file the header includes. The header is kept in such a build even when the program touches no pin, since it is where the line is, and it may count on the sized numbers (uint32_t and the rest), bool, size_t and ZENO_LED without including anything. In a checked build the whole runtime stands above the header, so this was always true there.

A minimal build for a computer is as it was, byte for byte: print is printf, only the C library's half is written, and print("Hello") is still one puts.

52.5 A second board: the same chip, on its own registers

boards/lm3s6965evb is the chip QEMU emulates, with a header of its own. board.h is the board layer written for real: a pin is a bit of a GPIO port, the clock is the SysTick timer, a serial port is a UART, print goes out of UART0, and a warning and the end of the program go to the debugger (semihosting). startup.c asks the C library for nothing.

pins print C library under it
boards/qemu-cortex-m3 simulated: a line of text for each change newlib's fwrite newlib, whole
boards/lm3s6965evb the chip's ports A to G the board's UART0 memcpy, strlen; snprintf only for a float

Why keep the first. Its simulated pins print what a computer prints, so every example with a pin in it can be held to the computer byte for byte (51.7), and it is the proof that a board with no header and a full C library still builds. The second is the proof of this chapter, and the pattern for a real board.

The pins are numbered port by port, 0 to 7 for PA0 to PA7 up to 48 to 55 for port G, because that is the order of the data sheet and needs no table. The LED is pin 13 to a Zeno program, as everywhere (5.12b), and PF0 on this board, where the board's LED is. PB5, which the numbering would make 13, is not reached. That is the price of led meaning the same in every program.

What is tried, and what is not. QEMU emulates the processor, the SysTick timer, the direction and the level of every pin, and the data and the flags of the UARTs. A program that drives a pin and reads it back, sleeps, prints, reads a line and stops with an error does all of that through the same registers a real chip has, and the tests hold it to the answers. QEMU does not emulate a pull-up (an input with one reads low there), the speed of a UART, or the clocks of the ports. Those lines are written from the data sheet and have been run nowhere. None of the folder has run on the chip itself.

Two functions stay for the C library's sake, in startup.c: _sbrk, the memory snprintf takes while it makes a float into text, and __assert_func, what newlib calls if it finds a fault in itself. Newlib's own __assert_func prints with fprintf, which would bring every stream back into any program with a float in it. The linker leaves both out of a program that has none.

The UART holds one byte at a time. The chip can queue sixteen, and turning the queue on empties it, in QEMU as on the chip: a byte typed before the program started would be lost. A board that is sent bytes faster than its program reads them wants the queue and an interrupt (52.9).

52.6 What it buys, measured

Flash and RAM in bytes, arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2 with newlib 4.4, the build that checks:

program before this chapter qemu-cortex-m3 lm3s6965evb
hello.zeno 9,772 9,472 936
blink.zeno 29,984 29,984 3,996
signal.zeno 31,296 31,016 4,844
buffer.zeno 35,536 15,888 7,464
modbus.zeno 34,520 14,452 9,720
words.zeno 38,432 18,704 10,408
primes.zeno 38,568 33,032 25,360
tour.zeno 50,184 44,504 36,840

The first column is the only board there was, qemu-cortex-m3, the commit before. The second column is the same board now: with fprintf out of the runtime (52.2), a program that shows no float lost 20 KB there too, with a whole C library still under it. blink did not move on that board, because its simulated pins print with printf. hello and blink take 20 bytes of RAM on the second board.

The last two rows show a float, and 28 KB of what is left is snprintf, strtod and the memory they ask for.

A program of whole numbers and text carries memcpy, memset and strlen of the C library and nothing else. blink is larger than hello because sleep(500 ms) counts in a double, and this processor does that in software.

In the minimal build buffer went from 33,584 bytes to 13,776 on the first board when print stopped being printf there (52.4). A program with a float in it has that machinery anyway, and pays a little for the change: primes went from 30,304 to 31,880, and 1 KB of RAM for the room where a number is made into text.

52.7 How it is held to its word

  • a_board_can_print_read_and_stop_by_itself runs on a computer, under every kind of build and the minimal ones, with a header that crosses the streams: what is printed comes out of the error stream, a warning out of the other, and the number a program stops with is 40 more than it gave. Nothing reaches the C library's side.
  • a_program_prints_through_the_registers_of_a_cortex_m3 runs on the emulated chip: the LED and pins driven and read back, the clock, a serial port, numbers of 64 bits, a float, a list, a warning, a line typed to input, and a division by zero that stops it with its file and line. Checked and minimal.
  • tools/board.py tries every program on both boards (51.7). On the day this was written: 228 of 228 programs on qemu-cortex-m3 and 208 of 208 on lm3s6965evb in the build that checks, and 212 of 212 and 193 of 193 in the minimal one. On the board with pins of its own a program that uses the board module is left out and counted: a simulated pin prints a line when it changes, and a real one does not.

52.8 --memory does not go with such a board yet

The report of --memory is written as the C library ends the program (atexit), and a board that stops itself does not end that way. The C says so when it is compiled (#error), and the build stops with that line, so nobody waits for a report that cannot come. On a board with no ZENO_BOARD_PRINTS it works as before.

52.9 Left for later

  • A float made into text, and read, without snprintf and strtod: the last 28 KB of C library in a program for a board.
  • The checks without GCC's built-ins (the rest of item 8).
  • The report of --memory through the board (52.8).
  • An analog pin, a PWM pin and an interrupt in the header of boards/lm3s6965evb: the chip and QEMU have a converter and timers.
  • The UART's queue and an interrupt for what comes in (52.5).
  • A board that runs alone, with no debugger: its warnings out of a serial port, and a loop or a reset where the program stops.
  • A trial on a real board.

53. A float and its digits, with no C library

Three things in the runtime were done by the C library: print(x) of a float found its digits with snprintf and strtod in a loop, {x:.2f} was snprintf, and float("2.5") was strtod. On a computer those are given. On a chip they are the largest thing in the program: 28 KB of flash on an ARM Cortex-M3 for the first float a program shows (52.6), with the memory snprintf asks for while it works.

This chapter is the third part of item 8 of missing.md. The runtime now does all three itself, with whole numbers, and exactly. snprintf, sprintf, strtod, strtof and atoi are not called anywhere in it. primes.zeno takes 7,884 bytes on that chip, where it took 25,360.

Nothing in the language changes. What a program prints changes in two places, and in both a build now prints what zeno run always did (53.2, 53.4).

53.1 Whole numbers, in rows of 32-bit words

A float is a whole number times a power of two: 0.1 is 3602879701896397 / 2^55. Its digits in base ten are worked out exactly, and exact sums on the smallest and the largest floats take whole numbers of more than a thousand bits. The runtime keeps such a number as a row of 32-bit words with its length beside it, and has a dozen small functions for them (zeno_big_times, zeno_big_shift, zeno_big_compare and their like): multiply by a small number, add, subtract, compare, double, halve. Every row is on the stack of the function that uses it, of a size fixed when the C is compiled. No memory is asked for.

Why whole numbers. Sums on floats are rounded, and a method that rounds on the way gives now and then another last digit, which is the one thing this code is for. With whole numbers the answer is the same on every processor, with or without floating point of its own.

Rejected. - A smaller printf (newlib has one, and vendors have theirs). Each rounds its own way and none gives "the fewest digits", so the loop round snprintf and strtod would stay, and what a program prints would depend on the C library under it. - The fast methods with tables (Grisu, Ryu). They are several times faster and carry tables of powers of ten, some 10 KB of them in Ryu, on a chip where flash is what this chapter is about. - __int128. 32-bit compilers do not have it.

53.2 The fewest digits that name a float

The rule is the one of 24.21 and does not change: the fewest digits that read back as this float and no other; of two such texts the nearer; of two equally near the one that ends in an even digit.

The method is Steele and White's, in the form Burger and Dybvig gave it ("Printing Floating-Point Numbers Quickly and Accurately", 1996). Each float owns a stretch of the number line: every number nearer to it than to the float on either side. Digits are taken off the front of the float's exact value one at a time, and after each the code asks whether what is written so far, or that with its last digit one higher, already lies inside the stretch. The first time one does, it stops.

One answer changes, and it is the build that was wrong. The C tried each length in turn with the float's exact value rounded to that length, and took the first that read back. But the fewest digits are not always the rounded ones. A power of two has the float below it half as far away as the float above, so its stretch reaches twice as far up as down:

print(2.0 ** -44.0)

zeno run printed 5.684341886080802e-14, 16 digits, which reads back as that float. The exact value rounded to 16 digits ends in ...801, which is below the stretch, so a build went on to 17 and printed 5.6843418860808015e-14. A build now prints what zeno run prints. It can only happen to a float that is exactly a power of two: 46 of the 2,098 there are had another text.

The C++ and Lua targets had the same fault, because their runtimes find the digits the way the C did, with their own %.16e. They keep that way, which is short, and at each length now try the rounded digits and then the digits one step higher: the stretch of a power of two reaches further up than down, so those are the only other ones that can name it. JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, PHP, Ruby and Rust were right already. tools/targets/edge-floats.zeno prints all 2,098 powers of two, on every target.

Which power of ten a float is under is guessed from its bits with whole numbers too (two * 78913 >> 18 is two * log10(2) near enough for every float), and put right by one comparison. There is no call to log10 or ceil.

53.3 An f32 takes the same road

The rule of 41.8 does not change: each length from 1 digit to 9, rounded from the exact value, until one reads back as the same f32. zeno_f32_text asks the same function for digits with that rule, where it called snprintf, strtof and strtod. zeno_f32_shown, which gave the float with those digits, is gone: nothing needs it.

53.4 {x:.2f} is exact, and a NaN is NaN

The float is split into its whole part and what is after the point. The whole part is divided by 1,000,000,000 until nothing is left, which gives its digits nine at a time. What is after the point is multiplied by ten once for each decimal, and what comes out over the point each time is the next digit. What is left at the end says which way the last digit goes: up when it is over half, and to the even digit when it is exactly half, as before ({0.125:.2f} is 0.12).

One answer changes. A float that is not a number printed as the C library writes it, nan or -nan, where zeno run prints NaN:

let x = float("nan")
print(f"{x:.2f}")

A build prints NaN now, and inf and -inf as before. Text is made the same way on Linux, macOS, Windows and a chip, whatever their C libraries do with a NaN.

53.5 float("2.5") gives the nearest float, however long the text

What is accepted does not change: a sign, then inf, infinity or nan in capitals or not, or digits with a point anywhere and e and a power after them; blanks around it. 1. and .5 are floats; ., 1e, 1_000.0, 0x10 and nan(1) are a ValueError.

The digits are gathered into a whole number n and a power of ten. For most text that is all there is to do: with no more than 15 digits and a power no more than 22, n and the power are both floats exactly, and the processor's one multiplication or division gives the nearest float by itself (Clinger, 1990). Any other text is n divided by a power of ten, or multiplied by one, as whole numbers: a long division gives 64 bits of the answer and says whether anything was left, and the 53 a float keeps are rounded from that, to even on a tie. The smallest floats, which keep fewer bits, come out of the same division.

No more than 770 digits are kept, with a note of whether any that were dropped was not 0. A text that lies exactly between two floats never has more than 767 digits, so text of any length is read as the nearest float, in a fixed 960 bytes of stack.

float( ) no longer makes a copy of its text to cut the blanks off.

53.6 What it costs, and what it buys, measured

On an ARM Cortex-M3 (arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2, -Os) the digits of a float take 1,192 bytes of flash, {x:.2f} 908, float( ) 1,428 and 184 of powers of ten, and the functions for long whole numbers under them some 700: 4.4 KB where the C library took 28. A program that uses one of the three carries only that one.

Flash in bytes, the build that checks:

program qemu-cortex-m3 before now lm3s6965evb before now
primes.zeno 33,032 16,172 25,360 7,884
tour.zeno 44,504 22,000 36,840 14,032
instruments.zeno 52,816 31,296 45,136 23,336

A program with no float in it is the same size as before. On lm3s6965evb a program now has of the C library memcpy, memset, strlen and their like, and the functions of math it calls. The soft floating point of a chip with none of its own comes with the compiler, and is some 3 KB.

The quick way of reading (53.5) costs flash on such a chip. Its one multiplication or division of floats brings the compiler's functions for them, 2.2 KB, into a program that reads a float and never multiplies or divides one itself: sentence.zeno is 19,932 bytes on lm3s6965evb and would be 17,696 without it. It stays, because a program that reads a float nearly always does sums with it and has those functions anyway, and without it reading is three and a half times slower than it was, on a computer too. Rejected: the quick way only where the processor has floating point of its own. Each compiler says that with a macro of its own, and the C Zeno writes would read text one way on one chip and another way on the next.

While it works, a float's digits take 800 bytes of stack, {x:.2f} 640, and a long text read as a float 960. The C library asked _sbrk for memory in their place, and kept 2 KB of its own: primes has 33,952 bytes of RAM in use on lm3s6965evb, where it had 36,028.

On a computer (a million of each, x86-64, -O2):

before now
str(x) of floats that need 17 digits 5.8 s 0.96 s
str(x) of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, ... 1.85 s 0.35 s
f"{x:.2f}" 0.51 s 0.06 s
float(text) of six short texts 0.11 s 0.11 s

Writing is five to eight times faster, because the old way called snprintf and strtod once for each length it tried. Reading is as fast as strtod for the short text programs mostly read, and three and a half times slower for text of 16 digits and more, which goes the long way (0.38 s for a million of them).

53.7 How it is held to its word

  • a_float_is_written_and_read_with_no_c_library types 14,118 floats at a program that prints each as it is and with 0, 2 and 9 decimals, 6,000 f32s, and some 11,400 texts to read: every kind of float (any bits, readings, every power of two, the smallest ones), text with too few digits and far too many, whole numbers exactly between two floats with a hair over and under, and halves of the smallest floats in 750 digits. What comes out has to be what Rust's own functions give, under zeno run, in a build and in a firmware build. It also reads the runtime for the five calls that are gone.
  • floats_are_written_and_read_on_a_cortex_m3 types some 400 of them at the serial port of both emulated boards: floats of every kind, f32s, text of 750 digits, text that is no float. Each board prints what zeno run prints, in the build that checks and in the minimal one. On lm3s6965evb there is no C library under the digits, and on both the processor is a 32-bit one with no floating point of its own. It has not run on a real chip.
  • While it was written the C was compared with the C library of this computer (glibc, which is exact) on several million floats and texts, a part of them with the address and undefined-behaviour checkers on.
  • tools/board.py (51.7): 228 of 228 programs on qemu-cortex-m3 and 208 of 208 on lm3s6965evb in the build that checks, 212 of 212 and 193 of 193 in the minimal one.

53.8 What stays with the C library

  • A minimal build for a computer still writes {x:.2f} as printf's own %.2f (30.6): printf is there anyway. So there a NaN with decimals is still nan. A minimal build for a board goes through the runtime (52.4) and prints NaN.
  • import c shows a pointer with snprintf("%p") (chapter 44). Only a program that imports C has it.
  • The simulated board prints a pin's change with printf (qemu-cortex-m3, and every computer).
  • math.sqrt, math.sin and the rest are the C library's.

53.9 Left for later

  • The checks without GCC's built-ins (the rest of item 8).
  • {x:.2f} through the runtime in a minimal build for a computer too, if the NaN there ever matters.
  • The rest of 52.9: --memory through the board, an analog pin, a PWM pin and an interrupt on boards/lm3s6965evb, a board that runs alone, and a trial on a real board.

54. The history: every commit, under its release

HISTORY.md, at the root of the repository, lists every commit, oldest first, under the release it went into, with one plain line on what it changed. zeno-lang.org shows the same file at /history/. It is there so that somebody who reads it from the top can follow how the language was built: this file says why Zeno is as it is, and that one says in what order it came to be.

(This chapter was numbered 49 for a few hours. The ticker's chapter had that number already, in commits that were waiting for the release of 0.6.0 to be over, and the code and the docs name the ticker's decisions by it in many places. This one was named in two.)

54.1 A script writes the file, from git and a file of notes

tools/history.py writes HISTORY.md. Git gives the commits, their order, their dates and the tags. tools/history-notes.txt gives the words: a line for each commit, a heading for a run of commits, and a paragraph for each release.

Why a script? A list of three hundred commits kept by hand is behind at the next commit, and nobody can see that one is missing. The script counts them, and --check fails when the file is behind. Why notes beside it? The first line of a commit message is written for somebody in the middle of the work ("Decisions 5.15: whoever receives a value owns it"). The page is for somebody who is not. Turned down:

  • git log alone. It has every commit and none of the story: no release, no word on what a run of commits was for.
  • The plain line inside each commit message. The commits that are there cannot be given one without writing the history again, which changes every hash and breaks every link to a commit.
  • git notes. GitHub does not show them, and a clone does not fetch them unless it is told to.

54.2 A release is a tag

A tag vX.Y.Z on a commit ends a release, and nothing else says so. The commits up to and with the tagged one are that release, and what follows the last tag is under "Unreleased". So a new tag makes a new heading by itself, and the notes cannot disagree with git about what a release holds.

The paragraph of a release is in the notes, under its number. The block named Unreleased goes with whichever release now holds its first commit: a release that is tagged before anybody has touched the notes still gets the paragraph that was written for its commits.

The script stops in a clone that has no tags or only part of the history, and says which git fetch to run. A clone made for one task is often shallow. Without this, every commit it has would be written under "Unreleased" and the file would look whole.

54.3 A commit with no note is still listed

A commit that has no line in the notes is listed with the first line of its own message, under the heading "Later commits" when it comes after the noted ones. The page says it has every commit, and it keeps saying so between the day a commit is pushed and the day somebody writes its line. --missing prints the lines to fill in.

Turned down: leaving such a commit out until it has a line. Then the page is whole only when somebody remembers.

54.4 Oldest first, and the name is not CHANGELOG

The first commit is at the top. The page is read as a story, and a story starts at its beginning. A changelog is the other way round, because it is for somebody who has one version and wants to know what the next one changes. Zeno has that already, in docs/releases/, one page for each version, which is also the text of the release on GitHub. Two files with one job would drift apart, so this one has another job and another name.

54.5 The commit that brings the page up to date is not on it

A commit that changes only HISTORY.md and the notes is not listed. A commit cannot hold its own name: the name is worked out from what the commit holds. So a commit gets its line in a later commit, and that later commit holds the two files and nothing else.

Turned down: listing it, one step late. Every time the page was brought up to date it would gain a line that says only that it was brought up to date, and would need bringing up to date again.

54.6 One file, shown in two places

The site's tools/build.py turns HISTORY.md into /history/, as it turns this file into /decisions/. Nothing is written twice. A short name of a commit is a link to the commit on GitHub, in the file and on the site, so the page can stay one line to a commit and the whole of each is one press away.

55. Checks in plain C, for a compiler that is neither GCC nor Clang

The C that zeno build writes is C as the standard of 1999 has it, but for a handful of things it asked of GCC and Clang by their own names for them:

  • __builtin_add_overflow, __builtin_sub_overflow and __builtin_mul_overflow, which say whether a sum, a difference or a product was too big (5.5e);
  • __builtin_ctzll and __builtin_unwind_init in the collector;
  • __attribute__((noreturn)) in front of a function that never comes back, and __attribute__((noinline)) in front of three that are to stay functions of their own.

A compiler that has none of those names stopped at the first. tcc, the Tiny C Compiler, is of that kind, and is the one that could be tried here. IAR's compiler, Keil's older one and the compilers some chip makers ship are too, as far as their manuals say: none of them can be run where Zeno is made.

This chapter is the last part of item 8 of missing.md. Each of those things is now written a second time in plain C, and one mark, ZENO_PLAIN_C, says which of the two a compiler gets. tcc builds every example, in every kind of build, and each does what it does built by gcc.

Nothing in the language changes, and a build by GCC or Clang does what it did.

55.1 One mark, decided in one place

At the top of runtime.c:

#if !defined(ZENO_PLAIN_C) && !defined(__clang__) && !(defined(__GNUC__) && __GNUC__ >= 5)
#define ZENO_PLAIN_C
#endif

Every place that has two forms asks #ifndef ZENO_PLAIN_C, and no place asks what the compiler is. GCC has had the three overflow built-ins since version 5, so an older GCC, which some chip makers still ship, gets the plain C as well.

Building with -DZENO_PLAIN_C asks GCC and Clang for the plain C too. That is what makes it testable: the plain C can be held to the built-ins on the same machine, by the same compiler, with no other compiler at hand.

Turned down: asking for each built-in by itself (__has_builtin). GCC only has that question since version 10, and five marks are thirty-two files to test where one mark is two.

Turned down: #define __attribute__(x), the one line that makes every attribute vanish. The name belongs to the compiler, and a compiler's own headers may use it.

55.2 The checks, written out

Four functions say whether a result fits and hand it over when it does: zeno_add_overflows, zeno_sub_overflows, zeno_mul_overflows and zeno_mul_overflows_u64. Each has the built-in and the plain C in it, and zeno_add, zeno_sub, zeno_mul, the u64 ones and int("...") call them.

A sum and a difference are worked out as numbers with no sign, which C lets wrap round, and the signs are looked at: a sum overflowed when a and b have one sign and the sum has the other. The result itself is then C's own a + b, worked out only once it is known to fit.

The plain C never works out a number that does not fit, since that is the thing C leaves undefined, and it never turns a number with no sign that is too big into one with a sign, which C leaves to the compiler (C99, 6.3.1.3). So it is the same on every compiler, and a compiler that builds on a mistake not happening has nothing to build on.

A product is taken as halves of 32 bits, so that every product of two halves fits in 64:

a * b = a1 * b1 * 2^64 + (a1 * b0 + a0 * b1) * 2^32 + a0 * b0

The first part fits only as 0, so one of the two top halves is 0. What is left of the middle is moved up 32 bits, so it must fit in 32. And adding the last part must not carry. For numbers with a sign the two are multiplied with their signs taken off, and the product has to fit with its sign put back: below zero there is room for one more.

Turned down: finding out by dividing (a > INT64_MAX / b, as CERT's rule INT32-C writes it). A Cortex-M3 has no instruction that divides 64 bits: it is a call into the compiler's library of some hundreds of steps, for every product a program works out.

Turned down: a number of 128 bits. __int128 is GCC's and Clang's again, and on a 32-bit processor they do not have it either.

A sum of two u64s needs no built-in in either form: with no sign C wraps round, to less than it began with. Both forms are now that one line.

55.3 The word in front of a function

ZENO_NORETURN is __attribute__((noreturn)) for GCC and Clang, _Noreturn for a plain compiler that reads the C of 2011, and nothing for one that does not. ZENO_NOINLINE is the attribute, or nothing.

With nothing there the C is still right. The first only lets the compiler leave out the way back from a call that never comes back, and the second is a hint about speed. A compiler may then warn that a function "might return no value" where its last line is a call that stops the program (tcc does). It never reaches the end, and C only minds if the value of such an end is used (C99, 6.9.1).

55.4 The top of the program stays out of main, in the compiler's word or without one

The collector looks for the program's variables on the stack below main's. So the top-level code is a function of its own, zeno_program, and it must stay one: put inside main by the compiler, its variables could lie above the place the collector starts from. That was __attribute__((noinline)), the one attribute that something depended on.

GCC and Clang keep the attribute, as ZENO_NOINLINE, and main calls the function by its name. A compiler that has no such word calls it by its address, read from a variable it cannot see through:

#ifndef ZENO_PLAIN_C
    zeno_program();
#else
    void (*volatile program)(void) = zeno_program; /* called so, it stays out of `main` */
    program();
#endif

No compiler can put a function inside main when it cannot know which function is called. A build with no collector has nothing that looks at the stack, and there main calls zeno_program by its name for every compiler.

Tried first, and turned down by the count before 0.7.0: one way for every compiler. The first form of this stage called through the pointer in every build with a collector, GCC's too, and took the attribute off everywhere, so that a build with no collector could have the one function put inside the other (4 to 32 bytes less on a chip). The comparison with 0.6.0 that a release is held to (docs/release.md) found both in the instructions a program runs, with the C of the program the same line for line:

bench/ program, instructions 0.6.0 pointer, no attribute attribute, by name
fib 30, --release 24,062,434 24,356,168 (+1.2 %) 24,060,625
trees 14, --fast --owned 288,528,748 291,298,958 (+1.0 %) 288,531,936

GCC makes a copy of fib for the one place that calls it when it can see that place, and cannot when the caller is reached through a pointer; and with zeno_program inside main it lays the loop of trees out differently. Neither is a mistake of the compiler's, and a few bytes on a chip are not worth one instruction in a hundred of every program on a computer. What a program asks for nothing of must cost it nothing (24.29, 34.5), so GCC and Clang are given what they were given in 0.6.0, and only a compiler that could not read that gets the other form.

55.5 The collector in plain C

The lowest bit of a word that is set is found by halving the word six times.

The registers are read with setjmp. A pointer may be nowhere in memory when the collector runs, only in a register. GCC and Clang have a name for putting the registers on the stack. Plain C has one thing that reads them: setjmp copies them into what it is handed. The collector looks through that like any other memory, and then calls the function that looks through the stack by its address, as in 55.4, so that it lies below everything on any compiler.

Two things about it are not as good as the rest of this chapter, and both are written down here and not hidden:

  • A C library may keep registers back from setjmp. The C library of Linux scrambles three of them on a 64-bit Intel processor (the stack pointer, the frame pointer and the place to go back to), so that what setjmp filled cannot be used to break into a program. A pointer that a compiler kept in the frame pointer and nowhere else would not be seen. With gcc 13 and Clang 18 told to take the plain C, the collector's own function puts that register on the stack as it begins, at -O1, -O2 and -Os, so it is seen there. Nothing in C promises that. GCC and Clang never take this path unless they are asked to, and tcc keeps nothing in a register across a call.
  • A firmware build with a collector cannot be built in plain C, and says so. A firmware build's promise is that its C has no setjmp in it at all (firmware.md), and that promise is worth more than this corner. So there the plain C is one line, #error, that says to build with GCC or Clang, or with --no-collector or --owned. A build for a board has no collector, and is not touched by this.

The collector is for a computer, where the compiler is nearly always one of the two. It was written in plain C all the same so that tcc could be used to try the whole of the runtime, and it found nothing.

55.6 Found on the way: floats on a compiler that is neither

a * b + c is two steps in Zeno, each rounded. A processor that has one instruction for both gives another last digit now and then, and a C compiler may use it unasked, so the runtime says not to. It said so to gcc and to Clang, each in its own words, and to no other compiler at all.

The line C itself has for it, #pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF (C99, 7.12.2), is now given to every compiler but gcc, which does not read it and keeps its own. A compiler for a Cortex-M4F or an M7 has such an instruction, so this is the kind of compiler it matters to. It could not be tried here: tcc never joins the two steps.

55.7 What it costs, measured

On a computer (x86-64, -O2), a loop of a hundred million rounds, each with two products, a sum, a difference and a count:

with the built-ins in plain C
gcc 13 0.19 s 0.23 s
Clang 18 0.19 s 0.24 s

Fifty million products that nearly fill an int take the same time either way (0.22 s with gcc, 0.29 s with Clang). The same two loops built by tcc take 4.7 s and 2.0 s, which is tcc's doing and not the checks': it does not optimize.

On a Cortex-M3, the functions themselves, in bytes (-O2):

with the built-in in plain C
a sum, a difference 28 42
a product 190 142, and 66 for the u64 one it calls
a product of u64s 76 66

And whole programs for boards/lm3s6965evb, in bytes of flash:

program with the built-ins in plain C
hello.zeno 936 932
scheduler.zeno 7,480 7,188
primes.zeno 7,884 7,780
modbus.zeno 9,720 9,596
tour.zeno 14,032 14,208
instruments.zeno 23,336 23,288

So on the chip the plain C costs nothing to speak of. A 32-bit processor has no overflow flag for a number of 64 bits, and what GCC writes for its own built-in there is about what the plain C says. How long each takes on a real chip was not measured: QEMU does not keep time the way a chip does.

55.8 How it is held to its word

  • plain_c_asks_gcc_for_nothing reads the runtime with the mark decided: told to be plain, no __builtin_ is left in it, and no __attribute__ but the one only Windows reads (55.9). The program written after it never has either.
  • plain_c_finds_an_overflow_where_the_built_ins_do takes the four functions as the runtime has them, writes each out in both forms in one C file, and holds the plain one to the built-in on every pair of 384 numbers at the edges (each power of two, one less, one more, and each of those below zero) and on twenty million pairs of every length, with the products that just fit and the ones that just do not. The file is read as the C of 1999 with nothing added. plain_c_finds_an_overflow_on_a_cortex_m3 runs the same on the emulated chip, where a number of 64 bits is two words.
  • a_program_overflows_in_plain_c_where_it_does_under_zeno_run types 3,000 pairs of ints and 3,000 of u64s at a program that prints each sum, difference and product, or that it was too big. What comes out has to be what Rust's own checked arithmetic gives: under zeno run, built, built as plain C, built as plain C with the collector run before every piece of memory is handed out, and built by tcc where there is one.
  • a_program_overflows_in_plain_c_on_a_cortex_m3: on both emulated boards, built as plain C, 300 pairs that only just fit are printed as zeno run prints them, and each of ten pairs that do not fit stops the program with the error, the line and the column of the one sum that was too big.
  • tools/plain.py builds every example, every sample of the book and the corner programs for the collector, --owned and --no-collector, and compiles the C three ways: as it is, as plain C read by the standard of 1999 (-DZENO_PLAIN_C -std=c99 -pedantic-errors, -O2), and with tcc. 266, 238 and 238 programs do the same in all three. With Clang in place of gcc the examples and the corner programs do too. The plain workflow runs it on GitHub.
  • While it was written the two forms were compared on 291 million pairs, and on 48 million with gcc's checker of undefined behaviour on.

No program of Zeno's has been built by IAR's, Keil's or a chip maker's compiler. None of them can be run here. What was tried is that the C asks for nothing outside the standard of 1999, and that a compiler which is neither GCC nor Clang (tcc 0.9.27) builds all of it.

55.9 What is still GCC's, or the system's

  • On Windows one function runs before main to keep line ends as they are, by __attribute__((constructor)). gcc and Clang are the compilers a build is tried with there. Microsoft's compiler wants more than this chapter gives it, and is a stage of its own.
  • import c (chapter 44) writes a few lines with _Generic, which is the C of 2011, and zeno run builds the library it loads with an attribute of GCC's. Only a program that imports C has them.
  • A board's own files are written for the board's compiler: startup.c and link.ld in the two folders that come with Zeno are for arm-none-eabi-gcc. A board for IAR or Keil is a folder with their start-up file and their linker's file in it.
  • The C of 1999 is asked of the compiler (Keil's older compiler reads it with --c99), and of the C library memcpy, strlen and their like, with the functions of math a program calls.
  • zeno build --llvm is Clang by its nature.

55.10 Left for later

  • A trial with a compiler of a chip maker, when one is at hand.
  • Microsoft's C compiler.
  • The registers read without setjmp where the C library has a better way, if a plain compiler on a computer ever needs it.

56. raises in a function type, and what a build still refuses

Item 9 of missing.md has one aim: a build should take what zeno run takes. Nine parts take it there (9.1 to 9.9 of plan-9-14.md). This chapter is written as they land, one section or more for each.

The first part is a function type that says what it raises:

function parse(text: str) -> int raises ValueError { ... }

function each(texts: list[str], convert: function(str) -> int raises ValueError) -> int raises ValueError {
    var total = 0
    for text in texts {
        total += convert(text)
    }
    return total
}

Until now a firmware build, and so a build with no collector, refused texts.map(parse) and each(texts, parse) with "cannot compile a function that can raise, used as a value, yet" (5.5l). Both build now, and print what zeno run prints.

56.1 The type, and what a call through it does

A function type is written as the first line of a function is, with no names: after what it returns it may say raises and one kind of error. A call through a value of that type can raise that kind, and is checked as a call of a function that says so: the caller catches it, or says raises itself.

error: `each` can raise ValueError here but does not say so. Add `raises ValueError` to it, or catch the error

var f = parse gives f the whole type, raises and all, in a firmware build (and with no collector). An ordinary build gives it the type it gave before, for the reason in 56.4.

Why this way of writing it. It is the function's own first line, so there is nothing new to learn, and the printer and every message already wrote a function that way. Two others were weighed in the plan: raising function(str) -> int is one more word in a place no other word goes, and cannot say which kind; function(str) -> int or raises ValueError reads as if the error were a value that comes back, which it is nowhere but in the C of a firmware build.

A fault on a type needs no rule of its own. In a firmware build a division by zero, a bad index and their like stop the program, so a function that says raises ZeroDivisionError with nothing in it that raises one by hand is refused (5.19m, 6.9). The plan asked whether a type that says raises ZeroDivisionError should be refused the same way. It is not: the only functions that can be put in such a type are ones that raise nothing, and ones that say raises ZeroDivisionError, which 5.19m has already held to raising it by hand. So the error that comes through the type is always one that travels as a value, and except ZeroDivisionError around the call catches it in every build. Refusing the type would refuse a program that is right.

56.2 raises after a result belongs to the function it ends

This line built before, and means that make raises Missing:

function make() -> function(int) -> int raises Missing { ... }

A type that read raises for itself would take the word from make, and the line would come to mean something else without a word of warning. The first rule of the plan forbids that. So raises belongs to the outermost function whose result it follows, in a first line and in a type alike. A function type that is itself the result, and raises, stands in brackets:

function make(n: int) -> (function(int) -> int raises ValueError) raises Missing { ... }

Brackets may stand around a function type and nothing else:

error: brackets in a type go only around a function type, as in `(function(int) -> int raises ValueError)`. One type is written without brackets

Why not (int) too. It would be a second way to write int (question 1 of the audit).

What the brackets also give. (function(int) -> int) or none is a function that may be missing, where function(int) -> int or none is, as it always was, a function whose answer may be none. That could not be written before. The printer and every message write the brackets back where they are needed, so a type in a message is one that can be copied into a program.

After raises, or none wants the brackets (from the review of this part). function() raises ValueError or none was taken at first, as a function that may be missing. A reader can as well take it to say that the function raises ValueError or nothing, so it is refused, and the message writes the type with its brackets:

error: `or none` after what a function type raises could mean that the function raises that or nothing. A function that may be missing is written with brackets: `(function() raises ValueError) or none`

No program had the line. function(int) or none and function(int) -> int or none keep their meanings.

Item 10 is not in the way. Several results will be written -> (int, str). One function type in brackets has no comma, so the two are told apart by the first comma.

56.3 One kind, and the comma

A function's first line may say raises ValueError, KeyError. A function type stands inside a list of its own:

function each(convert: function(str) -> int raises ValueError, text)

Is text a second kind, or a second parameter with no type? The second is legal, and was before this part. A rule for the parser would be a rule for the reader to know (question 2 of the audit). So in a type raises names one kind, and a type ends at the comma. A function that raises two kinds fits raises Error.

The message for a second kind comes from where it can be told:

  • After a field, a let or what a function returns no comma can follow a type, so the parser gives it.
  • In a list of parameters, the checker gives it when a parameter with no type has the name of a kind of error.
  • Inside [ ], as in list[function() raises ValueError, FileError], the checker gives it when the type after the comma is the name of a kind of error. It gave the message about how many types a list takes at first, which sent the reader the wrong way.
error: a function type names one kind of error after `raises`. A function that raises more than one kind fits `raises Error`, which catches every kind

Why one kind is enough for now. Every program found so far that hands a raising function on raises one kind, or wants any. A list can be let in later inside brackets of its own, and no type written today would change its meaning.

56.4 What fits: the test of except

A function fits a type that says raises K if every kind it raises is one that except K would catch: K itself, or anything when K is Error. A function that raises nothing fits too.

error: `convert` of `each` should be function(str) -> int raises ValueError, but this function can raise Missing, and the type says it raises only ValueError. Write `raises Error` on the type to take a function that raises any kind

Why the test of except. It is the one a reader already knows: a type that says raises K is a promise that except K around the call is enough.

The gap in an ordinary build. In an ordinary build and in zeno run, a function that raises was accepted where the type says nothing, and the call through the value was then checked as raising nothing. That is a hole in "a function says what it raises", and it is older than this part. It is left as it is in an ordinary build, on both sides: a function, or a value whose type says raises, put where a type says nothing, is not held to it there. A firmware build and a build with no collector hold it, since they call the two in different ways (56.5):

error: `f` of `apply` should be function(str) -> int, which raises nothing, but this function can raise ValueError. In a firmware build a call through a function type raises only what the type says: write `raises ValueError` after what it returns, or build without `--firmware`

Why it is not closed now. Closing it would refuse programs that build today, which the first rule of the plan forbids without asking. So it was measured, as the plan says, and the number goes to the owner of the language with the question. The check was run over 443 programs (every example, every program in tools/targets/, every sample of the book that zeno run runs, and the benchmarks):

  • Accepted by a strict check today and caught by closing the gap: 0. A firmware build is strict, and so is zeno check --strict.
  • Accepted when not strict: 2 programs, 19 places (tools/targets/edge-files.zeno and edge-bytes.zeno). Each hands a function written where a value goes, which reads a file and so can raise FileError, to a parameter of type function() -> str. A strict check refuses all 19 already, for another reason: the function written there does not say raises.
  • A value whose type says raises, put where a type says nothing: 0. No program could write one before this part.

56.5 How a firmware build calls it

In a firmware build an error travels as a value: a function that can raise answers true or false, and gives its answer through a last pointer (5.5l). A value of a type that says raises is called that way, in C:

int64_t t16;
if (!((bool (*)(zeno_closure *, const char *, int64_t *))z_convert->code)(z_convert, z_text, &t16)) { ...; return false; }

and in LLVM, call zeroext i1 with a ptr for the answer. What is held at that line (the copy of the list a for walks, the list map is making) is let go on the way out, as on any line that can fail.

A function that raises nothing, put where a raising type is wanted, is called through a small function written for it, the first time it is needed, which calls it and answers true:

static bool zeno_raising_wrap_double(zeno_closure *zeno_self, int64_t a0, int64_t *zeno_result) {
    (void)zeno_self;
    *zeno_result = z_double(a0);
    return true;
}

A function written where a value goes is compiled the raising way from the start when that is where it goes. The checker notes each such place (made_raising), and both compilers read the note, so neither works it out again.

The note is kept for each copy of a generic. It was kept by line and column at first, and the copies of a generic function share every line and column. So a line that hands size to a list of raising functions in one copy, and to a list of plain ones in the other, was refused by a firmware build that zeno run took (found in review). A note is now kept by a Spot: the declaration of the named function it is in, then the line and the column. Each copy has a declaration of its own, and each compiler knows which function it is writing.

A value that is already of a plain function type cannot become a raising one, and is refused:

error: `f` of `twice` should be function(int) -> int raises ValueError, and this is a function value that raises nothing. In a firmware build a function that can raise is called in another way from one that cannot, so one kept as the first cannot become the second. Give it the type `function(int) -> int raises ValueError` where it is made, or build without `--firmware`

Why it is refused and not carried. The plan left this open: it could be carried in a block of its own that holds the plain one and calls it, by the rule 9.2 is to bring. That is a block made and freed at each such place in a build with no collector, for a program that can say what it means where the value is made, by giving it the raising type there. The message says so. If a real program needs it, 9.2's rule is the way in.

An ordinary build changes not at all. Both kinds of function are called alike there (5.5i). Each compiler also checks, where it puts one function value in the place of another, that both are called the same way, so a gap in the checker would stop the build with a message and not write a wrong call.

The interpreter, the VM and the fifteen targets do not look at types, and needed nothing.

56.6 What it costs

Nothing for a program that does not use it. tools/same.py built every program of tools/targets.py and every benchmark, 444 in all, each of the fifteen ways, with the zeno of 0.7.0 and with this one. The 443 that were there before wrote the same C, the same IR, the same joined program and the same bytecode, 6,645 builds of 6,645. The fifteen that differ are those of tools/targets/edge-raises-in-types.zeno, which 0.7.0 cannot read. No engine file was touched.

After 56.8, with its fixes from the review: 445 programs, and again 6,645 of the 6,645 builds of the 443 old ones the same. The thirty that differ are the fifteen ways of each of the two new programs.

56.7 How it is held to its word

  • The parser (parser.rs): a_function_type_can_say_what_it_raises, raises_after_a_result_belongs_to_the_function_it_ends and brackets_go_round_a_function_type_and_nothing_else: each way of writing it, the type in a list of parameters with another after it, and each message.
  • The checker (checker.rs): a_call_through_a_function_type_that_raises_is_checked_as_raising, what_a_function_raises_fits_a_type_that_catches_it, an_ordinary_build_does_not_hold_what_a_function_raises_against_a_plain_type, a_firmware_build_cannot_make_a_plain_function_value_raise, a_second_kind_after_raises_in_a_type_is_named_as_one, a_function_type_in_a_message_is_written_as_in_a_program, a_fault_after_raises_in_a_type_is_one_raised_by_hand (56.1) and a_function_of_an_interface_says_what_its_function_types_raise.
  • Both compilers (emit_c.rs, emit_llvm.rs): raising_function_values_match_every_way builds tools/targets/edge-raises-in-types.zeno in a firmware build and with no collector, through C and through LLVM, and each must print what zeno run prints. With no collector it must end with 0 blocks left. The program hands raising functions, and plain ones made raising, to a parameter, into a field, into a list, to map, filter, reduce and sort, and fails in each a thousand times. The test also holds the C of the small functions above (and of the one for parse, which only passes its answer on) to what this chapter shows, and holds an ordinary build to having none. what_a_firmware_build_refuses_says_so lost its rows for a raising function used as a value.
  • The tests' own firmware build is now checked as zeno build --firmware checks it. The two compilers' tests checked a program for a firmware build with the rules of an ordinary one, and so never saw what the checker notes for a firmware build alone. With the note of 56.5 that mattered, so they use the firmware rules now. The same programs are left out of a firmware build as before, 48 of them in C and LLVM, counted at both ends. One is left out by another message: edge-u64.zeno was left out by the compiler with "nothing in this try can be caught", and is now left out by the checker, since it says raises OverflowError on a function that only multiplies (5.19m).
  • The targets: the same program is in tools/targets/, so every target prints what zeno run prints.
  • For 56.8: a_function_that_is_kept_takes_what_it_uses in the checker has compose and each refusal in its words, and a_second_kind_inside_brackets_is_named_as_one the message inside [ ]. Both compilers: a_kept_function_takes_what_it_uses_every_way builds tools/targets/edge-kept-functions.zeno every way, with the same memory report from C and LLVM and 0 blocks left. It keeps functions in a variable, a field and a list, gives one to a parameter that says take, makes them a thousand times, calls them after the function that made them returned, fails a thousand times through a type that says raises, and calls make(2)("5") on both paths. each_copy_of_a_generic_makes_its_own_functions_raising builds the program of the review as firmware, through C and LLVM.

56.8 A function that is kept takes what it uses

function compose(f: take function(int) -> int, g: take function(int) -> int) -> function(int) -> int {
    return function(n: int) -> int { return f(g(n)) }
}

A build with no collector refused this with "this function uses a value from outside it that has one owner, so it must be gone before that value is..." (5.17d). A function written where a value goes only looked at what it used, and so lived for its line.

The rule added: a function that is kept takes what it uses. If it is returned, put in a variable or a field, appended, or given to a parameter that says take, each value with one owner that it uses is given to it, as let b = a gives it. The function owns them from then on, and frees them when it is freed. A function that is only passed along, to map or to a parameter that looks, looks as before.

Why no word at the function, as Rust's move. The line already says the function is kept: it is after return or =, or goes to a parameter that says take. A function that is kept and still only looked would be gone before it could be called, so there is no second meaning for a word to tell apart. A function's first line says take for a parameter because a call does not show what the function does with it; here the line shows it.

Where "kept" is known. A function written where a value goes has its type worked out where it is written, and only the place it goes knows whether it is kept: take in the checker, which every let, return, field, append and parameter that says take goes through. So take marks the function it is about to check, and the function, when it is checked, gives away what it uses.

By the one rule of let b = a. The steps of giving a value away (a loop or a case looking at it, a line that already used it, a let at the top of the file that a function reads, and the record of where it went, which a loop and a try read) were made one function, give_away, in a commit of their own that changed nothing. A kept function calls it for each value it takes, so the two cannot drift apart, and each message is the one let b = a gets.

What it may take is the surrounding function's to give: its own value, or a parameter that says take. A parameter that only looks gets the message every look gets, to write take on it. A value of a function further out cannot be taken by a function written two levels in: the function in between may be called again, and would have nothing left to give the second time. The message says to hand the value in as a parameter that says take. self cannot be taken either: it is the object the method was called on, and take cannot be written on it, so the message says to put what the function needs in a let first.

A var is refused in every build. A var can be given a new value after the function took the old one, and the two would then hold different things, or would have to share one variable, which a value with one owner cannot do. With no collector a var of the function around was refused already, by design (5.17c). With a collector, the first half of 9.2 took a var whose type says owned: zeno build then wrote a program that stopped with a fault of memory, and zeno build --llvm printed the length of the old list where zeno run printed the new one (found in the review, plan, Changes 4). 0.7.0 refused that program, so nothing that built before is touched. The message says to declare it with let, and does not speak of a collector:

error: this function is kept, so it takes `xs`, but `xs` is a `var`: the function around it could give it a new value after this one took it. Declare it with `let`

And each compiler refuses, rather than writes, a taken value it has no plain variable for, so a mistake in the checker cannot become a fault of memory again.

How it is built. The checker writes the names a kept function took into Types.taken, by its Spot (56.5): only names, since what each is, and so how it is freed, is for each copy of a generic to say. In the C the function's block holds each value. Making the block moves it in and leaves NULL behind, so the end of the surrounding function frees nothing, and the block's drop frees each by its kind. Through LLVM the value is loaded from its slot and null stored there, and the block's drop function frees it. With a collector the value moves the same way, and nothing is freed by hand.

Nothing changes where nothing has one owner. With a collector and no owned written, a list or an object is shared, a function does not use a value with one owner, and nothing moves: the C, the IR and the bytecode of every program of 0.7.0 are what they were (56.6).

Found on the way: a function called straight from the call that made it was never freed. make(2)("5") with no collector left one block, in 0.7.0 as well, whether the call worked or raised (found in the review of 9.1). The checker made the call of such a function the statement's only when its type was written owned, and a function type has one owner without the word. It is now the statement's, as any value made in the middle of a line is, and freed when the line is over.

56.9 A method used as a value

class Counter {
    count: int
    function bump(self, by: int) -> int {
        self.count += by
        return self.count
    }
}

let c = Counter(0)
let m = c.bump
print(m(1), m(2), [1, 2, 3].map(c.bump))

zeno run and every target always took c.bump as a value. Both compilers refused it, in every build, with a collector too: "cannot compile a method used as a value". It builds now, every way.

It is a function that calls the method. c.bump means function(by: int) -> int { return c.bump(by) }, and the checker writes exactly that function out, checks it as it checks one written by hand, and hands it to the compilers (Types.method_values, by the place of c.bump). So one rule answers both (plan, 9.2): passed along, it looks at c; kept, it takes c where c has one owner, by the rule of 56.8 and in its words; with a collector, where the object is shared, it shares it, as zeno run does. Its type is the method's, less self, with what the method raises (56.1). Nothing new was needed in either compiler but the step from c.bump to that function: the block, its drop, what it takes, and a raising call through it in a firmware build are those of any function written where a value goes.

Why not a block of its own, an object and a method, as zeno run holds it: that is a second kind of function value, with a second way to be called and freed, in two compilers and three kinds of build. Written out, it is the kind there already is, and the rules that hold for it hold here without a line more.

It is bound to the object of that line. zeno run reads c when it meets c.bump, and keeps that object. A function written by hand would read c when it is called, and see a var given another object in between, or a variable at the top of the file, which every function reads where it is. So the compilers hand the function a copy of what the variable holds on that line, and not the variable: var c = Counter(0), let m = c.bump, c = Counter(100), m(1) gives 1 everywhere. Where it takes the object, the object is moved out of the variable itself, as 56.8 says, and there is no copy to make.

What it can be. A method of an object that a variable holds, x.f with x a name: a let, a var, a parameter, self, a loop's variable. An object of an interface calls the method of its own class. A private method is still private. Any other object, as in make().size, a.b.size or xs[0].size, is as it was: zeno run takes it, and both compilers refuse it, and with one owner the checker says to call it there. So does a method of a copy of a generic class, and a method with types of its own.

Passed along, it is the line's. With no collector, one that is only passed along, apply(c.bump, 1), is freed when the line is over, as apply(function(n: int) -> int { ... }, 1) is. The checker moves the note that says so from the function it wrote to c.bump, which is what the compilers see (found by the test: one block was left).

Found on the way. A message about a function that is only looked at said "but this is a a function that is only looked at", and the same for a quantity: the type's own words already begin with "a". Only the words change.

What it costs. Nothing for a program that does not use it: tools/same.py finds the C, IR, zeno join and bytecode of 0.7.0 for every program that was there before. Of the 6,690 builds of 446 programs, 45 differ: the 15 ways of each of the three new programs of 9.1 and 9.2. And 8 more builds differ only in the words of a refusal, in builds that refused before and refuse still: tools/targets/edge-classes.zeno with no collector is refused at Node(10).sum, the next line, where it was refused at chain.sum; and tools/targets/values.zeno with no collector gets the message for a var of the function around, where it got the one for a method of a value that has one owner.

A method of an object that no variable holds is refused by both compilers with words that say what to write: "Put the object in a let first and use .size of that: then it builds".

Tests. The checker: its type, what it raises, passed along, kept, taken, a var and self refused with no collector, an interface, and make().size refused as before (a_method_used_as_a_value_is_a_function_that_calls_it). Both compilers: tools/targets/edge-method-values.zeno with no collector through C and LLVM, with the same memory report and 0 blocks left, and in the ordinary and firmware builds of both; the binding to the object of that line, at the top of a file and in a function with a var that is shared; and an owned object taken with a collector (a_method_used_as_a_value_every_way). The targets run the program, and nine print what zeno run prints here (Lua, Dart, Kotlin, C# and WebAssembly are not installed on this machine; the weekly check has them).

56.10 take in front of a place: moving out what may be none

class Slot {
    task: Task or none
}

let task = take slot.task       # slot.task is none now
if task is not none {
    run(task)
}

The need. With one owner, an object could not give away what a field holds, because nothing would be left in the field (5.8i). A list has pop(); a field had nothing, so a state machine could not hand on the buffer it held.

The rule. take in front of a field or an item of a list gives what is there and leaves none. The place must be one that may hold none, so that what is left is something its type already allows, and what comes back may be none too, and is tested as any such value is. It means the same in every build: where values are shared it still leaves none, so one program runs the same way under zeno run and with no collector. The plan weighs the other ways to write it (9.3); take is the word for "the value goes over, and the place holds nothing" since 5.19b, and it was reserved already, so no new word is needed and no program that builds today changes.

Where it goes. In front of a field, take slot.task, or of an item of a list, take tasks[i], reached in any way: take slots[i].task, take make().task. It binds as a minus does, to the whole place after it. A variable is not a place for it, since let b = a gives a away already, and the parser says so:

error: `take` goes in front of a field or an item, as in `take slot.task`, and leaves `none` there. `task` is a variable: `let other = task` already gives what it holds away

A place that cannot hold none gets a message that says how to make it one, and for a list, that pop() takes an item out:

error: `take` leaves `none` in `id`, and `id` is written `int`, which does not allow `none`. If it may be empty, declare it as `id: int or none`
error: `take` leaves `none` in the place of the item, and the items of this list are written `Task`, which does not allow `none`. To take the item out, use `pop()`. To leave `none` in its place, make it a `list[Task or none]`

A value of a dict is not a place for it yet: a dict cannot hold a value that may be none (get gives none for a key that is not there), so there is nothing to leave.

The guards. A value that has one owner leaves the object or the list it was in. So the three guards of pop() (5.15e) hold, by the same code (takes_out in the checker): only the owner may, not while a loop walks the owner, and not on a line that has already looked at it. A method may take out what its own object holds, and whoever calls the method is held to the rule in its place (5.19k), as for pop(). After a take, on the same line, the place holds none, so a look at it there needs no guard.

Reading such a field, which a line cannot do with one owner, keeps its words, and adds what take would do: "To move it out and leave none in the field, write take s.task". The same for an item. It says what take does rather than that it is the answer, since the line may be walking a chain, at = at.next, which take would cut. The words of that refusal change in 15 builds that refused before and refuse still: book/11-classes#11, book/13-none#8 and tools/targets/edge-big.zeno, in the five builds with one owner.

How it is built. One new expression, ExprKind::Take(place), last of its kind. The parser reads take where a minus may go. The checker gives it the type of the place (take_out). The interpreter reads the place and stores none; the VM does the same with two new instructions, TakeField and TakeIndex, which no program of before uses. Both compilers read the value into a variable of their own and write none where it was, so nothing is freed there: whoever receives the value owns it, and if nobody does, the statement does, as with any value made in the middle of a line. With no collector, text that a field or a list kept leaves its keeper as pop() makes it leave a list (zeno_text_take). lower.rs makes it two statements for the targets, keep what is there and then store none, so no target's runtime changes. zeno join writes it (take slot.task), with the brackets every operator gets there.

What it costs. Nothing for a program that does not use it: the C, IR, zeno join and bytecode of every program that was there before are those of 0.7.0 (tools/same.py).

Tests. The parser: where take binds, and its two messages. The checker: the type in every build, a place that cannot hold none, text, the three guards, a method that takes out of its own object, and the message for reading such a field (take_leaves_none_where_a_value_was). Both compilers: tools/targets/edge-take.zeno, a scheduler that hands its task on, fields and items of an object, of text and of a number that may be none, a list of a fixed length, a thousand rounds, and a value that nobody receives, with no collector through C and LLVM with the same memory report and 0 blocks left, and in the ordinary and firmware builds of both. A bad index stops the program at the take, at the same line and column, in each build of C. The C writes none where the value was and frees nothing there (take_leaves_none_every_way). The targets run the program, and nine print what zeno run prints here.

56.11 A value with one owner as what a type parameter stands for

class Stack[T] {
    items: list[T]
    function push(self, x: take T) { self.items.append(x) }
}
let frames: Stack[Frame] = Stack([])      # refused with no collector until 0.8.0

The need. A firmware program wants a queue of frames, a ring of buffers, a Box of what a sensor read. With no collector every list and object has one owner, and none of them could fill a type parameter: same([1, 2]), Box(Frame(1, [])) and Stack[Frame] were refused in every build with no collector (5.16i). A generic was a tool for numbers only there.

The rule. A copy of a generic is checked as if it had been written by hand with the type in the place of T (3.16d). With no collector that rule was not followed: the checker stopped at the call. The stop is taken away, and nothing else is added. Stack[Frame] is then a class with a list of frames, which a build with no collector has taken since 5.15c, and every rule of one owner holds of it in the words it has for a class written by hand.

take T. 5.19f refused it, "because T may be a number". It is now read for whatever T stands for: in a copy where T is copied, the word changes nothing, which is what it already does where values are shared (5.19a). So function same[T](x: take T) -> T is right for an int and for a list, in every build. A generic that keeps or returns what it is given and does not say take is wrong for a list, and the error is inside the copy, with the note that names the copy and the line that asked for it. The other ways were weighed. Making take implied for a T would make count[T](xs: list[T]) take a list it only looks at, and the caller lose it. Refusing a list for a T that is not taken would be a rule a hand-written class does not have. Only the checked copy says the same thing as a class written by hand, so it is the one rule there is. Whether a written type is a type parameter is known by the variable the name finds, which the outline and each copy record (type_params).

What the call does. What T stands for is known only once every argument has been read, so a call cannot ask the copy what each parameter does. It goes by what the generic wrote: a field of a generic class, and a parameter written take T, take the value; a parameter written T looks at it, and one written list[T] already did. A look is never what fills T: T is the value, and a look at a list fills it with the list (unlent). The copy then says whether the look may be kept, as a hand-written function would. With no collector a list that fills T is an owned list, whatever the argument was called when it was read, so Box([1]) and let b: Box[list[int]] ask for the same copy.

Names. With no collector every list has one owner, so owned says nothing in the name of a copy: the copy of Box for a list of ints is Box[list[int]], and z_Box_list_int in the C (5.14c). With a collector Box[owned list[int]] and Box[list[int]] are two copies, and keep owned in the name.

An error in a field of a copy. It had no note, since the fields of a copy were worked out outside the note that the methods get. A field of Stack[Packet] that cannot hold an owned Packet now says which copy it is in, as a mistake in a method does.

How it is built. Only the checker changed. The refusal in the [ ] of a generic and the two in infer went, take T is read, a call of a generic takes or looks as above, and the names of copies drop owned with no collector. The compilers build a copy as they build any class, and free what it holds by Drops, so neither emit_c.rs nor emit_llvm.rs needed a line. The interpreter, the VM and the targets were never told what owns what.

What it costs. Nothing for a program that does not use it: the C, IR, zeno join and bytecode of every program that was there before are those of 0.7.0 (tools/same.py). Two programs that were refused with one owner are refused still, with the words a hand-written copy gets: book/19-generics#7 returns an item of a list it only looked at, and tools/targets/edge-modules keeps a T it was only lent, each in the five builds with one owner.

Tests. The checker: same, Box and Stack with a list, an object and an enum value; a parameter written T that looks, and one written take T that takes; take T with a number in every build; the error inside a copy, with its note; take on a copied type that is no type parameter, still refused; an owned class with a collector (a_value_with_one_owner_can_fill_a_type_parameter).
