Both compilers: tools/targets/edge-generic-owned.zeno, same, Box, Stack, Pair and a Slot that hands on with take, with a list, an object and an enum value, a stack that hands its items back, copies printed, and a thousand rounds, with no collector through C and LLVM with the same memory report and 0 blocks left, and in the ordinary and firmware builds of both. The same test builds the kept function of 56.5 and 56.8 in a generic, taking a list in one copy and a number in another, which waited for this part, and an owned class copy with a collector (a_value_with_one_owner_fills_a_type_parameter_every_way). The targets run the program, and nine print what zeno run prints here.

56.12 A dict that owns its values

let channels: dict[str, Channel] = [:]     # refused with no collector until 0.8.0
channels["volts"] = Channel("volts", [12, 13])
channels["volts"] = Channel("volts", [14])    # the old one is freed
let amps = channels.pop("amps")

The need. A program with no collector could keep lists and objects in a list, in a field and, since 56.11, in a generic, but not under a key: a dict's values had to be copied when stored (10.14). A table of channels by name, or of handlers by command, had to be a list with a second dict of positions beside it.

The rule. A dict owns its values, as a list owns its items (5.15c). 10.14 wrote out what that means for each way into a dict, and the plan kept it (9.5), so this part builds what was written:

Written With one owner
d[key] a look at the value
d[key] = value takes the new value, and frees the one that was there
d.pop(key) hands the value to whoever receives it
d.clear(), and the end of the dict free every value
for key, value in d a look at each value, for the body
d.get(key) a look, or none
d.get(key, instead) refused
d.values() refused

A look is the look a parameter gets: it is read, changed in place and passed on, and not kept. The message for keeping one names the owner and the way out, pop(key), as the message for an item of a list names pop().

The two refusals. get(key, instead) gives either a look at a value the dict owns or instead, which only the line owns, and nothing after the line can tell which, so nothing could know whether to free it. Making instead a look too would leave the value it was made from with no owner; making the dict's value a copy would copy a list on every call. get(key) and a test say the same thing with an owner for every value, so the message says to write that. values() would be a second list of the same objects, which is a second owner of each; the loop with two names gives the same values one at a time as looks, so the message says to write that. keys() is not touched: a key is a number or text, which is copied.

The guards. pop, a store and clear free a value or hand it over, so they are held to the three guards of a list's pop() (5.15e), by the same code (takes_out): only the owner, not while a loop walks the dict, not on a line that has already looked at it. The loop message says "a dict" and "its values", and each says what was being done: "take a value out of", "replace a value of".

Only with one owner. With a collector nothing changes. A dict of lists or of shared objects was fine there; a dict of objects of an owned class is still refused by zeno build, as it was ("cannot compile a dict with these keys and values yet"), since a dict that is itself shared cannot be the owner of what it holds (5.15c). The rules above are asked for only where every value has one owner, so zeno run and a build with a collector check every program as before.

How it is built. The checker: a dict's index lends the value when it is owned, get(key) gives a look or none, and the two refusals and the guards are beside those of a list. runtime.c is not changed, since any change there changes the C of every program. Instead each program with such a dict gets three functions of its own for each kind of value, zeno_dict_put_values_{kind}, zeno_dict_clear_values_{kind} and zeno_dict_drop_values_{kind}, written by Drops beside the free functions of lists. They free a value with the free function its kind already has, and call the runtime's own zeno_dict_set, zeno_dict_clear and zeno_dict_drop. A store over a key that is not there frees NULL, which does nothing. The LLVM build defines the same three in IR. A loop over a dict written where the loop walks it frees the values with the dict when there is one name, and with the list of values the loop made when there are two. A list of dicts that own their values gets a free function of its own name, so that it cannot meet the one for a list of plain dicts.

What it costs. Nothing for a program that does not use it: the C, IR, zeno join and bytecode of every program that was there before are those of 0.7.0 (tools/same.py). The words of a refusal change in the builds with one owner of six programs that are refused still, for another reason further down: examples/channels.zeno keeps what get gives, and edge-fixed, edge-json, edge-lists, io and text meet a rule of one owner that was behind the dict's. Two pieces of the book that were refused now build with no collector and print what zeno run prints, with 0 blocks left: book/10-dicts#3 and book/15-function-values#3.

Found on the way. A function that is given a parameter that may be none, and reads a field of it after testing it, read the field before the test in every build of C and LLVM of 0.7.0, because the compilers read a parameter's fields once at the start of a function that cannot change them (22.8). A function such as id_of(f: Frame or none) then read through NULL when given none. Such a parameter is now left out of that read. No program in the repository wrote one, so no C changed (a_parameter_that_may_be_none_is_read_after_its_test).

Tests. The checker: each row of the table, keeping a look from [ ] and from get, the two refusals, the three guards, and a build with a collector as it was (a_dict_owns_its_values). Both compilers: tools/targets/edge-dict-owned.zeno, a dict of objects and one of lists each way in the table, a dict of enum values, a dict in a field and dicts in a list, a dict made where a loop walks it, and a thousand stores over one key, with no collector through C and LLVM with the same memory report and 0 blocks left, and in the ordinary and firmware builds of both. The C of the three functions, the name of a list of dicts that own their values, and the refusal with a collector (a_dict_owns_its_values_every_way). The targets run the program.

56.13 What was known when the benchmarks stopped

On 2026-11-19 the owner of the language stopped the benchmarks for items 9 to 13: the parts are tested and pushed, and the engines are timed later if he asks. tools/same.py stays, as a test. This is what had been measured by then, on the build machine (4 cores, Linux).

Counts (cachegrind, the sizes of bench/run.py --count), 0.7.0 against 9.1 to 9.4 with the cures below:

zeno run --vm zeno run
fib -0.51% 0.00%
loop -0.57% 0.00%
sort +0.08% -0.02%
strings -0.11% 0.00%
trees -0.18% +0.14%
nbody -0.15% -0.21%

The count of trees under zeno run moves by 0.1 to 0.3% from one run of the same build to the next, with where malloc puts things and the seeds of the hash tables; the best of two runs at size 12 was -0.01%.

Cures that brought the counts back. 9.1 made ast::Type bigger, which cost zeno run 0.57%: the kind after raises is boxed now. 9.3's two arms cost the VM 0.6%: they call a cold function of their own (take_out), and the two instructions come after the superinstructions. The interpreter's arm for take is in a cold function too, since it had grown the frame of eval from 0x448 to 0x478 bytes.

The clock (bench/compare.py, best of 6 rounds, the VM, builds under names of the same length, before the interpreter's cure): fib +4.0%, loop -2.8%, sort +1.9%, strings +0.1%, trees +5.1%, nbody +4.5%. An earlier run of 4 rounds on a busy machine gave, for zeno run, fib +3.9% and strings +4.0%, and the others within 1%. Fewer instructions taking longer points to where the code lies (24.29, 50.7), but the cause was not run down: the noise floor and a bisect by the clock were begun and stopped.

56.14 A list of numbers that may be none, with no collector

var readings: list[float or none] = [21.5, none, 22.0]   # refused with no collector until 0.8.0
readings.append(none)
readings[1] = 21.0              # a new box, and the old one freed
let last = readings.pop()       # the box freed, the number kept

The need. A number that may be none is a number and a flag, and the two do not fit in the 64 bits of a slot of a list (5.11i), so a list holds the address of a small box for each number, and NULL for none. With a collector the collector frees the boxes. With no collector nothing did, and zeno build --no-collector refused the list (5.16h). A list of readings where some are missing is the plainest list a sensor gives.

Two ways, and the one built. The plan (9.6) chose A: a second, packed list of flags beside the values, one byte an item, used with no collector alone. It allowed B, the boxes owned by the list, if A turned out to reach past the runtime's list functions and the places both compilers read and write an item. It does:

  • A list is a zeno_list in runtime.c, and runtime.c is pasted whole into the C of every program. A field of flags in zeno_list changes the C of every program, which the rule that a program that does not ask builds as before (tools/same.py) does not allow.
  • The other way to A is a second kind of list, with the flags, written into each program that needs it. Then every function on lists has a twin for it (append, insert, pop, a store, slice, +, *, reverse, find, in, map, filter, reduce, a loop's copy, the free), in C and in IR, and every place either compiler picks a list function picks between the two.

B needs neither. The free and the copy that keeps a box of its own exist already for text (5.9x), and a box is freed with the same zeno_free as any block of the pool. So B is built, with no collector alone, and A stays on the list (56.18).

The rule. With no collector, a list owns the box of each number that may be none, as it owns its copy of each text. Each way into a list makes a box in the pool for a number, and none for none. A read takes the number out and leaves the box. A store makes the new box and frees the old. pop and take read the number out and free the box. clear and the end of the list free every box. A list made from another (+, *, a slice, filter, map, the copy a loop walks) gets boxes of its own. find and in put the number they look for in a box in the text room, given back when the statement is over. The same holds for float, bool and the sized numbers.

Only with no collector. A build with a collector writes what 0.7.0 wrote: the boxes are the collector's, in the text room (zeno_box_int), as before. Nothing is asked for by a word, since the only programs that change are ones --no-collector refused.

How it is built. runtime.c is not changed. Drops writes, for a program that has such a list, the functions it uses: zeno_box_keep_{kind} (a box from the pool, or NULL), zeno_box_take_{kind} (the number, and the box freed), zeno_list_keep_boxes_{kind} (a box of its own for each item of a list just made) and zeno_list_drop_boxes (every box freed, then the list). A list of such lists gets the free function of its depth, as lists of text do. The store makes the new box before it frees the old one, so that C and LLVM take blocks from the pool in the same order and give the same memory report. The LLVM build defines the same functions in IR, as zeno.box.keep.int and the rest.

What it costs. Each number that is there takes a block of the pool: 8 bytes and the pool's few bytes beside it, against 9 bytes an item for A. A list filled from empty holds 679 numbers in the 32,768 bytes of the pool by default, and the 680th stops the program with the message of a full pool (5.9j), in C and in LLVM alike. A number that stands for "nothing" in a plain list, or an enum with a case for the missing value, costs less on a small board, and none-list.md says so. Nothing for a program that does not have such a list: every program that built before writes the C, IR, zeno join and bytecode of 0.7.0 (tools/same.py). The words of a refusal change in the builds with no collector of tools/targets/edge-repeat.zeno, which is refused still, for another reason further down.

Tests. Both compilers: tools/targets/edge-none-list.zeno has lists of ints, floats, u8s and bools that may be none, with none first and last, every method above, map, filter and reduce, such a list in a field and in a list, a loop whose body appends to the list it walks, and six hundred numbers stored and replaced, and a list that outgrows the pool stops with the message of a full pool. It is built with no collector through C and LLVM, with the same memory report and 0 blocks left, and in the ordinary and firmware builds of both, each printing what zeno run prints. The same test reads the C of the helpers and checks that a build with a collector writes zeno_box_int and no zeno_box_keep_int (a_list_of_numbers_that_may_be_none_every_way). The targets run the program. The page is none-list.md.

56.15 The size of the pool on the command line, and spare blocks that are checked

zeno build --no-collector --pool 2104 readings.zeno     # -DZENO_POOL=2104
zeno build --no-collector --text-room 64 readings.zeno  # -DZENO_TEXT_ROOM=64
zeno build --no-collector --memory late.zeno            # a write after free stops it

The need. The pool and the text room of a build with no collector are fixed when it is built (5.9c, 5.9j), and --memory says exactly how big each must be. But the only way to give a build that size was to run the C compiler by hand with -DZENO_POOL=, which zeno build --board does not let a person do at all. And a write to a block after it was given back went unseen: valgrind and the address sanitizer see the pool as one array (5.9k).

Both sizes, and the words. --pool N and --text-room N, both, because a person who finds one looks for the other, and --memory prints both. = may stand for the space, as with --target and --board. Each hands its -D to the C compiler, or to clang with the runtime file beside the IR, and to the board's compiler with --board. The C and the IR do not change: the size is in the command, where it was by hand, so a C file written with --pool is the C file written without it.

Where they are refused. They mean something only where the pool and the room are arrays of a fixed size: a build with no collector, for a chip. With a collector there is no pool; with memory owned on a computer the pool and the room grow, and their first sizes are not what a person means by the size; --web, --target and every command but build compile nothing. Each is refused with what to do instead, and not ignored, because an option that is taken and does nothing leaves a person sure of a size the program does not have. A size must be a whole number above zero and at most 2,147,483,647, since the runtime prints it in its messages as a C int; and given once.

The check, and why it is asked for by --memory. A block that is given back is filled with 0xA5 past the link to the next spare block. When the block is handed out again, every such byte must still be 0xA5, and the link must be NULL or a spare block of the same size in the pool (zeno_in_pool), or the program stops with "a block of memory was written to after it was given back". The link is looked at before it is followed, because a write over it is the worst case: it would hand out an address that is no block at all. 0xA5 and not zero, because zero is what a block most often holds. It is a check for trying a program, so it goes with the option for trying one, --memory, and not with a word of its own (the plan, 9.7); it is a check, so a minimal build leaves it out (30.2).

Only where it is asked for. runtime.c is not changed, since it is written whole into the C of every program, and a check behind an #ifdef there would still change the text of every C file (tools/same.py). with_spares_checked writes it into the runtime of a build that asks: two prototypes after zeno_spare, a call in zeno_alloc_raw before the link is followed, a call in zeno_free before the block goes on its list, and the two functions after zeno_in_pool, each behind #ifdef ZENO_MEMORY_REPORT, so the C file built by hand without that flag has not a byte of it. The LLVM build writes the same runtime beside its IR. Each place it goes is found by text that must be in the runtime once, so a change to the runtime that moves one stops the tests rather than leaving the check out.

What it costs. Nothing without --memory: the C of every program is what 0.7.0 wrote, with or without --pool. With it, a block given back is written once more and read once more when it comes off its list, in proportion to its size. No block is bigger, and the report is the same line for line.

Found on the way. docs/pool.md said buffer.zeno needs 25,384 bytes of pool; the compiler of today needs 17,184 for it, and a pool of 20,000 runs it, so a change since the page was written made it cheaper. It was not run down. The page and its exercise 2 give the numbers of today.

Tests. The options: both ways of writing each, the flags they make, and each refusal of a size (the_pool_and_the_text_room_are_sized_on_the_command_line). The size: a program runs in the pool its report names and stops a byte below, with the flags --pool makes (with_no_collector_the_pool_has_an_end). The check: a write into a block and one into its link after free, through C and LLVM, each stopped; the same C without --memory runs to the end; the C differs from the plain C by the check alone; and a program that gives back hundreds of blocks and keeps to its own runs as zeno run runs it, with 0 blocks left (with_memory_a_write_to_a_block_given_back_stops_the_program). The page is pool-size.md.

56.16 A function inside a function, and a default that is worked out

function g(n: int, top: int = n * 10) -> int {
    let a = sq(2)                 # above its line
    function sq(x: int) -> int {  # uses nothing around it
        return x * x
    }
    let k = n * 2
    function add(x: int) -> int { # uses `k`
        return x + k
    }
    return a + add(1)
}

The need. Both compilers refused a function with a name written inside a function, and a default that is more than a literal. zeno run takes both, so a program that used either could not be built at all, and the plan (9.8) puts them first among the refusals of a build.

Not "a let at its line". The plan's first way was to make each such function a function value in a let at its own line. That refuses what zeno run takes: a call above the function's line runs there, and so do two such functions that call each other. What zeno run refuses is a use above a let the function needs, and the checker already says so in every engine ("k is declared further down than the first use of add, which needs it"). The build stands on that rule instead.

Three kinds. inner_plan, which both compilers call so that they agree, sorts the functions of a block by what each uses that it does not declare (free_names):

  • Nothing of the function around it (only its parameters, the file's names and other functions of this kind): a function of the file, under a name of its own, zeno_inner_N_name in C and @zeno.inner.N.name in LLVM, since two functions may each have an sq inside. It is in sight from the start of its block to the end, and compiled after the function it is in, seeing what it saw there. A call above its line and two that call each other work, and it costs what a function of the file costs. This is the common case.
  • A let, a var, a parameter or an import around it, or a call to one of this kind: a closure, made once, just after the last declaration of its block it uses, and after each closure beside it that it calls. The checker holds every use below that line. Inside its body its own name is the closure, so it can call itself.
  • Two of the second kind that call each other: each would have to be made first. Refused, with a message that says to give one to the other as a parameter; left for later.

Who owns the closure. With a collector the closure is the collector's, as any function value is. With no collector the block owns it and frees it as it ends, so it may be called and not used as a value, and a function written where a value goes may not call it, since that one may outlive the block. Copying it on each use was the other way (the planning thread's point 3); it was not taken, because a function value with no collector already has one owner and a let of a function written where a value goes is the way to one that can be given. Both are refused with a message that says so. A var around it that it changes is shared, and with no collector refused as before.

Defaults. A default that is more than a literal is worked out at a call that leaves the argument out, in the order of the parameters, after the arguments given (which keep the order they are written in). It reads what it reads where the function is written: the file's variables and functions, the parameters before it, and self in a method. The compiler swaps its scopes for those while it writes the default, so a variable of the calling function with the same name is not seen, and the default sees the inner functions that were in sight where its function is written. In C each given argument is held in a variable first, so that a default reads it once; in LLVM each is a value already. A default on a closure is refused for now: the call goes through a function value, which has no defaults.

Opt-in. Nothing asks for this but the program itself: only a program that a build refused before builds in a new way, and the C and the IR of every other program are what they were (tools/same.py).

The other refusals. As the plan asks, every other refusal of the two compilers was listed and tried against zeno run. Nearly all are guards behind the checker, which refuses the program first. The ones a program can reach are in compiler.md, each with its reason. The message for print([]) and [none] alone said "a list of these"; it now says that a build needs to know what the list holds, and how to say it.

Tests. functions_inside_functions_every_way holds tools/targets/edge-inner-functions.zeno to zeno run in every build of both compilers and with memory that grows, with 0 blocks left: a call above the line, two of the first kind calling each other, one calling itself, one made in a loop, one in a method, three deep, one that raises, and defaults that read earlier parameters, the file's variables, a function with a side effect, and self. With a collector, a var changed after the function was written and a function returned as a value. It checks where each kind goes in the C and the IR, and every refusal word for word through both. The page is inner-functions.md.

56.17 The sweep: what a build still refuses, and why

The need. Each page that names what a build refuses was written at the step that built it, and later steps took rows away without always striking them. The plan (9.9) asks for every refusal named in no-collector.md, firmware.md, functions-and-errors.md, one-owner.md, chapter 11 and part 7 of missing.md to be run again, and for each page to list what is refused by design, with the reason, and nothing else.

What was found. Run again on the compiler of 9.8:

  • Built now, and struck: keeping a function that looks (9.2, a kept function takes), a list or an object for T (9.5), a list of numbers that may be none (9.6), raise e (5.9d), moving out of a field (5.8i, 56.10), the pool's size and checked spare blocks (5.9j, 5.9k, 56.15).
  • Refused by design with no collector, and missing from the table of no-collector.md, so added: replacing what a field holds through a parameter that only looks; taking an item out of a list a for walks (5.15e); keeping an item that [ ] only looks at; a kept function that uses a var from outside it; and the function inside a function of 56.16, used as a value. The table has seven rows now, each the rule of one owner or of a block that owns what it made.
  • What every build refuses is the table of compiler.md (56.16).

One test holds both. what_a_build_with_no_collector_refuses_says_so has a program for each row of both tables and the words of its refusal. A row of no-collector.md must be taken by zeno run and by a build with a collector, through C and LLVM, and refused with no collector in its words by both. A row of compiler.md must be taken by zeno run and refused in its words by both compilers, and refused with no collector too. It reads the two tables from the pages: a row on a page with no program, or a program with no row, fails it. The older test of that name, which holds the one-owner refusals one by one and a program of the lines beside them that build, is what_one_owner_turns_down_says_so now.

Words that were changed. Four messages said less than they could, and the sweep put them right. print([]) and [none] alone said "a list of these"; they say that a build needs to know what the list holds now, and how to say it. A variable that only holds none had "yet" at the end of its advice. A method that comes with Zeno, used as a value, said ".append on this" in C and "on a list" in LLVM; both say what it is now. LLVM said "a function or a block" where C said "a function or block"; one wording now. Each of these programs was refused before and is refused now.

tools/same.py against 9.7 (c7b5d39): 451 programs, 15 ways, 6765 builds, 6704 the same and 61 different, all programs refused before. edge-inner-functions.zeno and the book's sample 08-functions#14 build now (56.16). edge-order.zeno is refused at a later line, a built-in used as a value, where it was refused at a default. The book's samples 09-lists#0 and 08-functions#1, and edge-enum-numbers.zeno through LLVM, are refused in the new words above. Not one program that built before is written differently.

56.18 Left for later

  • A list of kinds after raises in a type, inside brackets of its own. Refused with "a function type names one kind of error after raises...".
  • A plain function value made raising where it is used. Refused with "...so one kept as the first cannot become the second...". The way in is the rule of 9.2.
  • Closing the gap of 56.4 in an ordinary build. A question for the owner of the language, with the numbers above.
  • A method of an object that no variable holds, used as a value: make().size, a.b.size, xs[0].size. Both compilers refuse it as before. Put the object in a let first.
  • A method of a copy of a generic class, or one with types of its own, used as a value. Refused by both compilers as before.
  • A method that comes with Zeno used as a value: xs.append, text.upper. Refused by both compilers as before.
  • take in front of a value of a dict. A dict cannot hold a value that may be none yet. Refused with "...and not a value out of a dict yet".
  • get(key, instead) and values() on a dict that owns its values. Refused, with what to write instead (56.12).
  • A dict of objects of an owned class, with a collector. Refused by zeno build as before, in words that say why since 56.19; zeno run runs it.
  • A u64 that may be none (56.19). Refused by both compilers, in every build.
  • take with one owner on the line that writes the place: self.current = take self.waiting[0] is refused, as self.current = self.waiting.pop() was, because the line looks at self before it takes out of it. Two lines do it.
  • A list of objects of an owned class inside the [ ] of a generic, with a collector: Box[list[Packet]]. Refused, as such a list is inside any other type: "...and owned cannot be written inside another type yet". With no collector Box[list[Frame]] builds.
  • A packed list of flags beside the numbers (way A of 56.14), so that an item that may be none takes 9 bytes and no block. It needs a field in zeno_list or a second kind of list with every list function twice; see 56.14.
  • Two functions inside a function that call each other and use variables around them (56.16). Refused with "...Give one of them to the other as a parameter".
  • A default that is more than a literal on a function inside a function that uses variables around it (56.16). Refused; give the argument at the call.
  • A generic function, a class or an enum inside a function or a block. Refused by both compilers; write it at the top of the file.
  • Named arguments to a function held in a variable, and a built-in function used as a value (xs.map(str)). Refused by both compilers; see compiler.md for the reasons.

56.19 What the review of item 9 found, and a matrix that looks first

The need. The review of item 9 tried programs of its own and found four that zeno run ran and a build refused, which the sweep of 56.17 had not tried: in on a list of numbers or text that may be none (LLVM took it, C refused it), 3 in range(5), [3] in rows with no collector, and a list made in the default of a parameter that only looks, with no collector, which was told to "give it a name with let" though a default has nowhere to write one. A sweep that runs only what the pages name finds only what the pages name. So the review asked for a tool that tries every operation on every type in every build, and a test that fails when it finds a refusal no table lists.

The four.

  • x in xs, where the items may be none: C now makes x what the list holds first, as LLVM did.
  • range(...) anywhere but after for is the list of numbers that zeno run makes, new at each call: zeno_range_list in the runtime, with each number worked out without a sign so that a step of more than half of what an int holds cannot overflow on the way. So 3 in range(5), let r = range(5), total(range(5)) and range(3) + range(2) build, with no collector too, where the statement or the let owns the list. A for over a range still builds no list. A step of 0 is the ValueError of zeno run; a firmware build stops there, as it does for any fault it cannot carry as a value.
  • [3] in rows only looks at the items, so the checker compares an item with one owner as the list it is.
  • A list, a dict or an object made in the default of a parameter that only looks is the statement's, as one written in the call is: made at each call that leaves the argument out, and freed when the call's line is over.

Why a default was ever a problem. Each compiler worked a default out from a copy of it, made when it gathered the parameters of a call, and the checker notes what it learns by the address of each node it saw: that a list starts out owned, that a value is the statement's, that a list is of bytes. A copy has new addresses, so what was noted was lost, and a default holding lists, or bytes, was refused in every build or with no collector. A default is now held as Arc<Expr> in the tree, and a copy of the parameters shares it, so the compilers work out the node the checker saw. Function::fresh still gives a copy of a generic its own default, as it must.

tools/refused.py. Each program is one operation on one type: shown, compared, looked for with in, given to a parameter that looks or that takes, returned, kept in a list, a field or a dict, used as a default, walked, captured by a function that is kept, sorted, sliced, added. The types are the numbers, text, bool, u8, u64, each kind that may be none, lists of each, lists of lists, of objects and of bytes, dicts, a class, an owned class, an enum and a function. 705 programs, of which zeno run takes 674, built six ways (C and LLVM, each with a collector, with --firmware and with --no-collector) with CC and CLANG set to true, so nothing is compiled: 4,044 builds in about ten seconds. It fails on a refusal that matches no row of the two tables, on a program that C builds and LLVM refuses or the other way round, or both refuse in different words, and when tools/refused.txt is not what it found. That file holds each refusal with its row; the table test reads it and fails on a row that is not on its page or has no program in the test. A workflow, refused.yml, runs both on each push that changes the compiler.

What its first run found. No disagreement between C and LLVM. Eleven different refusals, of which these are built now:

  • A default holding lists, or bytes (above).
  • Two functions of one type in a list, [add, function(n: int) -> int { return n * 2 }], was a list of things whose type was not known; it is a list of that function type, as if the type were written.
  • [["a", none], [none]], [[1, none], []] and [none] in grid: the lists beside [none] or [], or the list on the right of in, say what it holds, and the compilers are now told.

And these are by design, and are rows now:

  • With no collector: returning or keeping what a parameter only looks at; filter on a list of lists or of objects; keeping an item that a for or a list comprehension walks. Each would give a value a second owner, and each message says what to write instead. Using a value after it was given away was a row already.
  • In every build: a u64 that may be none. A value that may be none and is not a pointer is a flag and the value, and a build has those pairs for an int, a float and a bool; a fourth for a u64 is left for later. The message said "this kind of value that may be none"; it says "a u64 that may be none" now.
  • With a collector: a dict of objects of an owned class (56.12). Its message said "cannot compile a dict with these keys and values yet", as if it were to come; it says why now, and what to write: "...keeps a dict where anything may share it, as there is a collector, and an object of an owned class has one owner. Make it a plain class, or build with --no-collector, where a dict owns its values". The table test holds that a build with no collector takes this row's program.

The review should run python3 tools/refused.py before each later review; adding an operation or a type to it is one line.

tools/same.py is always against a binary built from the tag. The comparison that says which programs a step changed is between a zeno built from tag v0.7.0 (17453fd) and the new one, never an older local build, whose own changes would hide among the step's. At the acceptance of item 9 (6d22db6): 451 programs, 15 ways, 6,765 builds, 6,523 the same and 242 different: 114 from the eight new programs in tools/targets/, 128 from 21 older programs that 0.7.0 refused. None is a program that 0.7.0 built.

After these follow-ups: 6,492 the same and 273 different, 31 more than at item 9. Against item 9 itself (f10c24b) that is 36 builds: two of the book's samples, 07-control-flow#6 (print(range(5))) and 09-lists#13 (let numbers = range(1, 11)), build now in each of their thirteen ways and print what zeno run prints, and edge-lists.zeno and 08-functions#7 are refused at the same line as before with two errors fewer after it, in the five ways with one owner, since [1] in [[1], [2]] builds there now. None of the 36 is a program that 0.7.0 or item 9 built.

The runtime grows only for a program that asks. zeno_range_list was first written into the runtime of every build. A C compiler drops a static function nobody calls, so no program got bigger; but every C file and every runtime beside the IR was written differently, which left same.py against the tag blind (3,091 builds differed by that function alone), and a C compiler that keeps what nobody calls, which the plain C of decision 55 allows, would put it in a board's flash unasked. The review ruled that the runtime of a program that uses nothing new must be, to the byte, the runtime 0.7.0 wrote. So the runtime has pieces, as it has the parts of a board (decision 45.4): PIECES in emit_c.rs names each, with the function by which a program uses it; runtime.c marks it #ifdef its name; C writes it when the program calls uses_piece, and LLVM when its IR declares the function (pieces_in_ir). zeno_range_list is the first. The test a_program_that_uses_no_piece_gets_the_runtime_of_0_7_0 holds the length and a hash of the runtime with no piece, for a build with a collector, --firmware, --no-collector and --owned, to what 0.7.0 wrote for print(1). Whatever is added to the runtime from now on is a piece. Making same.py skip the runtime was turned down: it would hide exactly this.

57. Several values from one function

function divide(a: int, b: int) -> (int, int) {
    return a // b, a % b
}

let quotient, remainder = divide(7, 2)

var low = 3
var high = 1
low, high = high, low

Item 10 of missing.md: a function that gives back two things at once, as a driver's read gives a value and a status. It is 10.1 to 10.4 of plan-9-14.md. Like everything added after 0.7.0 it is asked for by what is written (brackets after ->, commas after return and before =); a program that writes none of it means what it meant, builds to the same C, and runs the same bytecode.

57.1 The rules

  1. A function may give two or more values. Its first line says -> (int, str), and each return gives that many, with commas.
  2. They are received by that many names: let q, r = divide(7, 2), var q, r = ..., or q, r = ... for places that exist (a variable, a field, an item). Every value is received. _ in the place of a name receives one and drops it.
  3. Several values are not a value. They cannot be put in one variable, in a list, in a field, passed as one argument, used with an operator, or printed. Each is refused with one message: "divide gives 2 values. Receive each: let a, b = divide(...). To keep them together, declare a class".
  4. The right of = is one call that gives that many values, or that many values written out. All of the right is worked out, left to right, before anything on the left is given a value; then the left is filled left to right. That is what makes low, high = high, low a swap.
  5. (int, str) is written only after ->, in a function's first line or in a function type. Nowhere else is it a type.

Why every value must be received. A function that gives a value and a status is written so that the status is looked at. let value, _ = port.read() says in the line that it was dropped on purpose, and a call written as a statement, divide(7, 2), is refused as rule 3 refuses any other use of the values as one.

Why let a, b = 1, 2 is taken. Rule 4 needs values written out for the swap; refusing them after let would be an exception to it.

The messages, each with what to write:

  • "divide gives 2 values, and there are 3 places on the left of =. Receive each, and write _ for one that is not wanted"
  • "there are 2 places on the left of =, and the right gives one value, int. Give 2, as in a, b = 1, 2, or call a function that gives 2"
  • "this function gives 2 values, and this is one. Give each, as in return a, b", and its other side: "this function gives one value, int, and this return gives 2. A function that gives 2 says so in its first line, as in -> (int, int)"
  • "the function given to map gives 2 values, and map needs one value from each call. To keep them together, declare a class and return one object" (and filter, reduce, sort)
  • "a is on the left of = twice. Each place receives one value": which of the two a name would keep is a rule nobody can see. Items, xs[i], xs[j] = ..., are told apart only as the program runs, and are filled left to right.
  • "_ on the left of = drops a value, but here _ is a variable, which would be given it instead. Give the variable another name": _ is a legal name in 0.7.0, and where one is in sight _ on the left would quietly mean two things.
  • divide(divide(9, 2)) gives rule 3's message, and not "divide needs a value for b", which is what follows from it.
  • In the parser: "one value is written without brackets: -> int. Brackets hold two or more: -> (int, str)"; "several values cannot be none together. One of them can: (int, str or none)"; "a const names one value. Write a const for each"; "+= and the others change one place each. Write a line for each place"; and "(int, str) is written only after ->, ... declare a class" for the type anywhere else.

57.2 How it is written: the ways weighed

Written Verdict
A -> (int, str), return a, b, let a, b = f() Chosen. Go's shape: brackets in the first line, bare commas where values are given and received, and no tuple as a value. for key, value in ages already receives two names with a bare comma
B -> int, str In a function type among parameters the comma reads two ways: function(int) -> int, str. The brackets are the fence
C return (a, b), let (a, b) = f() (a, b) on the value side looks like a value that could be kept, and rule 3 says it cannot
D -> int and str The type would say one thing and return a, b another, and int or none and str reads against or and and everywhere else
E Named results, -> (quotient: int, remainder: int) That is a class. A class is how Zeno names the parts of a thing

Why not a tuple as a value, as Python and Rust have. It would be a second way to write a class with fields nobody named, and reading[1] says less than reading.status. What is asked for is to give back two things at once, and that needs no new kind of value in a program that says its types.

57.3 With no types written

A program with no types can carry several values through names the checker knows nothing about:

function pair(n) {
    return n, str(n) + "!"
}
function twice(make, n) {
    return make(n)
}
let shown = twice(pair, 3)      # the checker cannot see two values here
print(shown)                    # <2 values: 3, 3!>
let a, b, c = twice(pair, 3)    # stops: this gives 2 values, and there are 3 places

What the checker can see, it refuses before the run, with or without types: let x = pair(3) names pair, whose return n, ... says it gives two. What it cannot see is held in three ways, the same in zeno run, zeno run --vm and all thirteen targets:

  1. Where the values are received, the count is checked: "this gives 2 values, and there are 3 places on the left of =", and "there are 2 places on the left of =, and the right gives one value, an int".
  2. Shown, they never read as values: <2 values: 3, 3!>, as a function shows as <function pair>. Without the brackets [shown] would print [3, 3!], a list of two, where there is a list of one thing that is no value.
  3. An operator, an index, a field or len on them gets the message any wrong kind of value gets, with the kind named "2 values": "+ does not work between 2 values and an int". == is true only of the same values, as for a function or an event.

Why not refused at every use. Rule 3 at run time would be a test in every call, every store and every argument of every program, including the ones that never write return a, b, and bytecode that is no longer 0.7.0's. A program with no types already gives up the checks types bring; this is one of them, and the place it is caught, the line that receives, is the line that is wrong. The review of item 10 asked for rule 3's own words after the wrong-kind message as well. That is not done: the message comes from some thirty places in each of fourteen engines (every operator, index and call of a built-in), and a hint added to each is more code that can disagree than the words are worth. The type name "2 values" says what is there, and this section says why.

57.4 How it is built

  • The tree: Type::Several, only after ->; ExprKind::Several, only after return and on the right of the new statement; StmtKind::Receive { declare, places, value }, where a place is a new name with an optional type, _, or a place that exists. Three new kinds and no change to an old one, so every stage that was not told of them failed to build until it was.
  • The checker: a function's returns may be several. A call that gives several is accepted only as the right of a Receive with as many places, or after return in a function that gives the same. Each place gets its type, and with one owner each value is given to its place. A function type and an interface's function compare their results as any type does, and a generic's parameters are worked out from each value.
  • The interpreter and the VM: one new variant of Value, Several(Rc<[Value]>), the last, made only by return a, b and taken apart only by a Receive; one new instruction for each. A value, an instruction, a statement, an expression and a type are each the size they were in 0.7.0, and a test holds them there (a_value_an_instruction_and_the_tree_are_no_bigger_than_in_0_7_0).
  • Both compilers: the first value comes back as a function's answer does. Each further one goes out through a pointer the caller passes after the arguments:
static int64_t z_divide(int64_t z_a, int64_t z_b, int64_t *zeno_gives_2);

In a firmware build a function that can raise gives back true or false (5.5l), and its answer goes out through zeno_result, after the pointers for the further values. Why pointers and not a struct: it is what a firmware build already does with an answer that can fail, a struct for each shape of result is one more type for each, and C compilers for small chips return a struct through memory in any case. One rule, the same in every build. - Text with no collector: the first text comes back in the text room, as one text does (5.9n). Each further text is kept by copy (5.9l) by the function and owned by whoever receives it; a _ gives it back at once. Two faults the tests of every build found here are mended and tested (a third is in 57.5): an object received as a further value kept the type "owned" inside the list of values and could not be read, and the text room was not given back after a Receive, so a loop of them ran out of room. The review found a fourth: values written out, return make(n), fail(n) or let xs, s = make(n), fail(n), where a later one raised after an earlier one had made a list, left the list behind, since the failure leaves at once and the list had not reached its place. Each value that has to be freed is now held until all are worked out, as an argument is held until its call, and edge-several-2.zeno counts the blocks of all three forms. - The targets: lower.rs makes return a, b a call of several(...), and a Receive a temporary and one call of received(value, count, at, line) for each place, which checks the count (57.3). Two functions and a wrapper type in each runtime. - printer.rs, modules.rs, and the language server, whose hover shows divide: function(a: int, b: int) -> (int, str) and each name that received a value with its own type.

57.5 What it costs a program that does not use it

Nothing that could be found. runtime.c is unchanged, so the runtime test of 56.19 holds. tools/same.py against the zeno built from the tag v0.7.0: 6,795 builds, 6,492 the same and 303 different, which are the 273 of item 9 and the two new programs about several values (edge-several and edge-several-2, which 0.7.0 refused); no program 0.7.0 built is built differently. tools/refused.py has three more operations (a value received first, received later, and swapped) on every type, and found one more fault, mended: a function written among the arguments of a call that gives several values took, with its own return, the places the call was to give them to. The bytecode of the 84 programs in examples/ and tools/targets/ that are not about several values: identical to 0.7.0's for every program 0.7.0 could parse (five programs that use item 9's take differ, because 0.7.0 refused them). The sizes are in 57.4. Speed was not timed (section 6 of the plan's changes).

57.6 Left for later

  • Swapping two items that have one owner: xs[i], xs[j] = xs[j], xs[i] reads each item as a look, and with no collector a list of objects or lists refuses it with the message any item that is only looked at gets. A swap(i, j) method on a list would be the way in.
  • Several values in a for: for q, r in pairs().
  • A default for one of several results.

58. Generics, and what interfaces left out

Item 11 of missing.md, as plan-9-14.md plans it. 58.1 to 58.19 are generic enums, bounds, generic interfaces and a method with a type parameter of its own (11.1, 11.2, 11.3 and 11.5). 58.20 onward are the three things 10.10 left out of interfaces (11.4). Each is asked for by what a program writes: enum Name[T], [T is Shape], interface Name[T], the name Ordered where the program has none of its own, a default in an interface, a class whose function takes out, the word owned in front of interface. A program that writes none of them is checked, run and built as before: tools/same.py finds every C file, IR file, joined program and bytecode the same as before each part, for every program but the new one of the part.

58.1 Generic enums

enum Maybe[T] {
    Nothing
    Just(value: T)
}

function first_even(numbers: list[int]) -> Maybe[int] {
    for n in numbers {
        if n % 2 == 0 { return Just(n) }
    }
    return Nothing
}

The rules are those of a generic class (3.16 to 3.16c), and nothing new: square brackets after the name, a capital for each parameter, and the types worked out where the enum is used, never written there. Maybe[int] written as a type is a copy of the enum for int. A case is written by its name alone, as any case is.

  • Just(3) is a Maybe[int] by what it carries. It is worked out as a call of a generic function is (3.16b): from the values, then from an argument that is a function, then from the place the result goes. Ok(3) of Result[T, E] says T and not E, so it needs a place that says the rest: let r: Result[int, str] = Ok(3).
  • Nothing carries nothing, so it takes its type from the place it goes: a variable, a parameter, a field and its default, an item of a list or a value of a dict whose type is said, what the function returns, the other side of == or !=, and an argument of a generic, once the other arguments have said what T is (or_else(Nothing, 5), Link(3, End)).
  • Where nothing says, it is an error that shows how to write the type: "Nothing is a case of the generic enum Maybe, and nothing here says which Maybe it is. Put it where its type is written, as in let x: Maybe[int] = Nothing". The same for Ok(3) with nothing to say E.
  • A match on a Maybe[int] must handle each case, and the message names the case left out as for any enum: "this match does not handle Nothing". A case of Maybe against a value that is not a Maybe "can never match" it.
  • A case name is one enum's alone in a file, generic or not: the rule of 13.9 that two enums cannot both have a Nothing stays as it was, with the same message, naming whichever is written first.
  • A generic enum cannot give its cases numbers (Ack = 6): a case with a number carries nothing (35.1), and a generic enum is for carrying a T. The message says to take the number away.
  • Maybe(3), calling the enum, says that a value of an enum is one of its cases. let f = Just is refused as let f = first is (3.16e). Maybe with no types where a type goes says how many it takes.
  • What a reader sees is Maybe[int] in every message, and what print shows is the case, Just(3) or Nothing, as for any enum, in every engine and every build.

Why the place says the type of Nothing, and not a default. Rust and Swift work it out from every later use of the variable as well, which is a second kind of inference that no other part of Zeno has: a line would mean something that depends on a line below it. Java makes Optional.empty() a value of any type, which needs erasure, the road 5.14 turned down. The rule here is the one 3.16b already gives a generic class built with no argument that says (let s: Stack[int] = Stack(items=[])), and a Nothing with nothing to say what it is was never meant to be written. print(Nothing) is refused for that reason: it would print the same for every T, but the compilers need one copy to print it from, and a rule with an exception for print is two rules.

Why not T or none. It exists and is still the short way when nothing needs to be said about the absence. A Maybe[T] is what a program writes when the absence is a case of its own, or when T may itself be none: Maybe[int or none] keeps "nothing found" and "found a none" apart, which int or none or none cannot. Result[T, E] carries a reason, which none does not.

How it is built. The parser reads [T] after the name of an enum (Enum::type_params); its refusal is gone. In the checker a generic enum is a Generic whose Template is the enum, and a copy is an EnumInfo with its origin, made by copy_enum as copy_class makes a class (5.14). The cases of the generic are declared as Ty::GenericCase, the generic and the place of the case. A call of one is a call of a generic whose parameters are the values that case carries and whose result is Maybe[T] (case_outline), so the one infer of 3.16b works out its types; it then is a call of the copy's case, checked as any. A bare case reads the type of its place from expected_case, which expecting notes for a name as it notes the type of a call's place (generic_bare_case). In a call of a generic, a bare case waits (Later) until the other arguments have given the types, and then takes the type its parameter has in the copy (settle_later). In a match, a case finds itself in the copy that is matched (copy_matched). A generic enum that nothing uses is checked once with T as "anything", as a generic class is, and a match in it on a value of unknown type is not reported as missing a case, since each copy is checked for that.

Which copy each case means is noted in copy_called, the table a call of a generic already used (5.14): the call for Just(3), the name for Nothing. It is keyed by the node in the syntax tree, and a copy of a generic function has a tree of its own (Function::fresh, 5.14c), so return Just(x) inside wrap[T] is noted once for each copy of wrap, with the copy of Maybe that copy means. Item 9 once had notes keyed by line and column, which the copies share; these are not. The test calls wrap and none_of with an int and with text in one program, built every way.

The compilers write one enum for each copy (z_Maybe_int, its cases zeno_new_Maybe_int_Just and zeno_case_Maybe_int_Nothing), and nothing for the generic. A copy's cases are left out of the table that finds a case by its name alone, since every copy has a Just; a case of a copy is found by the copy the checker noted, and a pattern finds its case in the enum of the value matched (case_in). An enum that is not generic goes the way it went, and tools/same.py shows that no program without a generic enum is built differently. With no collector a Maybe[Frame] owns its frame and a Maybe[list[int]] its list, as an enum that carries them does (5.16); a name a case gives to what it carries is a look, by the rules of match. The interpreter and the VM run the generic as it is written. The targets do not look at types.

Tests. checker::tests::a_generic_enum_takes_its_types_from_where_it_is_used, what_a_generic_enum_says_when_it_cannot, and emit_c::tests::a_generic_enum_every_way with tools/targets/edge-generic-enum.zeno: Maybe, Result and a Chain[T] that holds itself, over numbers, text, a list and an object; Nothing in each place that says its type; copies made inside generic functions and a generic class; Maybe[Maybe[int]] and Maybe[int] or none; a thousand rounds; and every way out of a match (its end, return, break, continue, an error raised inside and caught outside); and several values from one function (chapter 57), one of them a Maybe[T], from a generic function and a plain one. It prints what zeno run prints in the six builds, and with no collector 0 blocks are left. tools/refused.py has Opt[int], Opt[str], Opt[list[int]] and Opt[P] among its types; every refusal it finds for them is one a plain enum or a list gets in the same place.

58.2 A look at a copy, given to a parameter of a generic

function size[T](s: Stack[T]) -> int { return len(s.items) }

let s = Stack([1, 2])
print(size(s))

With no collector, 0.7.0 refused this: "s of size should be Stack[T], but this is a Stack[int] that is only looked at". The argument is a look at a value that s owns, and the parameter, which has no take, looks: it is the right thing to pass. Working out T did not see through the look. It does now, for a Stack[T] and a Maybe[T] alike. The same program with a generic enum was the first to meet it (count(chain) of 58.1), and it is mended in the one place both go through (bind). A program 0.7.0 built is not touched: the change is only reached where the refusal was.

58.3 Bounds: function largest[T is Ordered]

function largest[T is Ordered](items: list[T]) -> T {
    var best = items[0]
    for item in items {
        if item > best { best = item }
    }
    return best
}

function total[S is Shape](shapes: list[S]) -> float { ... }

The rule. A type parameter may say is and an interface, on a function, a class or an enum. Each use is checked against it before a copy is made or found: the type that T stands for must be a class that says it is the interface, or the interface itself. If it is not, the error is at the use, where the program can mend it, and names both: "Task is not Shape, which total asks of S. It is one if it says so: class Task is Shape, with what Shape lists". Before, the same mistake was found inside the copy, with a note saying which copy; now the generic's own line says what it needs, and the call is told. A line that asks twice, as let r: Range[Task] = Range(...) does with the type and the call, is told once.

How it is written.

Written Verdict
A [T is Ordered] Chosen. It is the sentence a class already says, class Circle is Shape, with a word that was reserved already
B [T: Ordered] A colon in Zeno says "this name has this type" (port: int). T does not have the type Ordered
C function largest[T](...) where T is Ordered A second place to look for what the first has room for

Ordered comes with Zeno. A type is Ordered when < works on two values of it: every kind of number (int, float, f32, u64 and the sized whole numbers), a quantity, and text. It is what largest, a sort of one's own or a Range[T] need. It is a question the checker answers about a type, not an interface that a program can see, since no class could list the functions it would have. A class cannot be Ordered yet: what < means for objects of a class is "operators for a class" in missing.md, which comes later by the same road, and each message that meets it says so: largest([Task(1)]), class Task is Ordered, and Ordered written as a plain type. A program that declares its own Ordered has its own, as with every name that comes with Zeno: the name is looked up in the program first, and the one that comes with Zeno is only reached where the program has none. So no program that built before changes meaning, and nothing is reserved.

After is comes an interface. [T is int] says that after is comes an interface, such as Ordered or one the program declares; [T is Task], a class, says to write Task itself where T is used, or to declare an interface that Task is. A name that is not declared is "there is no type called" it, as anywhere a type goes.

The body is still checked for each copy (3.16d). A bound is a promise checked at the use. It is not all that the body may do: a generic with no bound that uses > is accepted, and stays accepted, and smaller[T is Ordered] may call a function that is no part of Ordered. Making the bound the whole truth would refuse generics that build now, and would need a bound for each operator before the first could be used; C++ took this road with concepts for the same reason. What a bound buys is what missing.md asked for: the error moves from inside the generic to the call.

Why a bound, and not a parameter of the interface's type. shapes: list[Shape] does not take a list[Circle] (10.7): a list of circles cannot take a square. [S is Shape](shapes: list[S]) takes a list of circles as one, and gives back an S that is a Circle, with its fields.

How it is built. ast::TypeParam is a name and the type after is, if any; Function, Class and Enum keep a list of them, and param_names gives the names where only they matter. The parser reads is and a type after each name; the printer writes it back. In the checker each Generic keeps its bounds as written, and asks works them out once, in the generic's own scope, so a program's own Ordered is found first. meets_bounds is asked by copy_function, copy_class and copy_enum before a copy is made or looked up; a copy that does not meet its bounds is not made. Nothing else changes: inside a copy T is the real type, so a call of the interface's functions is checked as on any object, and a bound makes no code. The compilers, the interpreter, the VM and the targets need nothing; a test holds that the C of a program with bounds is the C of the same program without them.

Tests. parser::tests (the bound read back); checker::tests::a_type_parameter_may_ask_for_an_interface, a_type_that_lacks_what_is_asked_is_refused_at_the_call and what_a_bound_says_when_it_is_written_wrong; emit_c::tests::a_bound_every_way with tools/targets/edge-bounds.zeno: largest over ints, floats, text, volts, milliseconds, u8, i16, f32 and u64; total over a list of circles, a list of squares and a list of shapes; a generic class Range[T is Ordered] whose methods call two other bounded generics, Pair[K is Ordered, V], a generic enum Span[T is Ordered], and a thousand rounds. It prints what zeno run prints in the six builds, with 0 blocks left with no collector, and its C with and without the bounds is the same.

58.4 One interface for each type parameter

[T is Ordered, U] must read one way: a comma begins the next type parameter. So [T is Ordered, Shape] does not ask two things of T; it makes Shape a second type parameter, which would hide the interface of that name inside the generic. Where a name after a comma is an interface of the program and an earlier parameter has a bound, that is refused: "Shape after a comma is a second type parameter, which hides the interface Shape. A type parameter asks for one interface: [T is ...]. If Shape is meant to be a type parameter, give it another name". A program that needs two has not been written yet, and how to write two is left for when one is; the message keeps that room free.

58.5 A generic that nothing uses, checked as its bound

A generic that nothing uses has no copy to check, so it is checked once on its own (5.14d), with each type parameter standing for "anything". A type parameter with a bound of the program's own now stands for that interface instead. So function f[S is Shape](s: S) that calls s.perimeter(), which Shape does not list, is found though nothing calls f, with the message any call through an interface gets. A parameter that is Ordered, or has no bound, still stands for "anything": Ordered has no functions to list, and a generic with no bound promised nothing. Once a copy is made, the copy is checked as before, with the real type.

58.6 Generic interfaces

interface Source[T] {
    function next(self) -> T or none
}

class Countdown is Source[int] { ... }
class Repeat[T] is Source[T] { ... }

function drain(source: Source[int]) -> int { ... }

The rule. An interface may have type parameters, written as a class writes them. An interface is a class to every stage after the parser (10.9), and a generic class has copies (5.14), so Source[int] is a copy of the interface: an interface of its own, whose next gives an int or none. A class says which copy it is after is, with the types: class Countdown is Source[int]. A generic class may say is Source[T], and each of its copies is the copy of Source for its own T: Repeat[int] is a Source[int], Repeat[str] a Source[str]. Everything else is the rules of an interface, unchanged (10.4 to 10.8, 58.20 to 58.22): the class has each function of the copy, written the same way; an object of the class goes where the copy is wanted; a list of them written out is a list of the copy; a bound may be a copy, [S is Source[str]] (58.3).

Source[int] and Source[str] are two interfaces. A Countdown does not go where a Source[str] is wanted, and a Source[str] does not go where a Source[int] is: "a should be Source[int], but this is Source[str]". A class may be two copies, is Source[int], Source[str], if it has the functions of both, which can only be when they do not meet; a class that has the functions of Source[int] and says Source[str] is told what Source[str] asks for.

Each copy is an interface of its own for 58.21 and 58.22 too. A copy has its own place in the checker's tables, so when Slot, a Holder[list[int]], takes out what it holds and Name, a Holder[str], does not, a call through a Holder[list[int]] is for its owner only and one through a Holder[str] is for anybody. An owned interface Holder[T] makes every copy owned, and each takes only an owned class.

The messages. class Words is Source, with no types, says that Source has type parameters and shows the class with them. is Shape[int] on an interface with none says to write it without [ ]. The wrong number of types is said as for a class. Source() says that an interface has nothing to build, as for one with no types, and Source kept as a value says it is written where a type goes.

Why copies, and not one interface over every T. The road of Java, where Source<Integer> and Source<String> are one interface at run time, is erasure, which 5.14 turned down for classes: a next() would give back "anything", and every caller would need a cast that the checker cannot see. A copy is what a generic class already is, so nothing new had to be decided for the C, the LLVM, an object with one owner, or --memory.

How it is built. The parser's refusal is gone: an interface reads [T] after its name into Class::type_params, and Class::is is a list of types where it was a list of names, so that Source[int] can be written there (interface_named). modules.rs renames the names in it as in any type, inside the class's own type parameters. In the checker a generic interface is a Generic whose template is a class that is an interface, and copy_class makes its copies as it makes a class's. In fill_class, a name after is is looked up as before, and a name with types is resolved as a type, which makes or finds the copy; a copy is the same ClassInfo each time, so is_one, fits and stands_for compare it as they compare any interface. The compilers read the name of each interface after is from the checker, which notes what each written type stands for (Types::interface_name): Source[int] for a copy, and the name as written for an interface with no types, as before. Both compilers register a copy of an interface as they register a copy of a class, and write the switch of 10.9 for each copy the program uses, over the classes that are that copy. A program with no generic interface reads the same names as before, and tools/same.py shows its C, IR, joined program and bytecode the same. The interpreter, the VM and the targets do not look at interfaces' types.

Tests. parser::tests::interfaces; checker::tests::an_interface_may_have_types_of_its_own, what_a_generic_interface_says_when_it_cannot and each_copy_of_a_generic_interface_is_held_to_taking_out_by_itself; emit_c::tests::a_generic_interface_every_way with tools/targets/edge-generic-interface.zeno: Countdown is Source[int], Words is Source[str] and Repeat[T] is Source[T], used through Source[int], in a list, as a bound, in a generic function over list[Source[T]], and a thousand rounds; and an owned interface Holder[T] whose classes take out what they hold and whose functions have a default, Slot is Holder[list[int]] and Cell[T] is Holder[T], in an owned list. It prints what zeno run prints in the six builds, with 0 blocks left with no collector, and in each target whose tools are installed. A program in two files with class Count is sources.Source[int] was tried by hand in three builds.

58.7 A method with a type parameter of its own stays refused

class Box[T] {
    item: T
    function convert[U](self, change: function(T) -> U) -> Box[U] { ... }
}

The plan builds this only if 58.1 to 58.6 make it a small step. They do not, and it stays refused. A copy of a generic is made where it is called, and today what is called with a dot is one function: a method read from an object is a BoundMethod that holds one FunctionInfo. A method with its own U would need, each its own work and none shared with what 58.1 to 58.6 built:

  • a bound generic as the type of box.convert, and the call of a method going through call_generic with the object as a first argument that says nothing about U;
  • its copies made inside each copy of the class, Box[int] having convert[str] and convert[float], and checked with self of that copy;
  • in both compilers, those copies registered as methods of the class copy and compiled with it, and each call reading which copy the checker chose, where a method call today finds its function by name;
  • with no collector, the rules of self (a look, or take where the method takes out, 5.19k and 58.21) held for each copy, and a method value of one (56.9) refused.

That is about a dozen places in four files for the item that the plan calls the least needed, and no program in the repository, the book or a review has asked for it. The same work is done today by a function of the file that takes the object first, which every build takes:

function convert[T, U](box: Box[T], change: function(T) -> U) -> Box[U] {
    return Box(change(box.item))
}

So the message says that, with the names filled in: "the method convert cannot have type parameters of its own yet. Write it as a function of the file that takes the object first: function convert[T, U](box: Box[T], ...)". It was "The class can have them: class Box[T]", which in a generic class named a class that already has them. A method of an interface stays refused by the parser, as the plan says: it would be a copy for each U in each class behind each switch.

Tests. checker::tests::what_a_generic_cannot_do_yet, for a plain class and a generic one.

58.8 A generic given a list whose items are not all one type

first([200 ms, 1 s]) runs with zeno run, which keeps each item as it is and prints 200 ms, and every build refused it, in 0.7.0 too, with "first cannot tell what T is from this call: no argument says", which pointed at the wrong thing. The list does say something: that its items are two types. A build gives a list one type (the row of compiler.md on such lists), and making the list one of ms would change what it prints, 1000 ms where zeno run prints 1 s. So it stays refused, by that row, and the message now says why and what to write: "first cannot tell what T is from this list: its items are not all one type, but a quantity in ms and a quantity in s, and a build gives a list one type. Write them all in one unit, such as ms". For an int beside a float it says to write each as a float; for anything else, to make them one type or an enum with a case for each, as the row does.

The checker notes each list written out whose items it could not join into one type, with the types they are (mixed), and the one place where a generic cannot tell a type reads it. Nothing else changes: a list that is one type is never noted, and zeno run takes what it took. The row names the case, and tools/refused.py has two programs beyond its matrix, first given a list of two units and of an int and a float, so a later change to either message is seen.

Tests. checker::tests::a_generic_given_a_list_of_two_types_says_why_in_a_build.

58.20 A default on a parameter of an interface's function

enum Mode {
    Slow
    Fast
}

interface Motor {
    function spin(self, speed: int = 1_000, wait: ms = 5 ms, mode: Mode = Fast)
}

class Fan is Motor {
    function spin(self, speed: int = 1000, wait: ms = 5 ms, mode: Mode = Mode.Fast) { ... }
}

function drive(motor: Motor) {
    motor.spin()             # 1000, 5 ms, Fast
    motor.spin(wait = 20 ms)
}

The rule. A parameter of a function of an interface may have a default. It is a plain value: a number, with a minus in front of it or not; text (not an f-string); true, false, none; a quantity such as 5 ms; or a case of an enum that carries nothing, bare or with the enum's name. Anything else is refused where it is written, with what is allowed. The class writes the same default, and "the same" is the same value: 1_000 and 1000 are, Fast and Mode.Fast are. A default that differs, or none where the interface has one, is refused at the class, with both defaults and both lines. Had Fan above written speed: int = 2000:

error: `spin` of `Fan` gives `speed` the default `2000`, on line 11,
and `Motor` gives it `1000`, on line 7. Write the same default in
both, so that a call through a `Motor` and a call on a `Fan` mean the
same

Where the interface writes none, the class may have its own. It could in 0.7.0 (10.6 compared names and types, and said nothing of defaults), and such a program must go on being taken. A call through the interface then gives every argument, and one that leaves it out is refused at the call ("spin needs a value for speed"), so the two calls still cannot differ without the reader being told.

Why the same, and not "the class's own wins". motor.spin() is one line that runs a different class each time. If each class could fill in its own default, the line would mean a different speed for each motor, and nothing on the line or in the interface would say so. With one value written twice, the interface tells the whole truth, and the class says nothing that contradicts it. It is 10.6 again: the same first line twice needs no working out.

Why only a plain value. "The same" then has one meaning, which the checker and the reader both see at a glance. 2 * 3 and 6, or len(names) and a number, would need the checker to work values out (and len(names) is not the same at every call), and a rule that says "the same when worked out" is a rule nobody can check by eye. A quantity is allowed because a timeout with a unit is the default firmware writes most. A case of an enum that carries values is not plain: it is a function that makes one.

5 ms and 5000 us. The planner's rule counts them the same value, and the comparison does. In practice it does not arise: the unit is part of the parameter's type (wait: ms), so a default in another unit is refused as the wrong type before the two are compared.

How a call fills it in. Nothing new: every engine already fills a left-out argument from the default of the function it calls, and a call through an interface calls the interface's function. Since the class's default is the same value, a call on the object gives what a call through the interface gives. The checker checks the interface's default as it checks any default (its type, and what a quantity in it needs), so the compilers find it noted.

Tests. The checker: every kind of plain value, equal in another spelling; a call through the interface that leaves it out; the class's own default where the interface has none, and a call through the interface that leaves that out; each kind unequal, and none where there is one; a default in the interface that is a sum, a call, a list, an f-string and a case that carries values; one of the wrong type. Every build: tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno prints what zeno run prints, through C and LLVM, with a collector, in firmware, and with none (0 blocks left), and in each target language.

58.21 A function that takes out what its object owns, standing for one of an interface

interface Pile {
    function take_last(self) -> Task
    function size(self) -> int
}

class Stack is Pile {
    tasks: list[Task]

    function take_last(self) -> Task {
        return self.tasks.pop()
    }
    ...
}

function drain(pile: take Pile) {          # the owner: allowed
    while pile.size() > 0 {
        print(pile.take_last().name)
    }
}

function peek(pile: Pile) -> str {         # only looks: refused
    return pile.take_last().name
}
error: only the owner can call `take_last`, which takes out or
replaces something the object owns (`Stack` is a `Pile`, and its
`take_last` does): somebody else may have been lent it. Here `pile`
only looks at it

The rule. A function that takes out or replaces what its object owns (5.19k) may stand for one of an interface. A call through the interface is then held to the guards of 5.15e, as a call on the object is: only the owner may make it, not inside a loop or a match that is looking at what it would take, and not on a line that has already looked at the object. The interface's function says nothing about it, and nothing is written: it takes out if the function of any class that is the interface does, and the whole program is known (7.11).

How the checker knows. It keeps the set of functions of interfaces that some class's function takes out for, with the name of one such class for the message. A class adds to it where 0.7.0 refused it. A call through the interface whose function is in the set is held to the guards. The checker already reads the program several times over, until a reading learns nothing new (for the types of parameters with none written); the set is carried from each reading to the next in the same way, and what is reported comes from a reading in which the set did not grow. So a call read before the class that takes out (later in the file, in another file, or in a copy of a generic class made later) is held to the same guards as a call read after it. The set only grows, and it is never larger than the number of functions of interfaces, so the readings end.

Why not work it out at the first call (as the plan first said). Two things break it. A class whose function calls through its own interface (a tree whose count adds up the count of its children) is still being checked at that call, and the checker answers "takes out" for a method still being checked, since that can only refuse; such programs were taken by 0.7.0 and would be refused. And a copy of a generic class that is the interface may be made after the first call. The set, carried over the readings, has neither fault.

Why not a word on the function (function take_last(self) takes). 5.19k turned it down for a method: a word that must be kept in step with the body is a second place to be wrong. An interface's function has no body, so the word would have something to say there; but then a class whose function stopped taking out would be told to keep a word that is no longer true of it, or every interface with it would change. The program is all there, and the checker can read it.

What it costs. A class that takes out makes every call of that function through the interface owner-only, even for the classes that do not take out. That is the price of a call that runs one of several functions: the caller cannot know which. A program that needs the looser call writes two functions.

A program of 0.7.0 has an empty set (each class that took out was refused), so every call through an interface is checked as it was.

Tests. The checker: drain and peek above, with no collector; peek written before Stack, with Stack in a second file, and with a copy of a generic class Box[T] is Pile made after peek; the loop's message (for one in piles around piles[0].take_last()) and the line's (print(pile.size(), pile.take_last().name)); an interface whose classes take nothing out, as before; a class that calls through its own interface, where count (which takes nothing out) is called on a loop's item, strip (which does) is called on an item it popped, and strip called on a loop's item is refused. Every build: tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno drains a Stack and a Queue through a Pile, takes out of a list[Pile] by index, a thousand rounds, and the tree.

58.22 owned interface

owned interface Shape {
