    function area(self) -> float
}

owned class Circle is Shape { ... }
owned class Square is Shape { ... }

let shapes: owned list[Shape] = [Circle(1.0), Square(2.0)]

The rule. owned may stand in front of interface, as it stands in front of class (5.8b). Each object that is an owned interface has one owner, which frees it, with a collector as without one: it moves when it is given away, a list of them is an owned list, a parameter looks at one unless it says take, and a field holding one is in an owned class. Only an owned class can be an owned interface, and an owned class can only be an owned interface. Each mismatch is refused at the class, and says which word to write:

error: `Dot` is an owned class, and `Shape` is not an `owned
interface`: an object with one owner cannot be where a shared one is
wanted. Write `owned interface Shape`, or take `owned` off `Dot`

error: `Dot` is not an owned class, and `Shape` is an `owned
interface`, whose objects each have one owner. Write `owned class
Dot`, or take `owned` off `Shape`

Why taking out was not the whole question. 10.10 said the two refusals were one question, about a function that takes out called through an interface. 58.21 answers that. But with a collector a value of an interface is shared, and an object of an owned class put where a Shape is wanted would be an owned thing inside a shared one, which 5.8 forbids: the shared Shape could be copied anywhere, and the owner would free the object under it.

How Verdict
A owned interface Shape: its objects have one owner, only an owned class can be one, and an owned class can only be one Chosen. It is the sentence owned class already is, with the word already reserved, on the first line of the interface where its reader looks
B An object of an interface is owned when what was put into it is The same type would be shared at one line and owned at the next, and nothing on the page would say which. 5.8b turned down the same thing for classes
C An interface is owned when its classes are, worked out Nothing written says it, against the rule that a feature is asked for by a word; and one more class could change every use of the interface
D Leave the refusal 10.10 left it open, and a Resource (12.1) needs it

With no collector, and in a file that says memory owned, nothing changes. Every object has one owner there already, the interface's too: the word is allowed and says nothing new, and a class without owned may be an interface with it, as it may hold anything owned.

How it is built. The parser reads owned before interface (the word was reserved by 5.19c, so no program had it as a name) and marks the interface owned, as it does a class. To the checker an interface is a class (10.9), so an owned one is an owned class: its objects are owned, the functions of it look at their object, and every rule of 5.8 applies with nothing added. The rule above replaces the old refusal. The compilers already free an object through its interface (the switch of 10.9 has a case for each class), which a build with no collector has done since 10.10; a build with a collector now does it for an owned interface.

Tests. The checker: both mismatches; both words, and neither; with no collector both mismatches are taken; a memory owned file with a plain interface and class. With a collector: an owned interface in an owned list, as a parameter that looks and one that takes, as a field and one that may be none; given away and used after; a list that is not owned; a function that replaces what its object owns, called through the interface by a parameter that only looks (refused, by 58.21). Every build: tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno has Shape with a Circle that replaces its centre, a Frame that holds one and may hold a spare, and a thousand rounds; with no collector 0 blocks are left, and with a collector the C build runs under valgrind with nothing wrong.

58.23 What interfaces still leave out

  • A default body for a function of an interface. A class writes each function (10.5).
  • An interface that is another interface. A class names both.
  • A way back from an interface to the class (10.8).
  • A default that is not a plain value (58.20), and a class whose default differs from the interface's.
  • A call through an interface that takes out, made by somebody who only looks, even when the class behind it does not take out (58.21). It is the guard, and not a gap: the caller cannot know which class it is.

Generic interfaces and functions with type parameters of their own are 58.1 to 58.19.

Where 58.20 to 58.22 meet several values (57). A function of an interface may give two results and have a default, take out and give two results, or be a function of an owned interface that does both; the end of tools/targets/edge-interfaces.zeno does each, in every build.

59. Cleaning up when a block ends, files in pieces, and folders

Item 12 of plan-9-14.md has three parts: a value that is cleaned up when its block ends (12.1), a file read and written in pieces (12.2), and folders (12.3). The third is cut loose from the other two and lands first. Its sections begin at 59.20, so that the first two parts keep the numbers before it.

59.1 is Resource: something that is put back when its owner ends

owned class Selected is Resource {
    line: Pin

    function release(self) {
        self.line.on()              # chip select is high again
    }
}

function read_id(bus: Bus, line: Pin) -> u8 {
    line.off()
    let chosen = Selected(line)
    return bus.transfer(0x9F)
}                                   # chosen.release() runs here, however the block is left

An open file, a chip-select line and a lock each have a second half that must happen on every way out of a block. Until now it was written before each return, and forgotten before one of them. Now the class says it once: an owned class that is Resource has its release called when the owner of the object ends. The choice of this over defer, finally and a block of Python's with is 12.1 of the plan; here is what was built.

Resource comes with Zeno, as owned interface Resource { function release(self) } (58.22). It is written into a program only when the program names it and has no Resource of its own, so a program that never says the word is the program it was: the same C, IR and bytecode, which tools/same.py holds. A program with its own Resource means its own, and nothing is released: it is an interface like any other. It is not a reserved word.

The rules.

  1. Only an owned class can be one: a shared object has no owner whose end could be the moment. class Plain is Resource is refused, and says Declare it `owned class Plain is Resource`.
  2. release takes self alone and gives nothing, as the interface says. It may not say raises: it runs at the end of a block, where an error has nowhere to go, and the message says to catch the error inside it.
  3. release cannot be called by hand. It runs once, and the message says how to end a resource sooner: give it to a function that takes it, function done(held: take Held) { }.
  4. It runs when the owner ends: when the block of the let that holds it is left by reaching its end, by return, break or continue, or by an error passing through. Of two in one block, the one made last is released first. After return x + y the value is worked out first and the release runs second, so the value may use the resource. A loop's body is a block, so one made in each turn is released at the end of each turn.
  5. A resource has one owner, like every owned value. return gives it to the caller, a parameter that says take takes it, let b = a moves it. Whoever has it at the end releases it; one that was given away is not released by the one who gave it, on any path: given away in one branch of an if, it is released at the end of the block only when the other branch ran.
  6. It does not run when the program is stopped: by program.exit, or by a fault of a firmware build (5.5l). Stopping ends no block. A failed assert is not a stop: it stands only in a test, and leaves its test as an error would, so what the blocks of the test own is released, and the next test can open the same file (plan, Changes 18).
  7. Where a resource can be, in this version: in a let, or in a parameter. The rest is 59.2.

An error passes through as it was. The release runs, and then the error goes on with its kind, its message and its line unchanged, to the except that catches it or out of the program. An error that nothing catches releases on its way out, top of the file included, and is reported after the lines each release printed, exactly as it is reported in a program with no resource. (raise e names the line of the raise, so the engines do not pass it on that way.)

59.2 Where a resource can be: a let, or a parameter

The compilers free an owned value on every road it can take, and for them a release in front of the free would be all there is to do. But the interpreter, the VM and the fifteen targets free nothing: their values are shared, and collected by the language they are written in. For them "the owner ends" has to be made into something that runs, and for a let in a block that is one thing: code at each way out of the block. For a field or an item of a list it would be chapters 5.15 to 5.17 again, in every engine. A let covers the guard of a block, which is what the needs above are. The rest is refused, each with a message that says what to write, so letting it in later changes no program (11.6). With a collector and with none the checker says the same words.

Where What is said
var h = Held("a") h holds a resource, which is released when its owner ends, so the variable cannot be given another value. Declare it with let
a list or a dict of them, Held or none, a field of any class, a case of an enum, a type parameter, what a function gives when it is one of those what would hold a resource. A resource is released when its owner ends, and its owner is a let or a parameter, never a list, a dict, a field, a case of an enum, or none or a type parameter. Keep it in a let of its own
print(Held("a").name), or a call standing alone this call gives a resource, and nothing keeps it, so it would be released at once. Keep it in a let, which releases it when its block ends: let held = ...
one of several values (item 10): return Held("a"), 1, let a, b = Held("a"), 1, let n, h = 1, Held("b"), and a, b = ... a resource cannot be one of several values: its owner, which releases it, is a let of its own. Give it back alone, and receive it alone: let held = ...
a default that makes one: function f(h: Held = Held("d")) a default cannot make a resource: h would be made at each call that leaves it out, where no let owns it. Pass one at the call instead
a function that is kept, using a resource of the block around it this function is kept, so it would take h, a resource, and nothing would release it when its block ends. Pass h to the function as a parameter instead
a parameter whose type is not written the type of x of show is not written, so a resource cannot go to it. Write its type: x: Held
the top of a file that imports web a page stays open after the program's last line, so the top of its file never ends, and h would never be released. Make it inside the function that uses it

A call that gives a resource may be received by a let, by return, or by a parameter that takes it, done(Held("passed")): in each the value has an owner the moment it is made. A resource may be held as the interface, let r: Resource = h, and a parameter may look at one as Resource; the release is then found through the interface, as any function of it is (10.9).

Where it meets chapter 58. A type parameter never holds a resource, so function named[T is Resource](x: T) may be written, and a call that gives it a Held is refused with the message of the second row, naming `T` of `named`; so is Box[Held] for a generic class, Just(Held("a")) for a generic enum, and class Maker is Source[Held] for a generic interface. A bound that could be met by nothing is not refused where it is written: it is refused the first time it is asked, at the call, as every bound is checked (58.3).

The last row is the page's: a program that imports web goes on after its last line, answering the page, so the top of its file never ends. A function of the page may make one, as any function may.

59.3 The top of a file, its tests, and how a program stops

The top of a file is a block. A resource made there is released after the last line, when the program ends as it should, last made first, and before an error that nothing caught is reported.

When a file is run for its tests, the top ends after its last test (plan, Changes 18). zeno test runs the file, then its tests, and the tests see the file's variables, as testing.md has always said. A resource of the top would be released before the tests if the top ended at its last line, and a test that reached it through a function would use something given back. So in zeno test and in zeno test --build a resource of the top is released after the last test, and in zeno run and zeno build after the last line. A list that the top owns in a build with no collector already went this way, given back after the tests; a resource goes the same road, its release in front of that giving back.

Refusing a test that uses a resource of the top was weighed and not taken: a test can reach it through a function it calls, or a function held as a value, and no check could see every road.

program.exit and a firmware fault release nothing, at the top or in any block (rule 6).

59.4 How it is built

The checker is the only part that knows which let holds a resource, and the engines learn it from the program it gives back. After the rules pass, checked rewrites the program, as it does for sized numbers (10.27): the statements after a resource's let, to the end of its block, go into a new statement, StmtKind::Scoped { name, body }, the second inside the first; a body whose parameter takes a resource is wrapped the same way; and each use that gives the resource away (to a take parameter, by return, by let b = a) becomes ExprKind::Give(name). Both are made only by the checker, and no program can write them. A Scoped opens no scope of its own: the names made in its body belong to the block it stands in, so the hoisting of functions and the free of other owned values see the block whole (ast::flat). A program with no resource is not rewritten, and the test a_program_with_no_resource_is_not_rewritten holds it.

The meaning of Scoped, for every engine: run the body; however it is left, if the name still holds its object, call its release; then go on leaving the same way. Give(name) reads the name and leaves it empty.

  • The interpreter: one arm, which runs the body, looks at how it ended, and calls release unless the name was emptied. Give reads the variable and leaves none in it. The top of a file under zeno test runs the file's tests at the end of its innermost Scoped.
  • The VM: the body runs in a try of its own; at its end the try is closed and the resource released, and an error that comes to its handler releases and is raised again as it was (Reraise). return, break and continue release, last made first, the resources they leave, after the value of a return is worked out; each try begun inside is closed before the release, so an error in a release cannot be caught by a try already left. One new instruction, Release, calls release unless the variable holds none, and keeps the place of the error passing through. The variable is found where its let is, so an inner block that uses the name again does not hide it. Op is still 12 bytes.
  • C and LLVM: every way out of a block already frees what the block owns (5.8h), and the release goes in front of that, block by block, innermost first. The release takes the object out of the variable first (NULL after), so that it runs once whatever happens inside it. In an ordinary build an error jumps over the blocks between a raise and its except (5.5i), so there the body is a frame of the kind a try has, which keeps the error aside, releases, and raises it again unchanged; it costs what a try costs, and only in a block that owns a resource. A firmware build passes errors as values, and needs no frame. Under zeno test --build the tests run before the last resource of the top is released. Nothing in runtime.c changed.
  • The fifteen targets (lower.rs): Scoped becomes a lowered try that catches what the program raises, releases, and raises it again as it was, with the release also written at the end and at each return, break and continue that leaves it. A mistake of the program and program.exit go past every target's try. No new lowered statement and no runtime changed: the ones that were there are enough.

Tests. The checker: each refusal of 59.2, with a collector and with none, and what is taken; a Resource of the program's own; a program with none is not rewritten; the shape of the rewrite. Both engines: an error that ends the program releases on its way out and is reported unchanged; program.exit releases nothing; under zeno test the top ends after its last test, and a failed assert releases what its test held. The six builds, against the interpreter and the VM, with no block left with no collector: return from inside a try, break and continue from inner blocks and a match, a resource held as Resource, a name used again in an inner block, an inner function written after the let and called above it, a release that catches its own error, an uncaught error reported unchanged after the releases; and in zeno test --build a failed assert, one inside a try, an error raised by a test, and the top of the file released after the last test. Every engine and build: tools/targets/edge-resource.zeno prints a line from each release on every way out: the end, return with a value that uses the resource, break, continue, a loop that makes one each turn, an error through two blocks that each own one, an error caught inside, two in one block, one given away, handed back, taken by a parameter, moved by let, given away on one path of an if and of a match, a name used again inside, and one at the top of the file.

59.5 What a resource still leaves out

  • A resource in a field, a list, a dict, or none, a case of an enum, or as a type parameter (59.2). An owned class that holds a resource would release it when the class is freed, which the compilers could do and the other engines could not.
  • Several values that hold one (item 10).
  • A var. Giving it a new value would release the old one, at a line where nothing is written.
  • A release that raises.

59.6 A file read and written in pieces: files.Reader and files.Writer

import files

let source = files.read_from("big.log")
let errors = files.write_to("errors.log")

for line in source {
    if line.find("error") is not none {
        errors.write(line + "\n")
    }
}
Written Gives
files.read_from(path) a files.Reader, at the start of the file
files.write_to(path) a files.Writer on a new, empty file, as files.write begins one
files.append_to(path) a files.Writer at the end of the file, made if it is not there, as files.append
reader.read_line() the next line without its line end, or none after the last (6.17, 6.18)
reader.read_bytes(count) up to count bytes as a list[u8]: fewer at the end, none after it
for line in reader each line in turn (59.7)
writer.write(text), writer.write_bytes(bytes) writes, and adds no line end (6.13)

All of them but for raise FileError, with the messages of files.read and files.write: there is no file `big.log`, cannot read `big.log`, cannot write `errors.log`, and `big.log` does not hold text for a line that is not UTF-8 or holds a zero byte, which is what files.read says of such a file. A Reader and a Writer are resources (59.1): the file is closed when the owner ends. There is no close, which is what 6.12 wanted of an open file: nothing to forget.

Why three functions and two types, and not open(path, "r"): 12.2 of the plan. A wrong letter is found when the program runs, and reading from a file opened for writing is a mistake the checker finds.

Written in Zeno, over six small built-ins (plan, Changes 20). The two classes are in library/files.zeno, as owned class Reader is Resource and owned class Writer is Resource, with read_line, read_bytes, write and write_bytes as their functions and a release that closes the file. Each holds the number of its open file and its path, both private. So the release, its order, every way out of a block and every engine and target come from 59.1 with nothing new. What asks the machine is six built-ins beside files.read, one for each thing done to an open file: handle_open(path, how) gives the number (0 to read, 1 to write from empty, 2 to add to the end), and handle_line, handle_bytes, handle_write, handle_write_bytes and handle_close take it, and the path for their messages. The library gives a program only the functions it reaches (33), and the six are pieces of the runtime (56.19), so a program that reads no file in pieces is built as it was, to the byte.

How Verdict
A Two classes in Zeno over six built-ins Chosen. One place for the classes, and the built-ins are small enough to write sixteen times
B Two types built into Zeno, as a Serial is A new type, its methods and its release in the interpreter, the VM, C, LLVM and fifteen runtimes, twice; and a second road for a resource beside 59.1's

What a program cannot touch. Only read_from, write_to and append_to make one: files.Reader(3, "x") is refused, because the class has private fields (10.2), and so is reading reader.file. In C the number is the address of the open file, so a made-up one would be a wild address. The six built-ins are callable only from library/files.zeno: to any other file they are names the module does not have, module `files` has no `handle_open`, the words a program would have got before they were there. The checker knows the file a call is written in (the line of a span says it), and asks it.

A write hands its text to the system before it gives back. Zeno holds nothing back for the close: release raises nothing (59.1), so what could not be written at the close would be lost without a word. So the write that meets a full disk raises FileError on its own line, and a program can catch it there (tested with /dev/full on Linux). A writer that gathers its pieces before it writes them is left for later.

Bytes on every system. The file is opened as bytes, so a line end is what 6.17 says, \n with a \r before it going too, and not what Windows makes of it. A file written in pieces is the bytes that were written.

A count below 0 is a ValueError: `read_bytes` was asked for -1 bytes, and a count of bytes is never below 0. It is a value no count can have, and it is said, rather than taken as 0 (which would hide the mistake) or as "all of it" (Python's read(-1), a second meaning for a number). The check is written once, in Zeno, in read_bytes.

On a board these are the C library's, and a board with no file system answers FileError, as files.read does there (6.20).

The end is where the file ends at that moment (plan, Changes 24). A read that found the end looks again the next time: what was written to the file since, by this program or another, is read. What is there without a line end is given as a line, as the last line of any file is; a "\n" written after it then ends an empty line. The reader does not wait for more. Each engine had a rule of its own before: zeno run, the VM and most targets read on, and the C library's getc remembers the end, so every build gave none for ever. clearerr (C, C++), a seek to where the stream is (PHP), and no "ended" mark kept beside a buffer (JS, TS, Dart) make them one. C# opens both kinds shared both ways, so that a file can be read while a Writer has it, as on every other system.

With no collector a line is built in the text room, as input()'s is, so a line longer than the room stops the program with the room's own message; the bytes of read_bytes are a list from the pool.

An error that nothing catches names library/files.zeno, the line in the library that called the built-in, and not the program's line (33.2: an error names where it was raised). It is in missing.md.

59.7 for line in reader

A loop over a dict is given its keys (6.38), and a loop over a reader is given its lines: it is what everyone writes first, and it holds one line at a time, where files.read(path).lines() holds the file.

It is not a new loop in each engine. The checker finds each for over a files.Reader, and checked makes it the loop it means, as it makes the rest of a resource's block a Scoped (59.4):

while true {
    let line..next = source.read_line()
    if line..next is none { break }
    let line = line..next
    ...the body...
}

No name a program writes has two dots in a row (35.2), so line..next is no one else's. break and continue mean what they mean in any for. Every engine, build and target runs a while, a call and an if, which they all could already.

A reader that a call gives has no owner to close it when the loop ends: for line in files.read_from(path) is refused by rule 7 of 59.1, in words of its own, a `for` cannot read from a reader that nothing keeps: it would be closed at once. Give it a name first, `let source = files.read_from(path)`, and then write `for line in source`. Two names, for i, line in source, are refused: a reader has lines, not places. A Writer cannot be looped over, as before.

Tests. Both engines: a file written by write_to, write_bytes and append_to, read by read_line, by for with continue, and by read_bytes across the end; a count below 0; a missing file; a write to /dev/full, caught at the write; each refusal above. Every engine, build and target: tools/targets/edge-files.zeno grows a file of a thousand lines with both line ends and none at the end, read by for and by read_line and held to lines(); a file opened three times in a row and then removed, which fails on Windows if the first was not closed; files of every shape of line end; bytes read in pieces across the end; a writer that adds and one that empties; a file that is not there, a folder, a missing folder, a line that is not text and a zero byte.

59.20 files.list(folder): the names, sorted by their characters

files.list("logs") gives the names of everything in the folder, as a list[str]: files and folders alike, with no . and no .., and each name without the folder in front of it. It raises FileError, and every kind of build can catch it, as files.read can.

Sorted, by the numbers of the characters. A system gives a folder's names in an order of its own: Linux in the order of a hash on some disks and of making on others, Windows by name in a way that ignores case, a board's card in the order the names were written. A program that prints a listing would print it differently from one machine to the next, and a test of it could not be written once. So the list is sorted, and by the one order every engine already has for text: the order of <, which is the order of the numbers of the characters, and for UTF-8 the order of the bytes. That makes "10" come before "9", "B" before "a", and "😀" after "ｚ".

Turned down: the order a person would sort in, "9" before "10" and case put aside. It is not one order: what it does with "é", "ß" or Tamil depends on a language, and the program would print what the machine's settings say. A program that wants it sorts the list itself.

Turned down: the system's own order. It is the reason for the rule.

Where the languages differ. Java, Kotlin, C#, Dart and JavaScript compare text by UTF-16, which puts a character from beyond the first 65,536 (two halves in UTF-16, 0xD800 and up) before one from 0xE000 to 0xFFFF, such as "ｚ". Each of those targets sorts with a comparison of its own that walks characters or bytes, not halves; the others (Rust, C, C++, Go, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lua) sort bytes or characters, which is the same order. tools/targets/edge-folders.zeno has a name on each side of that line.

A name that is not UTF-8 is a FileError: the folder `logs` holds a name that is not text. Linux lets a name be any bytes but / and zero. Turning such bytes into �, as Rust's lossy conversion does, would give a name that files.read cannot open; dropping it would give a list that is not what is there. Every name in Zeno is text, so a folder that holds one that is not cannot be listed. The JVM, .NET and Dart turn the name into text of their own before a program sees it, so on those four targets it arrives changed. That is said in folders.md, and not mended: there is no way to see the bytes.

The messages. Nothing at the path is there is no folder `logs`; anything else that stops it, a file at the path or a folder that may not be read, is cannot list the folder `logs`. They follow files.read's two, with "folder" where it says "file".

An empty path is no folder. Java takes "" for the folder the program runs in, and C's opendir, Rust's read_dir, Python, Go and Node do not. Zeno takes the second: there is no folder `, in every engine."."` is the folder the program runs in, on every system.

What the disk holds, and as files.read opens it (plan, Changes 28). Zeno lists the names the disk holds. On a disk that does not tell capitals from small letters, as on Windows and macOS out of the box, b and B are one file and one name; the tests use names that differ by more than case. And a name that files.list gives opens its file when it is handed to files.read, on every system. A C or LLVM build on Windows reads and writes through fopen, which takes a name through the machine's code page; 0.7.0's files.read and files.write do, and by 56.19 they stay as they were. So the pieces of files.list and files.make_folder take names the same way, with the C library's _findfirst64, _stat64 and _mkdir, and not its wide functions, which turned a name files.write had made into a second, other name: é came back as Ã©. A name the code page cannot hold, made by another program, is listed with question marks; folders.md says so.

59.21 files.make_folder(path): it worked if there is a folder at the end

files.make_folder("logs/2026/november") makes the folder and every folder above it that is not there, as mkdir -p, Python's os.makedirs(exist_ok=True) and Rust's create_dir_all do. It gives nothing, and raises cannot make the folder `...` as its FileError.

What counts is the end. It makes what it can, and then asks whether there is a folder at the path. A folder that was there already is no error, so a program can make its folders every time it starts without asking first. A file in the way, at the path or above it, is one; so is a folder that may not be written. Asking at the end, not reading the error of each mkdir, gives one answer from every system, including two programs that make the same folder at once.

Turned down: an error for a folder that is there, as plain mkdir gives. Every program would have to ask exists first, or catch an error that means nothing went wrong.

An empty path fails. No folder can be made at "".

On a board there are no folders, and both functions raise their FileError (cannot list the folder `...` and cannot make the folder `...`), which a program catches as it catches one from files.read.

59.22 files.join(first, second), written in Zeno

files.join("logs", "today.txt") is "logs/today.txt". One / goes between the two parts, whatever their ends hold: join("logs/", "/today.txt") is the same. A first part that is empty is no folder, and the second comes back as it is. Nothing else is changed: "a//" keeps its two, and .. stays.

/ everywhere. Every system Zeno runs on takes / between the parts of a path, Windows too, so the same path is the same text on every machine, and a program that prints one prints the same thing. Turned down: \ on Windows, as Python's os.path.join writes. The output of a program would then depend on the machine it ran on.

Written in Zeno, in library/files.zeno, as chapter 33 put math.hypot and random.pick. It is arithmetic on text, so it is written once, and every engine, build and target gets it from there. The file is the first part of a module whose other functions are built in; it imports files to say so, and a program that does not spell join gets none of it.

Turned down: a join of any number of parts. Zeno has no function of a count of arguments that is not known; join(join(a, b), c) says it in the words there are.

59.23 What is in the runtime, and what was left

Two pieces of the runtime. The C of list and of make_folder is written into runtime.c as two pieces of decision 56.19, ZENO_FILES_LIST and ZENO_FILES_MAKE_FOLDER, each found by its one function. A program that calls neither is given the runtime it was given before, to the byte, through C and LLVM alike. Each piece holds both systems: opendir and mkdir where there is POSIX, and the wide functions of Microsoft's C library on Windows, so that a name in Tamil arrives as UTF-8, as the command line does. A list of names made in a build with no collector is a list with an owner, as files.read_bytes gives, and its text is freed with it: the test runs it with 0 blocks left at the end.

tools/same.py against the zeno of 0.7.0: 6,492 of 6,780 builds the same and 288 different, which are the 273 that main before this part gave and the 15 builds of the new edge-folders.zeno. No program that was built before is built differently.

The targets. Each runtime has both, in its own language's words: fs.readdirSync in JavaScript, os.listdir in Python, Dir.children in Ruby, scandir in PHP, os.ReadDir in Go, Files.list on the JVM, Directory.EnumerateFileSystemEntries in C#, Directory.listSync in Dart, opendir in C++, std::fs::read_dir in Rust and WebAssembly. Lua itself cannot see into a folder: its runtime uses LuaFileSystem where it is installed, and find and mkdir -p where there is a POSIX shell, and on Windows without LuaFileSystem it raises the FileError. A page has no folders, and leaves out a program that makes one, as it leaves out one that writes a file.

Left for later, as the plan says: removing a folder, and saying whether a name is a folder (files.exists is false for one, which is enough to tell them apart for now). The Windows half of the C is built by the trial workflow on Windows, not by the tests on Linux.

60. Tools: a message on assert, and tests of a compiled program

Item 13 of missing.md is six small tools. Two are built now: a message on assert (13.1 of plan-9-14.md) and the same tests run on the compiled program (13.2). The other four are put off (section 5 of the plan's changes). Neither changes what a program means: the first is asked for by a second thing after assert, the second by zeno test --build, and a program or a command that does not write them does what it did.

60.1 A message on assert

test "the board answers a reset" {
    let reply = reset()
    assert reply == Reply.Ack, f"the board answered {reply} to the reset"
}
FAILED: the board answers a reset
error: the board answered Nak to the reset
this is false. The left of `==` is Nak, and the right is Ack
 --> board.zeno:8:12

The rule. After the condition of an assert, a comma and one text. When the assert fails, the text is printed on a line of its own above "this is false...", which stays as it was. When it passes, the text is not worked out.

Why it is added now. 10.17 turned it down because the test's name and the two sides of the comparison already say most of what a message says, and said it could be added later without changing anything. What it cannot say is why the values matter: "the board answered Nak to the reset" names the thing being tested in the words of the board, which == Ack does not. And a condition that is not a comparison, assert ring.is_full(), shows no values at all; the text is the only way for it to say more than "this is false".

Why a comma. It is how Python writes it, so the reader has seen it. assert is a statement and its condition is one expression, so a comma after the condition can mean nothing else; it is not a list, and not a call. The ways weighed:

Written Verdict
A assert c, "text" Chosen. One mark, read one way
B assert c else "text" else already begins a block after if; here it would begin a value
C assert(c, "text") Reads as a call of a function named assert, which the word was reserved to prevent (10.17)
D assert c with a comment after it, which a failure prints A comment that does something is a rule nobody can see

It must be text. An int or a list after the comma is refused with "what an assert prints when it fails must be text, but this is int. Write assert total == 6, f"the total was {total}"". An f-string makes anything text, so nothing is lost, and a message is never a value shown in a form the reader has to guess.

Worked out only when it fails. A passing test does not pay for building the text, and the text can use what is only there when something has gone wrong: f"the reply was {replies[9]}" in a test that passes never reads item 9. If working it out raises an error, the test fails with that error, as any error that leaves a test fails it (10.17); the line shown is the line of the assert.

One text. A second comma is refused with "an assert prints one text when it fails. Join the parts into one: ...", and a comma with nothing after it with "after the comma of an assert comes the text that a failure prints: ...". assert raises ValueError { } takes no text: the failure already says what was expected and what came.

What is not changed. The words "this is false..." and where a failure points. zeno run goes past tests, as before. A build leaves tests out (10.20), and so their messages with them.

How it is built. ast.rs: StmtKind::Assert holds the condition and an optional text. parser.rs reads the comma, checker.rs checks that the text is str, printer.rs writes it back, and Interpreter::assert works it out after the condition is found false and puts it above the line it always printed.

60.2 Tests of a compiled program: zeno test --build

$ zeno test --build --firmware board.zeno
board.zeno
  ok      three numbers add up
  FAILED  an empty list adds up to nothing

FAILED: an empty list adds up to nothing
error: an empty list should add up to 0
this is false. The left of `==` is 0, and the right is 1
  --> board.zeno:14:12
   |
14 |     assert total([]) == 1, "an empty list should add up to 0"
   |            ^


2 tests: 1 passed, 1 failed.

The rule. zeno test --build compiles each file with its tests in it, as zeno build would compile it, runs the program, and prints what zeno test prints, line for line. It takes what a build takes that still makes a program that checks itself: --firmware, --no-collector, --llvm, --release, --pool, --text-room, --memory and --board. --fast and --minimal leave out checks a test may be written to meet, and --web and --target make no program that this computer runs, so each is refused with that reason. With no --build, zeno test is what it was, and so is every build: a program that is not built for its tests has not one line of C more.

Why. zeno test runs the tests in the interpreter. The program that goes onto a board is the one C or LLVM makes of it, with no collector, errors as values, numbers of a fixed width and the runtime's own text and floats (chapter 53). 0.7.0 checks that the two agree by running each example both ways (the rule of chapter 5), but a test the user writes was never run in the build it is for. A test that shares a list is now refused with no collector, as the program would be, and a test that passes in the interpreter and fails in the build says where the two part.

Each test becomes a function at the end of its file. Before the checker, each test of the first file becomes a function with no parameters that may raise any error, written after the file's last statement (with_tests in src/test_build.rs). At the end it sees every variable of the file, as a test does, and is checked by the checker with the rules of the build, and compiled by each compiler as any other function: nothing in the compilers learns what a test is but assert. Its name, test 1, has a space in it, so no program can write it or call it. The tests of an imported file are left out, as zeno test leaves them out. --only takes its tests out before the checker, so a test that is not run is not built.

A failed assert leaves the test as return does. It writes its report, and then takes the road each build already has out of a try and past what must be freed. There is no new road, no block is left, and no except catches it, as none catches it in zeno test (10.17). An error that leaves a test, raised or not caught, is caught where main calls the test: in an ordinary build by the try of setjmp that try uses, in a firmware build by the false the test gives back (5.5).

An assert in a function written inside a test is refused. The parser takes it, and zeno test runs it, as 0.7.0 did. But the return of a failed assert would leave that function and not the test, and a firmware build has no other way out of a function whose type says it raises nothing; making one for this would be a second kind of error. So zeno test --build refuses it with "under zeno test --build an assert stands in the test itself, and not in a function written inside it. Let the function give back what it found, and assert that in the test". It is a refusal of this command, not of zeno build, which leaves tests out (10.20); it is written in docs/testing.md beside the table of what every build refuses.

The reports wait in a room of 8 KB. zeno test prints the line of each test as it runs, and the reports of the failures under them. So does the program: a failure writes its report into a static array of 8 KB, and the reports are printed after the last test. The room exists only in a test build, and asks nothing of the pool, so it works with no collector and on a board, where there is no malloc. A report that does not fit is left out whole, never cut, and counted; one line says how many were left out and that zeno test shows them all. 8 KB is some forty reports of the usual five lines; a board with less RAM than that is not one a test program is run on.

The command counts by marks, not by the number the program ends with. A program that an error or a fault stops already ends with 1, and program.exit can end it with any number, so "ended with 1" could mean one failed test, a fault, or neither. Instead the command gives the program the name of a file in ZENO_TEST_MARKS, and the program writes a mark there when its tests begin, one as each test ends, passed or failed, and one when they are all over, each written through at once. The command adds them up. With no mark of beginning the program stopped before its tests, and the command says "board.zeno stopped with this error before its tests. None of them was run.", as zeno test does. With no mark of the end it stopped in a test, which is counted as failed and named, and the command says how many after it were not run. Nothing the program prints is read for its meaning, so no line a program prints can be taken for a result. The program still ends with 1 if a test failed and 0 if none did, for a script that runs it.

Run by itself, it says its own totals. On a board, or run by hand, nothing gives the program a file of marks, and it prints the line of totals for its file itself. A program stopped before its last test, by a fault or by program.exit, prints the reports it holds before it ends, where the platform has a moment for that (atexit on a computer), so a fault in the fifth test does not cost the reports of the first four.

A report shows the line, in whatever file. An error that leaves a test is shown at the line that raised it, which may be in an imported file. A test build holds the text of every file of the program, as strings of C, and looks the line up; the report is the one zeno test prints, with the caret under the place and the note. On a board that text costs flash, in a test build only: the fifteen lines of board.zeno above are 286 bytes of it.

A board. zeno test --build --board boards/qemu-cortex-m3 board.zeno writes board-tests.c and builds board-tests.elf beside it, as zeno build --board does (51.5), and says the command that runs it. The tests run there, by whoever has the board, and the program prints the same lines through the board's zeno_board_print (chapter 52). Built and run so on QEMU's Cortex-M3, the program above prints what zeno test prints and ends with 1.

Where it differs from zeno test, on purpose.

zeno test zeno test --build
A fault of a firmware build: an index out of range, an overflow the test fails, and the next runs the program stops, as any firmware program does (5.5l); the command names the test it was in and how many were not run
program.exit in a test the test fails the program ends; the command says so as for a fault
An error before the tests the snippet of the line the compiled program's own message for an error nothing caught
A try that nothing in it can raise into, in a firmware build runs refused, as in any firmware program (5.5)
An assert in a function written in a test runs refused (above)

How it is built. src/test_build.rs makes the tests functions, refuses an assert in a function, and holds the part of the runtime that only a test build has. It is text of the test build, and not a piece of src/runtime.c (56.19), so nothing of it can reach another program. emit_c.rs and emit_llvm.rs each compile assert and assert raises in a test function (an assert that is not in one is nothing, as before), call each test after the program's statements, and end main with what zeno_tests_end gives back. main.rs reads --build, builds the program in a folder of its own, runs it with ZENO_TEST_MARKS set, and reads the marks.

Left for later. An assert in a function written in a test; a fault that fails its test and goes on, which needs a way back from a fault that a firmware build does not have; and reading the totals back from a board, which needs the board's serial port read by the command.

61. Another language's code in a Zeno file: inline blocks

Partha asked whether Zeno should be a superset of the big languages, so that their code could be pasted into a Zeno program. The answer agreed on was no, and this chapter is what is built in its place: a block that holds another language's code as it was written, which the program calls. inline.md is the walkthrough.

import c

let bits = inline c {
    #include <stdint.h>

    int ones(uint32_t x) {
        int count = 0;
        for (; x != 0; x &= x - 1) {
            count++;
        }
        return count;
    }
}

print(bits.ones(0xA5))

Nothing here changes a program that has no block. A block is asked for twice, by the word inline and by the import of its language, and tools/same.py shows the rest (61.18).

61.1 A block, and not a superset

The rule. Zeno is not a superset of any language. Code of another language goes in a block, is built or run by that language's own compiler, and is called through the bridge Zeno already has to it.

Why not a superset. A superset has to take every program of the other language for ever, with every mistake that language allows, so the first thing given up would be the checks Zeno exists for: an int that cannot overflow quietly, a name that cannot be none unseen. A superset of two languages cannot exist at all where they disagree: a / b, {}, 'x' and x = y each mean something else in C, Python and JavaScript. And a superset of one language makes Zeno a dialect of it. TypeScript is JavaScript with types and can never fix JavaScript's ==; C++ carried C's every rule for forty years.

What a block gives in its place. The same result for the person who has code already written: the code is used as it is, today, and not rewritten. It costs Zeno one new form and no new meaning: a block is a value, and that value is one the language had (a library of C, a module of Python or of Node).

The way Verdict
A Zeno as a superset of C, or of several languages Turned down, above
B The other language's code only in its own files, used through c.library("crc.c", ...) and python.module Works today, and stays. But ten lines of C want a file, a second list of declarations, and a reader who opens both
C A block in the .zeno file Chosen. The code sits beside the lines that call it
D A converter that rewrites the code as Zeno Built next, as zeno convert. It cannot take everything, and what it cannot take it leaves in a block, so it needs C first

61.2 How a block is written

The rule. let name = inline c {, the code on the lines below, further in, and a line that holds only }. The word after inline is the language, and is the name of the module its import gives.

Why these words. inline says what is done: the code is in the line of the program, and not in a file beside it. C, C++ and Rust programmers know the word for assembly written in the middle of C, which is the same idea. The language's word is the one the program already wrote in its import, so there is one name for each language and not two (node, and not js here and node there). The braces are Zeno's own, as for every other block of the language.

Written Verdict
A let bits = inline c { ... } Chosen
B c { ... } or c.inline { ... } A name and a { begins nothing else in Zeno, and c may be a variable. The reader could not tell a block from a mistake
C c.code("""..."""), a text given to a function The text would be Zeno's: its \n and {x} would be read by Zeno first, and C's "\n" has to be written "\\n". Pasted code would have to be edited, which is what a block is for avoiding
D extern "C" { ... }, as C++ and Rust write it There it declares what is elsewhere. Here the code is the thing itself
E @c on the line above, or a comment that does something A mark that changes what the next lines are is easy to miss, and a comment that runs is a rule nobody can see (60.1, D)
F Text between three backticks, as in a page of Markdown Nothing else in Zeno is written so, and a block has no name to be called through

61.3 Where a block ends, and why Zeno does not read inside it

The rule. The first line ends with the {. Every line of the block is further in than that first line. The block ends at a line that holds only }, as far in as the first line. What is between is not read as Zeno at all.

Why indentation ends it. To find the } that closes a block by counting braces, Zeno would have to know what a brace inside a string or a comment looks like in each language: "}", '}', /* } */, // }, # }, a template of JavaScript between backticks with ${...} inside it, a regular expression /}/, a raw string of Python. That is a small lexer for each language, each wrong somewhere, and the mistake it makes is the worst kind: the block ends early and the rest of the other language's code is read as Zeno, with messages about lines that are fine.

A line that holds only } at the first line's own indentation can be found with no knowledge of the other language. Code in a block is indented anyway, so a } of the other language is always further in. The rule can be said in one sentence and seen with the eye.

How the end is found Verdict
A A line holding only }, as far in as the opening line Chosen
B Counting { and } Wrong for a brace in a string or a comment, above
C Counting them with a lexer for each language Three lexers to keep right, and a fourth for each language added
D A word the writer picks, as a shell's <<END Never wrong, but a new form for the reader, and the writer has to pick a word
E Indentation alone, with no } Zeno's blocks end with }. One that did not would be the only one

A line that is not further in is a mistake, and is not taken for the end: "this line of the inline c block is not further in than the line that opens the block. Everything in the block is indented, and the block ends at a line that holds only }, as far in as the line that opened it". An empty line is allowed anywhere. A block with no such closing line is refused with "this inline c block has no end...", at the line that opened it.

This is the one place where indentation means something in Zeno. It was weighed against "the entire language must be unambiguous": the rule has one reading, a mistake against it is refused and not guessed at, and zeno format keeps to it. The other ways each have a case that reads two ways.

61.4 inline is not a reserved word

The rule. inline begins a block only where it is followed by a name, a {, and the end of the line. Everywhere else it is a name, as before: let inline = 3 means what it meant.

Why. A reserved word is taken from every program that used it as a name, and 0.9.0 is not allowed to change what a program of 0.8.0 means. A name, another name and { at the end of a line is nothing in Zeno today (two names side by side are always refused), so no program that was accepted can be read otherwise now. That is the test of 11.6.

The lexer looks ahead to the end of the line to decide. It is the one place it looks further than two characters, and it has to be the lexer: what follows is not made of Zeno's tokens.

61.5 A block is the whole value of a let

The rule. let name = inline c {. Not var, not const, not an argument, not part of a larger expression. It may be at the top of a file, in a function, or in a test.

Why a let. What a block gives never changes, so var would promise something that cannot happen, and is refused with "an inline block is the value of a let. What it gives never changes". A const is a value known when the program is checked, which a module of Python is not.

Why the whole value. print(inline c { ... }.f(1)) would put many lines of another language in the middle of a line of Zeno, with the end of the Zeno line after the block's }, and rule 61.3 could not hold. With a name, the block is in one place and its uses in another, each readable alone.

Why in a function too. A helper used by one function reads best there. The block is still made once: under zeno run the first time the line is reached, and in a build it is part of the program's C wherever it was written.

61.6 Which languages have a block

The rule. inline c, inline python, inline node. Any other word is refused with a message that names the three and says what to do in its place.

Language Verdict Why
C A block The most code already written, and all of a board's. It is also what zeno build writes, so a block of C costs a built program nothing
Python A block The most used language, with a library for everything. Zeno is not for firmware only
JavaScript, through Node A block The same, and the code of every web page
Assembly No block of its own: inside a block of C (61.15) It has no types, and it is a different language on every processor
C++ No block A built program is one file of C given to one C compiler (44.12). A block of C++ would need a second compiler in every build, and a way across for classes, templates and exceptions, which C does not have. C++ with extern "C" goes to c.library
Rust, Go No block Neither can be built from ten lines: each wants a project, its own build tool and minutes. Their libraries are used through import c (44.6)
Java No block A class needs javac and a file named after it. import java uses a jar
TypeScript No block Node does not run it everywhere yet. Its JavaScript is what inline node takes
Ruby, PHP, Lua, C# Later Each has its import already (chapters 37 to 40), and a block is the same few lines for each. Left until someone asks, since each is a language to test on three systems

Why inline node and not inline js. The block is a module of Node, with require and exports, and runs in the Node that import node starts. js would promise a browser's JavaScript too. inline js, inline javascript, inline py and inline asm are each answered by name.

61.7 A block needs the import of its language

The rule. A file with inline c and no import c is refused: "an inline c block needs import c at the top of the file. The import is what asks for the other language, and a file with no such line uses none".

Why. The first lines of a file say everything it needs from outside Zeno. A reader who sees no import python there knows the file runs with no Python on the machine, and that has been true since the first bridge (26.11). A block that brought the language in by itself, from line 200, would end that. It is also the opt-in rule of this project: a feature is asked for by a word the program writes, and here by two.

61.8 What a block of C gives

The rule. A library of C, the type c.library gives. Its functions are the ones written out in the block, with a body, that are not static. Each is typed from its own first line. Everything else in the block is the block's own: a static function, a variable, a #define, a typedef, a struct.

Why the same type. Everything chapter 44 decided then holds with nothing said twice: how a number is checked to fit, how a list is lent for a pointer, what a const means, what is refused. There is one table of how values go across, in c.md, and a reader who knows c.library knows a block.

Why nothing is declared. c.library is given declarations because a library that is already built says nothing about its functions. A block has the functions themselves, and their first lines are the declarations. Asking for them again would be the same words twice, and the second copy would one day disagree with the first.

Why static is the way to keep a function to the block. It is what C itself means by the word: a function no other file can see. Nothing new is learned, and code pasted from a .c file that was written well already says it.

Which functions Zeno sees Verdict
A Every function with a body that is not static Chosen
B Only those listed after the block, or marked with a comment A second list to keep right
C Every function, static or not A helper that takes a struct by value would refuse the whole block

A function Zeno cannot call that is not static is refused, with the reason c.library gives and one more sentence: "In an inline c block, a function that only the block calls is marked static, and Zeno leaves it alone". It is not passed over quietly: a function that is there and cannot be called would be found only at the call, with a worse message. A block with nothing to call is refused with "this inline c block has no function that Zeno can call...".

How the functions are found. bridge_c::block_declarations goes through the block once at the level of C's top: it steps over comments, strings, lines that begin with #, and bodies between braces, and keeps the first line of each function, the typedefs and the structs. What it keeps is given to the reader of declarations that c.library has, so both are read by one piece of code. Unlike 61.3, this reads C, and has to: but a mistake here cannot move the end of the block. The worst it can do is refuse a block or miss a function, and both are said in a message.

61.9 What zeno run does with a block of C

The rule. The block is built once into a small library by the C compiler of the machine, kept in the folder for what can be made again, and called through the helper that import c uses. It is built again when its text changes. zeno run --vm and zeno test do the same.

Why through the helper. It is what c.library("crc.c", ...) does, and it keeps the other language's mistakes out of zeno: a block that writes through a bad pointer stops the helper, and Zeno says "C stopped while Zeno was waiting for its answer" at the call (44.4). Building the block into zeno itself would be faster for each call and would let a block damage the interpreter.

61.10 What zeno build does with a block of C

The rule. Every build that writes C writes the block into the program's C, as it was written, after the runtime and before the program's own functions. A call of one of its functions is a call of C in the same file. Before the block is #line N "file.zeno", and after it #line K "program.c".

Why in the same file. It is the least there can be: no library beside the program, no second step of building, nothing between the call and the function, and the C compiler may put a small function in line. For firmware that is the whole point: a few instructions that must be C or assembly, on the board, with no cost.

Why #line. A mistake in the block is found by the C compiler when the program is built. Without the mark it would name a line of the program's C, five thousand lines down a file the writer never opened. With it, the message names the line of the .zeno file, and so does a debugger. The second #line gives the lines after the block back to the C file.

What a block can clash with. The block is in one file with the runtime and the program, so a name of the block could be one of theirs. Zeno's own names begin with zeno_ or z_, and the C compiler refuses a clash with a message that names both lines. A block can use the headers it includes, and those the runtime included before it.

All of them. zeno build, --firmware, --no-collector, --owned, --minimal, --release, --fast, --board, and zeno test --build. examples/bits.zeno prints the same from each.

61.11 What refuses a block

The rule. Where a block cannot work, it is an error with the line of the block. A block is never skipped.

inline c inline python, inline node
zeno build, and every build that writes C built in refused: a built program is C, and has no Python or Node inside it
zeno check --strict checked refused: what the block gives is known only when the program runs
zeno build --llvm refused refused
zeno build --target ... refused refused
The playground refused refused

Why refused and not left out. A program that built with its block missing would fail at the first call, or worse, build to something that does something else. Each of these already refuses the import (44.8, 26.11), so a block there was refused before it was read; the messages for the block itself are for the cases the import passes.

--llvm. The LLVM build writes IR, and C cannot be pasted into IR. It could compile the block with clang and link the two; that is left for later with the rest of import c under --llvm (44.10).

61.12 A block that cannot be started stops the program

The rule. A block of C that does not compile, or a block of Python or JavaScript with a mistake that stops it from starting, ends the program with what the other language said. No try catches it, and a function with a block in it needs no raises.

Why not an error to catch. An error that can be caught is for what may go differently next time: a file that is not there, a text that is not a number. A block that does not compile will not compile next time either. It is a mistake in the program, as a misspelt word of Zeno is, and those are never caught. If it were an error, every function with a block would need raises, to name something its caller can do nothing about.

When it is found. In a build, when the program is built. Under zeno run, when the line of the block is reached, and not before: zeno check does not start a C compiler or Python, and stays as quick as it was. What zeno check does find, for C, is everything about the calls: a function that is not there, an argument of the wrong type, too few arguments.

61.13 A block of Python is a module

The rule. The block gives a module of Python: what python.module would give if the lines were a .py file. It runs once, top to bottom, when the program reaches it. An error in it names the .zeno file and the line there.

How. inline.rs makes an empty module with Python's own types.ModuleType, compiles the text with compile, and runs it in the module with exec. The text is given as many empty lines in front as the .zeno file has above the block, and the file's own path, so the line numbers Python counts are the file's. Nothing was added to the helper of chapter 26: a block is made with the calls a Zeno program could have written itself.

Why the shared indentation is taken off. Python reads indentation, and a block is indented because it is in a block. The indentation every line shares is the block's and not the program's (61.16); each line keeps how far in it is from the others.

61.14 A block of JavaScript is a module of Node

The rule. The block gives what it puts in exports, or gives module.exports. It is a module as a .js file is: it has require, which finds packages from the folder of the .zeno file, and __filename.

Why a module of the older kind. Node makes one from a text with one call. A module with import and export can only be made from a file or an address, and what it exports is given later, through a promise. The older kind is what require gives, which is what node.module uses (chapter 28). A block that writes import is told so by Node.

61.15 Assembly

The rule. There is no inline asm. Assembly is written inside a block of C, as the C compiler takes it, and a whole file of assembly is given to c.library beside the .c files (.s, and .S for one with #include lines).

Why no block of its own. A block gives functions, and a function needs types for what it takes and gives. Assembly has none, so each routine would need a declaration of C written beside it anyway; with the assembly inside a C function, the function is the declaration. Assembly is also not one language. Each processor has its own instructions, and GCC, Clang, IAR and Keil each write them their own way. The C compiler of the board already knows both, and Zeno would have to learn them.

What it costs. One line more than a block of its own would: the C function's first line. It gains the registers the compiler picks for the arguments, and static inline if the writer wants it.

61.16 The indentation a block's lines share is not part of it

The rule. The spaces that every line of a block begins with are taken off before the other language is given the text. A line the C compiler names is the line of the .zeno file. A column it names is counted from where the block's lines begin.

Why. For Python the rule has no choice (61.13). For C and JavaScript the other way was weighed: giving C the lines as they are in the file, spaces and all, so that columns are the file's too. But then a text of C that runs over a line with \, or a template of JavaScript over several lines, would have the block's indentation inside it, and would change when zeno format moved the block. A column that is four less is seen at once, since the compiler shows the line; a text with four spaces more in it is not. One rule for three languages is also easier to say than one and an exception.

61.17 The formatter

The rule. zeno format leaves every line of a block as it was, and moves the block as one piece: its lines begin one step in from the line that opens it, and its } is under that line.

Why. The formatter lays out Zeno, and the text of a block is not Zeno. It can only move the block with its line, and it must, or a block in a function that was itself moved in would break rule 61.3.

61.18 Nothing changes for a program with no block

tools/same.py built the 481 programs it had before this chapter (every example, every program of tools/targets/, every sample of the book that runs, the benchmarks) fifteen ways each with 0.8.0 and with this compiler: 7215 builds, the same to the byte. The two new examples are the only programs that differ, and 0.8.0 refuses both.

inline is still a name (61.4), no module was added, and nothing of the runtime was touched.

61.19 Left for later

  • A library for a block of C: a block that needs -lz has nowhere to say so, and goes in a .c file given to c.library until it has.
  • A constant of a block: a #define or a variable is not seen by Zeno. c.library can declare a value (44.11).
  • Blocks of Ruby, PHP, Lua and C# (61.6).
  • zeno build --llvm with a block of C (61.11).
  • Colours inside a block in the editor: the VS Code and Vim files colour a block as its language where the editor has that language; the playground does not.
  • What c.library leaves for later is left here too: a function of Zeno given to C, a struct by value, small types given back as themselves.

How it is built. token.rs: TokenKind::Inline holds the language and the text. lexer.rs, inline_block: decides (61.4), reads the lines (61.3), takes off the shared indentation (61.16). parser.rs: ExprKind::Inline, only as the value of a let. checker.rs, inline: the import (61.7), and for C the library, by bridge_c::library_of_block. bridge_c.rs: block_declarations (61.8), and Block, which says where a block was written and writes its #lines. inline.rs: what zeno run does (61.9, 61.12 to 61.14). emit_c.rs: c_libraries writes the block and with_blocks_placed its line numbers (61.10). emit_llvm.rs and lower.rs refuse (61.11). format.rs, block (61.17).

62. A file of Python written again as Zeno: zeno convert

Partha asked for converters that write another language's code as Zeno, with Python first and then C, as the second half of what chapter 61 began: a block holds code as it was written, and a converter rewrites it. convert.md is the walkthrough.

zeno convert shop.py       # writes shop.zeno, and says what it did

Nothing here changes what any other command does. convert is a new command, and a program of Zeno is compiled as it was (62.20).

62.1 One promise: never silently wrong

The rule. What the converter writes runs, and prints what the Python printed, but for what a # convert: comment says. What it cannot write so, it does not write: it keeps that piece as Python.

Why. A converter that writes most of a program well and a few lines wrongly is worse than none. The person who reads its Zeno trusts it, and a wrong line found a month later costs more than the whole conversion saved. With the block of chapter 61, the converter never has to guess: there is always a way to write what it cannot read, which is to leave it as it was.

The way Verdict
A Write everything, as well as it can be guessed, and mark the guesses Turned down: a mark that is not read is a wrong program
B Refuse a file with anything it cannot read Turned down: nearly every real file has one line it cannot read
C Write what is sure, keep the rest in an inline python block that the Zeno calls Chosen

62.2 Inside zeno, written by hand

The rule. zeno convert is part of the zeno program. It reads Python with a reader of its own (convert_python.rs), with no library and no Python.

Why. Zeno has no dependencies (5.1, 5.2), and a converter that needed Python's own ast module would need a Python of the right version to convert, where the result needs one only for what is kept. A reader of its own also knows exactly what it read: a construct it does not know is a piece it keeps, with that as the reason, and not an error deep in a tree it did not make.

Not chosen. A separate program, or a repository of its own: the converter writes what Zeno's checker must take, and is checked by it in the same process (62.9), so it belongs with the checker.

62.3 Pieces: the statements at the left margin

The rule. The file is cut into pieces, each a statement that begins at the left margin with all that belongs to it. Each piece is written as Zeno, or as Zeno with a note, or kept whole.

Why. A piece is what a reader of Python sees as one thing: a function, a class, a loop, a line. Keeping one whole keeps its meaning, since nothing inside it is changed. A finer cut (one statement of a function in Zeno and the next in Python) would need the two sides to share the function's local variables, which they cannot.

62.4 What is kept goes into one block, in the place it ran

The rule. One inline python block, named py (or kept, ... if the file has that name). A kept import, def or class goes at the top of it and the Zeno reaches it as py.name. A kept piece that does something becomes def convert_step_N(): with global for what it gives a value, and the Zeno calls py.convert_step_N() where the piece was. if __name__ == "__main__": in kept text is if True:.

Why. A program's lines run in order, and a kept loop must run between the lines of Zeno above and below it. A function of the block, called there, does exactly that. One block, and not one for each piece, because the kept pieces share their names, as they did in the file.

62.5 Types from the program itself

The rule. The converter learns each type from what the program does: what a function is given at its calls, what it gives back, what goes into a list, a dict, a field. It goes over the whole file in rounds until a round learns nothing new, twelve at most. In the last round a type still not known is a reason to keep the piece.

Why. Most Python has no types written. A function's parameters are known from its calls, and those may be further down the file, and a list's items from an append in another function, so one pass in order cannot know them. A type written in the Python (-> int, x: float) is used where there is one, and checked against what the program does.

What a variable of Zeno needs. One type. A name that holds a whole number and later a float is a float from its first value, with a note (62.10); a name that holds a text and a number is kept.

62.6 What crosses between the two sides

The rule. A number, a text, a bool and none cross to the block and back. A value of Python's own stays in Python, and Zeno holds it as a handle. A list or a dict of Zeno goes to Python only if it is written out in the call, held by nothing else.

Why. The bridge copies a list of Zeno into Python (python.md). A copy of a list that the Zeno holds would not show what Python did to it, and a later line of Zeno would read the old one. A list written in the call has no other holder, so its copy is as good as it.

62.7 What a kept piece needs is kept with it

The rule. A piece that gives a value to a name a kept piece reads is kept too, if the kept piece can run after it: it is further down the file, or it is a function or a class, which run when called. A piece that gives a value to a name that a kept function or class defines is kept too, and so is one that gives a value to a name a kept piece gives one, if a function of Zeno reads that name. An import of a module Zeno has words for, and a name given one fixed value once in the file, are written on both sides.

Why. Python can only call Python, and a variable lives on one side. The order matters: a kept piece above a line of Zeno can never read what that line gives, so it does not pull the line into Python. Without that, one kept line near the end of a long file used to pull in every piece above it that shared a name with it.

62.8 A name both sides give values

The rule. Where a kept piece and a piece of Zeno both give values to a name, it is a variable on each side. The plan of the file checks that every line of Zeno that reads the name after the kept piece reads a value Zeno gave it after the kept piece, for certain: a line above it in the same block or further out. A try whose every except leaves (continue, return, raise, break) and reads nothing the try gives counts as run whole. A line that may read the kept value is kept, with "may still hold here the value that the piece at line N gave it".

The variable of a kept loop. A kept for whose variable is read only inside the loop, and by no function, has that variable for its own, as a for of Zeno does. A loop of Zeno elsewhere with the same name has nothing to do with it.

Why. Two loops with a variable name, one kept, are the usual case in a real file, and are not one variable in any sense the program uses. The check is what makes it safe to say so.

62.9 One piece kept at a time, and Zeno's checker has the last word

The rule. When some pieces cannot be written, one is kept: the first whose reason is its own and not "the type is not known". Then everything is done again. When every piece is written, the whole file is read by Zeno's own lexer, parser and checker, in the same process; a piece whose lines it refuses is kept, with the checker's message as the reason. If a refused line belongs to no piece, the whole file is kept as one block.

Why one at a time. What one piece cannot be written for is often what another became: a name holds a function because the line that gives it one is a lambda, and that line is kept; a type is not known because a value came from the block. Keeping every failing piece at once kept pieces for a reason that was gone a moment later. The rounds are fast, and a file of 250 lines with a dozen kept pieces converts in well under a second.

Why the checker. The converter writes text, and Zeno's checker is the only thing that knows for certain what Zeno takes. Nothing it refuses is given out.

62.10 Notes, once for each kind

The rule. Where Zeno runs the line and does what the Python did but prints or raises a little otherwise, a # convert: comment says so, above the first line of that kind. The report lists every line of every kind. The kinds: a value shown Zeno's way; a very large or very small float written otherwise; an error message in Zeno's words; an except that also catches what only Zeno raises; upper and lower on a to z only; math.round and a half; a variable that is a float from its first value.

Why once. A comment on every print of a list would bury the program. The report has every line for the person who wants them.

Why these are notes and not kept. Each is a difference a person expects of a new language and can see at once, and none changes what the program computes. Keeping every print of a list as Python would keep most programs whole.

62.11 What Python has and Zeno has not, written once as Zeno

The rule. sorted, list.remove, split with a number and a text times a number become calls of small functions of Zeno, written once at the top of a file that uses them, each with a comment: sorted, remove_item, split_at_most, repeated. A file that has a name the same as one keeps the line that would need it.

Why. Each is short in Python and has no one word in Zeno, and each is common. A function with its comment says plainly what is done, and the person can replace it. sorted is generic over Ordered, so one function serves lists of numbers and of texts.

Not chosen. Adding these to Zeno's library. That is a change to the language, and decision 6.1 says Zeno gets a method only where it cannot say the thing in one short expression already. It may come later; the converter does not decide it.

62.12 Where each name is declared

The rule. A name is declared with let (given once) or var where it gets its first value, if every use is in that block or further in. Otherwise it is declared before the outermost statement that holds all its uses, outside every loop, with the first value of its type (0, "", [], none).

Why. Python has one set of names for a whole function; Zeno has one for each block. The first value is never read by a program Python would run to the end, since Python would stop there with NameError (62.18).

62.13 A parameter given a new value

The rule. def f(n): n = n + 1 is function f(n_given: int) with var n = n_given as its first line; a call that names it says n_given=.

Why. A parameter of Zeno cannot change, and cannot be shadowed in the function's first block. The other name is the smallest change that keeps every line of the body as it was.

62.14 A loop's variable read after the loop

The rule. Where a for variable is read after the loop, given a value inside it, or is a plain variable as well, the loop of Zeno counts with word_item and its first line is word = word_item. The name is then planned as the plain variable it is.

Why. A for of Zeno has its variable to itself, and it is gone after the loop; in Python it stays. for line in lines: ... then print(line) is common.

62.15 Parts of texts and lists cut as Python cuts them

The rule. xs[a:b] is xs.slice(min(a, len(xs)), min(b, len(xs))), a negative literal end counts from the end and stops at 0, and the list must be a plain name or field so that it is worked out once.

Why. Python gives what there is of a part past the end; Zeno's slice raises IndexError. Clamping is what Python does, written out.

62.16 A question asked out

The rule. if x: is written as the question Python asks of that type: x != 0, x != "", len(x) > 0, x is not none. and and or are values only between bools.

Why. Zeno has no truth of a number or a list (2.4), and Python's a or b gives one of the two values, where Zeno's gives a bool.

62.17 A loop that changes what it goes over is kept

The rule. A for whose block may change the list or dict it goes over is kept, and so is one whose block calls a function of the file that may change it, by its name or a field of that name.

Why. A for of Zeno takes its items when it begins; Python takes each as it comes to it. The two agree as long as nothing changes the list.

62.18 What is not promised

A program Python stops with NameError or UnboundLocalError; whole numbers past 64 bits (loud in Zeno, but int() of a huge float gives Zeno's largest); what a kept function's annotation says it gives; one list under two names while a loop goes over one; strip and split on spaces outside ASCII; when a kept import runs; the last digit of sin. Each is in convert.md. Each is rare, and each but the first two would need the converter to run the program to know.

62.19 How it is checked

The rule. tools/convert.py converts each program in tools/convert, runs it with python3 and with zeno run, and compares what they print, or what Zeno prints with x.expect where a note says why it differs, and then the report must have that note. The first line of each program, # kept: N, is how many pieces are to be kept. cargo test convert has unit tests of the reader and the writer. The workflow convert.yml runs both on every push that changes the converter.

Why the count. A rule that stops working keeps a piece that was Zeno, and the program still prints the same. Only the count shows it.

62.20 Nothing else changes

convert is a new command. No word, rule or library of the language was changed for it, and tools/same.py builds every earlier program as before. The command writes a new file and will not write over one unless it is told --replace or given --to.

62.21 Left for later

  • C next: a file of C written as Zeno, what it cannot read left in an inline c block, and --declare header.h to write the declarations of c.library from a header.
  • A list or dict given to a function of the block where the Zeno never uses it again after the call, which would be safe.
  • lambda, functions inside functions, tuples as values, as Zeno gets them.
  • TypeScript and JavaScript, then Java.

How it is built. convert.rs: the command, Note, Report. convert_python.rs: lex, pieces, Parser. convert_python_write.rs: units_of, names_of, loop_names, spread, tables_of, round, plan with outlasting and after_kept_loops, Helper, assemble, convert. convert_python_values.rs: expr and the rest of an expression. convert_python_lines.rs: statement, for_loop, function, class.

Every journey is halfway done. Forever.

The runner has closed 0 of 1 halves

Zeno of Elea said Achilles can never catch the tortoise: first he must cover half the distance, then half of what is left, without end. It suits a compiler that will always be almost finished. The bar at the top of each page works the same way.
